When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, how must a bodhisattva mahāsattva be engaged so that he may be said to be 'engaged in the perfection of wisdom'?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the emptiness of form is to be called 'engaged. He who is engaged in the emptiness of feeling is to be called 'engaged.
He who is engaged in the emptiness of perception is to be called 'engaged.'"
One who is engaged in the emptiness of formations should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the ear should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the nose should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the tongue should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the body should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of form should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of sound should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of odor should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of taste should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the tangible is to be called "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of phenomena is to be called "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element is to be called "engaged."

One who is engaged in the emptiness of the auditory consciousness element should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of the olfactory consciousness element should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the gustatory consciousness element should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of the body-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the mind-consciousness element should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of suffering should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of origination should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of cessation should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the path should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of ignorance should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of volitional formations should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of consciousness should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of name-and-form should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of the six sense-bases should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of contact should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of feeling should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of craving should be said to be "engaged";
one who is engaged in the emptiness of grasping should be said to be "engaged."
One who is engaged in the emptiness of existence should be said to be "engaged"; one who is engaged in the emptiness of birth should be said to be "engaged";
[and one who is engaged] in the emptiness of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair should be said to be "engaged."
He should be called "engaged, engaged.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should be called "engaged, engaged" in internal emptiness; he should be called "engaged, engaged" in external emptiness.
One should say that he is engaged who is engaged in internal-external emptiness, up to one should say that he is engaged who is engaged in the emptiness of other-being;
for in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is to be called engaged when he is engaged in all these forms of emptiness.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through these emptinesses, he is neither to be called "engaged" nor "disengaged. Why is that?
Because he does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness as either engaged or disengaged.
This is the instruction on the truth of suffering.
He does not perceive form as having the nature of arising or the nature of ceasing;

he does not perceive feeling as having the nature of arising or the nature of ceasing; he does not perceive perception as having the nature of arising or the nature of ceasing; he does not perceive mental formations as having the nature of arising or the nature of ceasing.
He does not perceive consciousness as having the nature of arising or the nature of cessation;
he does not perceive form as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification;
he does not perceive feeling as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification.
He does not perceive perception as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification;
he does not perceive mental formations as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification;
he does not perceive consciousness as having the nature of affliction or the nature of purification.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive that form merges into feeling;
he does not perceive that feeling merges into perception; he does not perceive that perception merges into mental formations.
He does not perceive that volitional formations enter into consciousness;
he does not perceive that consciousness enters into phenomena; he does not perceive that a phenomenon enters into any other phenomenon.
For what reason?
Because, based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, no phenomenon whatsoever ever merges into any other phenomenon.
For what reason?
For it is thus, Śāriputra: that which is the emptiness of form is not form;
that which is the emptiness of feeling is not feeling; that which is the emptiness of perception is not perception.
That which is the emptiness of the formative forces is not those formative forces;
that which is the emptiness of consciousness is not that consciousness. For what reason?
Because that which is the emptiness of form does not exercise the function of forming.
That which is the emptiness of feeling does not feel; that which is the emptiness of perception does not perceive; that which is the emptiness of volitional formations does not form.
That which is the emptiness of consciousness does not cognize.
For what reason?
Because, Śāriputra, form is not one thing and emptiness another.
Emptiness is not other than form;
form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.
Feeling is not other than emptiness.
Emptiness is not other than feeling, and feeling is indeed emptiness;
emptiness is indeed feeling. Perception is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than perception.
Emptiness is not other than perception;
perception itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is perception.
Formative forces are not other than emptiness.
Emptiness is not other than the conditioned factors, and the conditioned factors themselves are emptiness;
emptiness itself is the conditioned factors. Consciousness is not other than emptiness.
Emptiness is not one thing and consciousness another;
consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness.
This is the instruction on the truth of origination.
Emptiness, Śāriputra, neither arises nor ceases; it is neither defiled nor purified;
it neither decreases nor increases.
It is neither past, nor future, nor present;

and that which is such contains therein no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no earth element, no water element, no fire element, no wind element, no space element, no consciousness element; and no sense-base of the eye.

There is no sphere of form, no sphere of the ear, no sphere of sound, no sphere of the nose, no sphere of odor, no sphere of the tongue, no sphere of taste, no sphere of the body, no sphere of the tangible, no sphere of the mind, and no sphere of mental objects; there is no eye-element, no form-element, and no eye-consciousness-element.
There is no ear element, no sound element, and no ear-consciousness element; no nose element, no odor element, and no nose-consciousness element;
no tongue element, no taste element, and no tongue-consciousness element.

There is no body-element, no tangible-object-element, and no body-consciousness-element; no mind-element, no mental-object-element, and no mind-consciousness-element; no arising of ignorance and no cessation of ignorance;
no arising of volitional formations and no cessation of volitional formations.

There is no arising of consciousness, nor cessation of consciousness; no arising of name-and-form, nor cessation of name-and-form; no arising of the six sense bases, nor cessation of the six sense bases.
There is neither the arising of contact nor the cessation of contact;
neither the arising of feeling nor the cessation of feeling;
neither the arising of craving nor the cessation of craving.
There is no arising of grasping, nor cessation of grasping;
there is no arising of existence, nor cessation of existence.

There is no arising of birth, nor cessation of birth; no arising of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, nor cessation of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no attainment and no realization; no stream-enterer and no fruit of stream-entry; no once-returner and no fruit of once-returning.
There is no once-returner, no fruit of once-returning; no arhat, no fruit of arhatship;
no pratyekabuddha, and no pratyekabodhi.
There is neither Buddha nor enlightenment;
for it is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is to be called "engaged, truly engaged.
Thus ends the instruction on the truth of cessation.

Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the perfection of generosity; he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the perfection of patience.
He does not perceive that he is engaged in the perfection of vigor, nor that he is disengaged from it;

he does not perceive that he is engaged in the perfection of meditative concentration, nor that he is disengaged from it; he does not perceive that he is engaged in the perfection of wisdom, nor that he is disengaged from it.
One does not perceive form as either joined or unjoined; one does not perceive feeling as either joined or unjoined; one does not perceive perception as either joined or unjoined.

He does not perceive formative forces as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive consciousness as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the eye as either engaged or disengaged.
He does not perceive the ear as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the nose as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the tongue as either engaged or disengaged.
He does not perceive the body as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive the mind as either engaged or disengaged; he does not perceive form as either engaged or disengaged.
He does not perceive sound as either conjoined or unconjoined; he does not perceive odor as either conjoined or unconjoined;
he does not perceive taste as either conjoined or unconjoined.

He does not perceive that one is engaged with or disengaged from the tangible; he does not perceive that one is engaged with or disengaged from mental phenomena; nor does he perceive [one as engaged or disengaged] with respect to the applications of mindfulness.
He does not perceive himself as "engaged" or "disengaged";
he does not perceive himself as engaged or disengaged in the right efforts; he does not perceive himself as engaged or disengaged in the bases of psychic power.
He does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with respect to the sense faculties;

he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with respect to the powers; he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with respect to the factors of enlightenment.
One does not perceive them as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the paths; one does not perceive them as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the four truths;
one does not perceive them as being "engaged" or "disengaged" with respect to the four grounds of self-confidence.
He does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the four analytical knowledges; he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the superknowledges;
he does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He does not perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with respect to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

nor does he perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor does he perceive himself as being either engaged or disengaged with respect to the knowledge of an omniscient one (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Therefore, Śāriputra, by this method also you should understand it thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus engaged in the perfection of wisdom is to be called "engaged.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not join emptiness with emptiness, nor is there a yoga of emptiness.

One does not join the signless with the signless, nor the application of the signless; one does not join the wishless with the wishless, nor the application of the wishless. Why is that? Because emptiness is neither a joining nor a non-joining.
Thus, the signless and the wishless are neither yoga nor non-yoga. Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this way is to be called "engaged" when engaged in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters into the emptiness of the specific characteristics of phenomena;
crossing over in this very manner, he does not join form nor disjoin it, and he does not join feeling nor disjoin it.
He does not join nor disjoin perception;
he does not join nor disjoin volitional formations;
he does not join nor disjoin consciousness.
One does not join form with the past limit, nor does one disjoin it;
one does not even perceive the past limit itself.
One does not join form with the future limit, nor does one disjoin it.
He does not perceive the future limit at all;
he neither joins form with the present nor disjoins it from it;
he does not even perceive the present itself.
One does not join feeling with the past limit, nor does one disjoin it;
one does not even perceive the past limit itself. One does not join feeling with the future limit, nor does one disjoin it.
He does not perceive the future limit at all;
he neither joins nor disjoins feeling with the present,
for he does not perceive the present at all.
One does not conjoin perception with the past limit, nor does one disjoin it;
one does not even perceive the past limit itself.
One does not conjoin perception with the future limit, nor does one disjoin it.
He does not perceive the future limit at all; he neither joins nor dissociates perception with the present,
and he does not even perceive the present.
One does not join the formative forces with the prior limit, nor does one disjoin them;
one does not even perceive the prior limit itself.
One does not join the formative forces with the posterior limit, nor does one disjoin them.
He does not perceive the future limit at all;
he neither joins nor disjoins the formative forces with the present,
and he does not perceive the present itself.
One does not conjoin consciousness with the past limit, nor does one disjoin it;
one does not even perceive the past limit itself.
One does not conjoin consciousness with the future limit, nor does one disjoin it.
One does not perceive the future limit at all;
one neither joins nor disjoins consciousness with the present,
and one does not perceive the present at all.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not join the past with the future, nor does he join the future with the past; he does not join the present with either the past or the future,
nor does he join the future with either the past or the present.

He does not join the past limit with the future limit or with the present, by virtue of the emptiness of the time-periods (*adhva-śūnyatā*). Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself in this way is to be called one who is engaged in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom applies himself in this manner:
Just as one who is practicing does not join all-knowledge with the past,
for he does not even perceive the past itself—
how could he join all-knowledge with the past? He does not join all-knowledge with the future.
He does not perceive the future at all;
how could he join omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the future? He does not join omniscience with the present;
he perceives only the present.
How does one apply [the mind] to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of the present?
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself in this way should be said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus ends the instruction on the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate form with omniscience, for he does not even perceive form; he does not associate feeling with omniscience, for he does not even perceive feeling;
he does not associate perception with omniscience, for he does not even perceive perception.

He does not join the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), for he does not even perceive the formative forces themselves; he does not join consciousness (*vijñāna*) with omniscience, for he does not even perceive consciousness itself;
he does not join the eye (*cakṣus*) with omniscience, for he does not even perceive the eye itself.
One does not join the ear with omniscience, for one does not even perceive the ear; one does not join the nose with omniscience, for one does not even perceive the nose;
one does not join the tongue with omniscience, for one does not even perceive the tongue.
One does not join the body with omniscience, for one does not even perceive the body; one does not join the mind with omniscience, for one does not even perceive the mind;
one does not join form with omniscience, for one does not even perceive form.

One does not associate sounds with the knowledge of all aspects, for one does not even perceive sounds; one does not associate odors with the knowledge of all aspects, for one does not even perceive odors;
one does not associate tastes with the knowledge of all aspects, for one does not even perceive tastes.
One does not join tangibility with the knowledge of all aspects, for one does not even perceive tangibility;
one does not join phenomena with the knowledge of all aspects, for one does not even perceive phenomena.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this way is to be called "engaged in the perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate the perfection of giving with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving itself;
he does not associate the perfection of ethical discipline with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of ethical discipline itself;
he does not associate the perfection of patience with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of patience itself.
He does not join the perfection of vigor with omniscience, nor does he perceive the perfection of vigor itself;
he does not join the perfection of meditation with omniscience,
nor does he perceive the perfection of meditation itself.

He does not join the perfection of wisdom with all-aspect omniscience, for he does not even perceive the perfection of wisdom itself; he does not join the applications of mindfulness with all-aspect omniscience, for he does not even perceive the applications of mindfulness themselves; nor does he join the right efforts.
One joins them with the knowledge of all aspects, yet does not perceive even the right efforts;

one does not join the bases of psychic power with the knowledge of all aspects, yet does not perceive even the bases of psychic power; one does not join the faculties with the knowledge of all aspects, yet does not perceive even the faculties.
He does not join the powers with all-aspect omniscience, nor does he perceive the powers themselves;

he does not join the factors of enlightenment with all-aspect omniscience, nor does he perceive the factors of enlightenment themselves; he does not join the paths with all-aspect omniscience, nor does he perceive the paths themselves.

One does not associate the analytical knowledges with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does one perceive even the analytical knowledges themselves; one does not associate the grounds of self-confidence with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does one perceive even the grounds of self-confidence themselves; one does not associate the superknowledges with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does one perceive even the superknowledges themselves.

He does not join the ten powers of a Tathāgata with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor does he perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata themselves; he does not join the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) with the knowledge of all aspects, nor does he perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha themselves.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner is said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not associate the Buddha with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), for he does not even perceive the Buddha; he does not associate omniscience with the Buddha, for he does not even perceive omniscience;
he does not associate awakening (*bodhi*) with omniscience, for he does not even perceive awakening.
One does not join omniscience with awakening, for one does not even perceive omniscience itself.
Why is that?
Because the Buddha is indeed omniscience, and omniscience is indeed the Buddha.
Awakening itself is the knowledge of all aspects, and the knowledge of all aspects itself is awakening.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself in this way should be said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus concludes the instruction on the Jewel of the Buddha.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apply himself to the thought that "form comes into being," nor does he apply himself to the thought that "form ceases to be";

he does not apply himself to the thought that "feeling comes into being," nor does he apply himself to the thought that "feeling ceases to be"; he does not apply himself to the thought that "perception comes into being," nor does he apply himself to the thought that "perception ceases to be."

One does not apply the thought that "formative forces come into being," nor does one apply the thought that "formative forces cease to be"; one does not apply the thought that "consciousness comes into being," nor does one apply the thought that "consciousness ceases to be."
One does not associate form with permanence, nor does one associate form with impermanence;
one does not associate form with pleasure, nor does one associate form with suffering;
one does not associate form with self, nor does one associate form with non-self.
One does not associate form with being peaceful, nor does one associate form with being unpeaceful;
one does not associate feeling with being permanent, nor does one associate feeling with being impermanent.
He does not associate feeling with pleasure, nor does he associate feeling with suffering;
he does not associate feeling with self, nor does he associate feeling with non-self;
he does not associate feeling with peace, nor does he associate feeling with lack of peace.
One does not associate perception with permanence, nor does one associate perception with impermanence;
one does not associate perception with pleasure, nor does one associate perception with suffering;
one does not associate perception with self, nor does one associate perception with non-self.
He does not associate perception with "peace," nor does he associate perception with "non-peace";
he does not associate volitional formations with "permanence," nor does he associate volitional formations with "impermanence";
he does not associate volitional formations with "happiness," nor does he associate volitional formations with "suffering."

One does not associate with the notion that "formations are the self," nor does one associate with the notion that "formations are not-self"; one does not associate with the notion that "formations are peaceful," nor does one associate with the notion that "formations are not peaceful"; one does not associate with the notion that "consciousness is permanent," nor does one associate with the notion that "consciousness is impermanent."
One does not associate consciousness with pleasure, nor does one associate consciousness with suffering;

one does not associate consciousness with self, nor does one associate consciousness with non-self; one does not associate consciousness with peace, nor does one associate consciousness with lack of peace.
One does not associate form with "empty," nor does one associate form with "not empty.
One does not course in the idea that form has signs, nor does one course in the idea that form is signless.
One does not course in the idea that form is with aspiration, nor does one course in the idea that form is without aspiration.
He does not course with the thought that "feeling is empty," nor does he course with the thought that "feeling is not empty";
he does not course with the thought that "feeling has signs," nor does he course with the thought that "feeling is signless";
he does not course with the thought that "feeling has aspirations," nor does he course with the thought that "feeling is aspirationless."

He does not course in the thought that "perception is empty," nor does he course in the thought that "perception is not empty"; he does not course in the thought that "perception has signs," nor does he course in the thought that "perception is signless"; he does not course in the thought that "perception is with aspiration," nor does he course in the thought that "perception is without aspiration."
He does not practice with the thought that "formative forces are empty," nor does he practice with the thought that "formative forces are not empty.
He does not practice with the thought that "formative forces have signs," nor does he practice with the thought that "formative forces are signless.
He does not practice with the thought that "formative forces are with aspiration," nor does he practice with the thought that "formative forces are without aspiration."
He does not course with the thought that consciousness is empty, nor does he course with the thought that consciousness is non-empty;
he does not course with the thought that consciousness has signs, nor does he course with the thought that consciousness is signless;
he does not course with the thought that consciousness is with aspiration, nor does he course with the thought that consciousness is without aspiration.
He who courses in this way does not apprehend that "he courses in the perfection of wisdom," nor does he apprehend that "he does not course";
he does not apprehend that "he both courses and does not course," nor does he apprehend that "he neither courses nor does not course."
"He does not practice" means he does not approach [them as real entities].
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way should be said to be "engaged in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of giving.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of ethical discipline;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of patience;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of vigor.

He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of meditation; he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the perfection of wisdom; he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the stage of non-retrogression.
He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of maturing sentient beings; he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of purifying a buddha-field;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the four grounds of self-confidence;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the four analytical knowledges;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of internal emptiness; one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of external emptiness;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of internal-and-external emptiness.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of emptiness;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the great emptiness; one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of the conditioned, nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of the unconditioned,
nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of absolute emptiness.

One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of non-dispersal,
nor for the sake of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He practices the perfection of wisdom;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of all phenomena,
nor does he practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of specific characteristics.

He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of non-apprehension; he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of existence.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of non-existence, nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the emptiness of other-nature.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of suchness;
one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the realm of phenomena; one does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the limit of reality.
For what reason?

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the differentiation of any dharma. Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not...
He practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the divine eye; he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the divine ear;
he does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the knowledge of others' minds.
One does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of recollecting past lives,
nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the various types of supernormal power;
and why is that?
For in this way, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not even perceive the perfection of wisdom itself;
how much less a bodhisattva, and how much less all the aspects and all the superknowledges?
It is in this manner, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is to be called "engaged."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: "With my divine eye, I shall know the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā," nor does he think: "With my divine ear, I shall hear their sounds."
"I shall know their very minds," and "having gone by means of supernatural power and recollecting their very past lives, I shall teach them the Dharma"—
Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva in this way.

"I shall know, with the divine eye, the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings in world-systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; I shall hear their sounds with the divine ear;
and I shall know their very minds."
"And having recollected their very former abodes, I shall go by means of miraculous power and teach the Dharma.

In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva that, "With my divine eye, I shall know the passing away and rebirth of beings in world systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges."
"By means of the divine ear, I shall hear their sounds;
I shall know their very thoughts;
and having gone by means of supernatural power, I shall teach the Dharma to them after recollecting their past lives."

In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "With my divine eye, I shall know the death and rebirth of beings in world-systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges," nor, "With my divine ear, I shall hear their sounds."
"I shall know their very minds," and "having gone by means of supernatural power and recollecting their very past lives, I shall teach them the Dharma"—
Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva in this way.

"I shall know, with the divine eye, the passing away and rebirth of beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northeastern direction; I shall hear their sounds with the divine ear;
and I shall know their very minds."
"Having recollected their very former abodes and having gone there by means of miraculous power, I shall teach the Dharma.
In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"With my divine eye, I shall know the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the eastern direction."
"By means of the divine ear, I shall hear their sounds;
I shall know their very thoughts;
and having recollectively remembered their former abodes, I shall go by means of supernatural power and teach them the Dharma."

In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "With my divine eye, I shall know the death and rebirth of beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the southwestern direction," or "With my divine ear, I shall hear their sounds."
"I shall know their very minds," and "Having gone by means of miraculous power and recollecting their very former abodes, I shall teach them the Dharma.
In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva [to think such things].

"I shall know, with the divine eye, the passing away and rebirth of beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the northwestern direction; I shall hear their sounds with the divine ear;
and I shall know their very minds."
"And having recalled their very former abodes, I shall go by means of miraculous power and teach them the Dharma.
For it is thus, Śāriputra, that it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"With my divine eye, [I shall see] in the world systems of the lower direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges..."
"Thinking, 'I shall know the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings,' 'With the divine ear, I shall hear their sounds,' and 'I shall know their very minds.'"
"And having recollecting their very former abodes, I shall go by means of supernatural power and teach the Dharma.

In this way, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "With my divine eye, I shall know the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings in world-systems in the upward direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges."

"Thinking, 'I shall hear their sounds with the divine ear,' and 'I shall know their very minds,' and 'Having recollecting their past abodes and having gone by means of psychic power, I shall teach them the Dharma.'"
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while leading immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings to final nirvāṇa is to be called "engaged.
For in this way, Śāriputra, while the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity,
and all other worldly afflictions whatsoever are shattered.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the eastern direction, and who teach the Dharma;

and their disciples; and the pratyekabuddhas; and the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [heavens]; and the Brahmapārṣadyas and the Brahmapurohitas—

The gods of the realm of Great Brahmā—those of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, and Utmost Purity; those of Limited Beauty, Immeasurable Beauty, and Total Purity; the Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Vast Fruit; the Non-Perceiving Beings; and the Pure Abodes—the Unshakable, the Heatless, the Clearly Visible, the Good to Behold, and the Highest Gods—they too protect that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
May no obstacle whatsoever befall this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; even those physical defects he may have shall become manifest in this very life.
Why is that?
For he pervades all sentient beings with loving-kindness.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southern direction, and who teach the Dharma, as well as their disciples—
And those who are Pratyekabuddhas;
and those who are the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin [heavens];
the Brahmapārṣadyas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmans, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, and the Parīttaśubhas.

The gods of the Apramāṇaśubhas, Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Asaṃjñisattvas, and the Śuddhāvāsa gods— the Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas— they too protect that bodhisattva mahāsattva,
lest anyone should create an obstacle for this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Whatever physical defects he may have, these too become manifest only in this present life;
for what reason?
Because he pervades all sentient beings with loving-kindness.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who in the western direction reside, maintain themselves, and sustain their lives in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and teach the Dharma; and those who are their disciples, and those who are Pratyekabuddhas; and the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, and the Nirmāṇarati [heavenly realms].

The Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmapārṣadyas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmans, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, the Bṛhatphalas,
the Asaṃjñisattvas, the Śuddhāvāsas, the Avṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭha gods— they too [beheld him].
They protect the bodhisattva mahāsattva so that no one whatsoever may create an obstacle for this bodhisattva mahāsattva;
even those bodily defects he may have become manifest in this very life.
For what reason?
Because he pervades all sentient beings with loving-kindness.
Śāriputra, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside in the worlds of the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—

Those who abide, remain, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma—whether they be their disciples (śrāvakas), or pratyekabuddhas, or the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin [heavens];
or the Brahmapārṣadya, the Brahmapurohita, or the Mahābrahmans; or the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, or Parīttaśubha [deities].

The gods of the Apramāṇaśubhas, Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Asaṃjñisattvas, Śuddhāvāsas, Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas— they too protect that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Let no one whatsoever create an obstacle for this bodhisattva mahāsattva; even those physical defects he may have shall become merely matters pertaining to the present life.
Why is that?
For he pervades all sentient beings with loving-kindness.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the northeastern direction—numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—and who teach the Dharma;

and those who are their disciples, those who are Pratyekabuddhas, and those who are gods from the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—they too provide protection for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"May there indeed be no obstacle for this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the eastern and southern directions—numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—and who teach the Dharma;

and those who are their disciples, and those who are Pratyekabuddhas; and those gods from the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—they too shall provide protection for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"May there indeed be no obstacle for this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the south-western direction—numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—and who teach the Dharma;

and those who are their disciples, and those who are Pratyekabuddhas; and those who are gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—they too shall provide protection for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"May no obstacle indeed arise for this bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the northwestern direction— numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— and who teach the Dharma;

And those who are their disciples, and those who are pratyekabuddhas, and those who are the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods— they too provide protection for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, thinking, "May no obstacle whatsoever befall this bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems in the direction below, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, and who teach the Dharma...

They teach it; and those who are their disciples, as well as the pratyekabuddhas, and the gods from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods— they too provide protection for that bodhisattva mahāsattva,
thinking, "May no obstacle indeed arise for this bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the upward direction—numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—and who teach the Dharma;
and their disciples, and the pratyekabuddhas, and the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—they too provide protection for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, thinking:
"May no obstacle whatsoever befall this bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom,

the gateways of dhāraṇīs and the gateways of samādhis appear before him with little difficulty; and in all places of rebirth, he pleases the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, such that he is never at any time separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

"Up until the point of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"— it is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom should be said to be "engaged.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him in this manner:
Is there any dharma that is either conjoined with or disjoined from other dharmas?
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:
"Might I more quickly awaken to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), or might I not awaken to it?"
For what reason?
Because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is not fully awakened to by means of the realm of phenomena.
It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be called "engaged."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive anything as distinct from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
nor does he create any differentiation of phenomena within the realm of phenomena,
nor does it occur to him thus:
Whether this dharmadhātu is thus realized or not realized, he does not perceive any dharma by which he might realize that dharmatā;
for he does not associate the dharmadhātu with being empty, nor does he associate it with being non-empty. Thus indeed...
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom should be said to be "engaged.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not join the eye-element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the eye-element;
he does not join the form-element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the form-element.
One does not join the eye-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does one join emptiness with the eye-consciousness element.
One does not join the ear element with emptiness, nor does one join emptiness with the ear element;
one does not join the sound element with emptiness, nor do they join emptiness with the sound element.
He does not join the ear-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the eye-element.
He does not join the nose-element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the nose-element;
he does not join the odor-element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the odor-element.
He does not join the nose-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the nose-consciousness element.
He does not join the tongue element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the tongue element;
he does not join the taste element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the taste element.
He does not join the tongue-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the tongue-consciousness element.
He does not join the body element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the body element;
he does not join the tangible object element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the tangible object element.
He does not join the body-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the body-consciousness element.
He does not join the mind element with emptiness, nor do they join emptiness with the mind element;
he does not join the phenomena element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the phenomena element.
He does not join the mind-consciousness element with emptiness, nor does he join emptiness with the mind-consciousness element. Why is that?
Śāriputra, this indeed is the supreme yoga for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, the yoga of emptiness.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in emptiness, he does not [fall] into the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
He falls [into the world], purifies the Buddha-field, matures sentient beings, and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra, among whatever applications there are for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the application of the perfection of wisdom is declared to be the foremost, the best, the eldest, the excellent, the most excellent, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the unequaled, the equal of the unequaled, and the sublime. Why is that?
For this, Śāriputra, is the unsurpassed yoga: namely, the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, the yoga of emptiness, the yoga of signlessness, and the yoga of wishlessness.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this way should be known as one who has received the prediction [of enlightenment], for he has drawn near to that prediction.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself in this way will accomplish the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable beings, yet it will not occur to him to think,
"The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will grant me a prophecy."
"I have drawn near to the prediction [of my future enlightenment]," "I shall purify the buddha-field," and "I shall bring sentient beings to maturity."
"I shall, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, set in motion the wheel of Dharma. For what reason?
Because he does not isolate the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), nor does he perceive any phenomenon other than the realm of phenomena.
Whoever should practice the perfection of wisdom, or whoever should be prophesied by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—for what reason is that?
Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the notion of a "being" does not arise. For what reason is that?
For in this way, a sentient being is ultimately neither born nor extinguished, because their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing.

And how can that which has neither arising nor ceasing practice the perfection of wisdom? Practicing in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] the perfection of wisdom through the non-arising of sentient beings.
One courses in the perfection of wisdom through the emptiness of sentient beings;
one courses in the perfection of wisdom through the non-apprehension of sentient beings;
one courses in the perfection of wisdom through the solitude of sentient beings.
For it is thus, Śāriputra, that the supreme yoga of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is this very yoga of emptiness, which stands surpassing all other yogas.
For practicing in this yoga, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth great compassion and brings forth great loving-kindness.
He does not give rise to a mind of stinginess,
he does not give rise to a mind of immorality, and he does not give rise to a mind of malice.
He does not give rise to a mind of indolence, he does not give rise to a distracted mind, and he does not give rise to a mind of faulty wisdom.
Thus was the instruction on the jewel of the Dharma.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, from where does that bodhisattva who dwells by means of this dwelling in the perfection of wisdom pass away before being reborn here?"
"Or, having passed away from here, where will he be reborn?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells by means of this dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, having passed away from here, is reborn in this very buddha-field."
Or, having passed away from other buddha-fields or having passed away from the Tuṣita gods, he is reborn here.
Thus is the eighth [type of] bodhisattva.
In this regard, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having passed away from among humans, is reborn into the very same class as humans, [he is the eighth].
Except for those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, that bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faculties are sluggish;
he does not quickly enter into the yoga of the perfection of wisdom,
nor does the gateway of dhāraṇī appear before him, nor the gateway of samādhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as to what you said:
"Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into this yoga of the perfection of wisdom, having passed away from here, where will he be reborn?
Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who enters into this yoga of the perfection of wisdom—
Having passed away from this buddha-field, he will travel from buddha-field to buddha-field;
in those buddha-fields, he will please the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and he shall never be separated from a Buddha.
Thus, Śāriputra, as for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who follows by faith, he who has passed away from other buddha-fields and is reborn here possesses sharp faculties;
he quickly attains this yoga.
Namely, the yoga of the perfection of wisdom;
even for one who has passed through various births, these most profound dharmas become manifest,
and subsequently he enters into the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.
In whichever Buddha-field he is reborn, there he will please the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who, having passed away from the Tuṣita gods, is reborn here, his faculties become even more acute;
the six perfections are not lost to him, and all the gateways of dhāraṇīs and samādhis become manifest before him.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who follow the Dharma of the bodhisattvas; practicing, striving, and exerting themselves in the perfection of wisdom, they bring sentient beings to maturity through the power of skillful means, yet they do not conceive pride on account of that fruit of stream-entry.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are stream-enterers but lack skill in means; they accomplish the four dhyānas and practice the perfections,
yet by virtue of that attainment of dhyāna, they are reborn among the long-lived gods.
If, having passed away from there, they are reborn among humans or gods,
they will please the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
yet even for them, their faculties will be dull and not sharp.
“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who enter the meditative absorptions and practice the perfection of wisdom,
yet through a lack of skill in means they relinquish those absorptions and are reborn in the desire realm.
For these bodhisattva mahāsattvas as well, Śāriputra, the faculties are blunt and not sharp.”
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are candidates for the second and third fruits, liberated through faith; having produced the four dhyānas, they attain the four immeasurables,
and they attain the four formless attainments, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
Possessing great compassion, they take birth through skill in means;

they do not do so by the power of the meditative absorptions, nor by the power of the immeasurables, nor by the power of the formless attainments. They are born in those places where they will please the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Furthermore, never being separated from their dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, they shall here in this very Fortunate Aeon realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained vision— those entering upon the second and third fruits— who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, through skill in means enter the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*),

the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); they cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
They enter the concentration on emptiness,
they enter the concentration on signlessness,
and they enter the concentration on wishlessness.

And they do not fall under their sway; rather, having pleased the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have appeared before them, and having practiced the holy life there, they are reborn once again into the company of the Tuṣita gods,
where they remain for the duration of their lifespan.

Having remained there for the duration of their lifespan, with unimpaired faculties, mindful and clearly comprehending, surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods, they manifest rebirth here and then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in various buddha-fields.
Thus is the once-returner.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the six supernormal knowledges and who are not reborn in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; rather, they travel from buddhafield to buddhafield,
honoring, respecting, revering, and worshiping the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the six superknowledges; sporting with those superknowledges, they travel from buddhafield to buddhafield, to those buddhafields where even the designation of the vehicle of the disciples or the vehicle of the solitary buddhas does not exist.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers; sporting with those supernormal powers, they travel from buddhafield to buddhafield, to those buddhafields where the lifespan is immeasurable.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers, who travel from world-system to world-system.

Having approached that place where there was no sound of "Buddha," no sound of "Dharma," and no sound of "Saṅgha," they remained there and spoke to sentient beings of the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," and the sound of "Saṅgha," as well as the praises of the Three Jewels.
By means of that sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," and the sound of "Saṅgha," when they pass away from there, they are reborn wherever the Buddha Bhagavats reside.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-returners; having produced the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments,
and being endowed with skillful means, they turn back from those meditative concentrations and attainments and are reborn in the desire realm.
They are reborn in great kṣatriya families, or in great brāhmaṇa families, or in great householder families for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
This is the "family-to-family" [rebirth] among humans.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; yet, through the power of skillful means or by virtue of their mastery over dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, they are reborn even among the gods of the Four Great Kings' realm,
and they are reborn among the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin realms.
Abiding there, they bring sentient beings to maturity,
purify the buddha-field,
and please the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having produced the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
pass away from those states and, through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), are reborn in the Brahma-world as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
There they become Brahmās, Great Brahmās, and they abide in those Brahma abodes.
Remaining there, they travel from buddha-field to buddha-field,
and they entreat those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are in those buddha-fields to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Thus is the "family-to-family" [rebirth] among the gods.
“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the four dhyānas up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and who, for the sake of awakening to them,
have attained the four noble truths yet do not fully penetrate them;
those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as being bound by only one more birth.”

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are "one-interval" practitioners (*ekavīcika*), who, from their first production of the thought of awakening, become attainers of the four dhyānas and attainers of the four immeasurables.
They become attainers of the four formless attainments;
they cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
and they realize the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Through skill in means, they are reborn among the gods of the Brahma-realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods;
there, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they act for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, by the very first production of the thought of awakening, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they turn the wheel of Dharma, accomplish the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable beings, and then pass into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
When they have attained final nirvāṇa, the True Dharma remains for an eon or the remainder of an eon.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, practicing the six perfections, pass from world-system to world-system; these are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
And there they will establish sentient beings in awakening; ever diligent for the sake of sentient beings, they never utter speech that is unbeneficial;
and ever diligent for the sake of sentient beings, they travel from buddhafield to buddhafield.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas also, for the sake of sentient beings, after incalculable and immeasurable eons, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in various buddha-fields.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, through the very first production of the thought of awakening, enter the fixed course of the bodhisattvas; these are those who attain parinirvāṇa through volitional effort.
They either abide on the stage of non-retrogression or they fully accomplish all the qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, by the very first production of the thought of awakening, apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.
Together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, they travel from buddha-field to buddha-field in order to purify their own buddha-fields,
and in various buddha-fields they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the six perfections, become universal monarchs and, placing the perfection of generosity foremost, provide all beings with every means of happiness:
food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink;

and likewise they shall supply perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, incense, beds, seats, shelters, houses, wealth, grain, jewels, pearls, gold, silver, coral, ornaments, and the necessities of life.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas for whom the Akaniṣṭha heaven is the limit; having established beings in the ten paths of wholesome action, they are reborn among the gods from the Brahmakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha realm, and in various buddhafields, they attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having accomplished the four dhyānas, they fall away from those dhyānas and, having attained the first dhyāna, are reborn among the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm.
Furthermore, having perfected those meditative concentrations and been reborn among the Akaniṣṭha deities, they awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in various buddha-fields.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having passed away from the Brahma-world, are reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; this is the "leaper."
Having bypassed one or two stages of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, they are reborn among the Akaniṣṭha gods and, in various Buddha-fields, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having manifested a physical body similar to that of a Tathāgata, [attain this]. This is the "half-leaper."
Having purified the Tuṣita heaven, they are reborn among the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha gods; there, through skill in means,
they teach the Dharma to beings in the hells and teach the Dharma to beings born in the animal realm.
They teach the Dharma to the beings of the world of Yama.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, established in the six perfections, having manifested a physical body just like that of a Tathāgata, approach as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
They teach the Dharma to sentient beings, attend upon the Tathāgatas,
and bring Buddha-fields to fulfillment.
And they hear the Dharma;
likewise in the eastern direction, the southern, the western, the northern, the northeast,
the southeast, the southwest, the northwest, above, below— in all ten directions, in each one.
In the east, having gone to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings,
bring Buddha-fields to completion,
and attend upon Buddhas.
And they hear the Dharma;
having emanated emanations from those buddha-fields, they bring about supreme, distinguished, and unsurpassed buddha-fields.

And bodhisattva mahāsattvas bound to only one more birth, being reborn in those various buddha-fields, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in many different buddha-fields.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, passing away from all those places, attain the meditative concentrations and formless attainments, and are reborn among the gods of the Brahma-realm up to the Śubhakṛtsna gods;
there they are reborn in the sphere of infinite space up to the peak of existence.
Then they are reborn in various buddha-fields.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas for whom the peak of existence is the limit; having attained the meditative concentrations and formless attainments, they are reborn from the sphere of infinite space up to the peak of existence.
Then they are reborn in various buddha-fields.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, being free from passion for the realm of form, while practicing the six perfections, possess bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and supreme, completely pure faculties.
Being endowed with these, those who possess such purified faculties become dear to many people and pleasing to them;
furthermore, those beings who behold those bodhisattva mahāsattvas [experience great joy].
Through that very clarity of mind, they attain final nirvana by means of the three vehicles in successive stages.
Thus, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train for the purification of body, train for the purification of speech, and train for the purification of mind.
There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the six perfections, obtain refined faculties.
With those refined faculties, they do not exalt themselves nor disparage others.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, abide in the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline, and never again are born in the states of woe, miserable destinies, or fallen realms, until they reach the stage of non-retrogression.

“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, never abandon the ten paths of wholesome action until they reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, established in the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline...”
Having become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), they give gifts to sentient beings and establish them precisely upon the ten paths of wholesome action.
Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, abiding in the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline, take possession of many hundreds of universal monarchies,
and they take possession of many hundreds of thousands of universal monarchies.
Abiding there, they please many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; they honor, revere, respect, and worship those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and thereafter they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, attaining parinirvāṇa in this very life, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, are attainers of the four dhyānas and attainers of the four formless attainments; sporting with these, they enter the first dhyāna.
Then, emerging from that, they enter the attainment of cessation; then, emerging from that, they enter the second dhyāna;
then, emerging from that, they enter the attainment of cessation.
Then, having emerged from that, they enter the third dhyāna;
then, having emerged from that, they enter the attainment of cessation;
then, having emerged from that, they enter the fourth dhyāna.
Then, emerging from that, they enter the attainment of cessation;
then, emerging from that, they enter the sphere of infinite space;
then, emerging from that, they enter the attainment of cessation.
Then, emerging from that, they enter the sphere of infinite consciousness;
then, emerging from that, they enter the attainment of cessation;
then, emerging from that, they enter the sphere of nothingness.
Then, having emerged from that, they enter the attainment of cessation;
then, having emerged from that, they enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
then, having emerged from that, they enter the attainment of cessation.

In this way, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing in the perfection of wisdom enter into a leap-over concentration (*avaskandaka-samādhi*) through skill in means and awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in various buddha-fields.
Thus [is] the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣī*).

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, established in the six perfections, bring forth the illumination of the Buddha-dharmas for sentient beings, and they themselves are never deprived of the illumination of the Buddha-dharmas until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are candidates for arhatship; they realize pratyekabodhi through skillful means in world systems devoid of Buddhas and free from śrāvakas.

Having ripened many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings in the three vehicles, they awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are pratyekabuddhas regarding the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
They are possessors of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet they do not attain the fruit of stream-entry,
nor do they attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship.
They do not attain the state of a pratyekabuddha;

rather, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, they, through skill in means, lead all sentient beings onto the path, purify them, and cause them to attain the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning.
They cause them to attain the fruit of non-returning,
they cause them to attain arhatship,
and they cause them to attain individual enlightenment.
Not realizing it themselves, they establish others therein.

Thus, Śāriputra, whatever knowledge and abandonment are attained by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— those fruits obtainable through the paths of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— are but the patience of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has attained the receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thus, Śāriputra, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell by means of this perfection of wisdom should be known as irreversible, for they establish others in a Dharma that they have not attained themselves.
“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who, abiding in the six perfections, purify the Tuṣita heaven.
Indeed, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, should be known as belonging to the Fortunate Aeon (bhadrakalpika).
Śāriputra, these are irreversible bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, for whom this arising occurs within the Buddha-dharmas; therefore—”

Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not allow any opportunity for faulty action of body, speech, or mind, and should train for the sake of the complete purity of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
This is the elucidation of the assembly of irreversible bodhisattvas.
Thus ends the instruction on the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is blameworthy bodily action, what is blameworthy verbal action, and what is blameworthy mental action?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"In this regard, Śāriputra, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: 'What is that body?'"
By which body might one undertake bodily action,
and what is that speech by which one might undertake vocal action?
"What is that mind by which I might initiate mental action?
Examining in this way, he perceives the body.
He perceives speech;
he perceives the mind.
Śāriputra, this undertaking of the actions of body, speech, and mind by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is faulty.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the body, does not perceive speech, and does not perceive the mind.

Śāriputra, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should give rise to a mind of stinginess, immorality, ill-will, laziness, distraction, or faulty wisdom through body, speech, or mind; that he should give rise to the corruption of body, speech, or mind— this is impossible, this has no occasion.
This is not possible. Why is that?
Because, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, he purifies the corruption of body and purifies the corruption of speech.
[He] purifies the corruption of the mind.
Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the corruption of body, speech, and mind?"
The Blessed One said:
"Insofar as, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a body, nor does he perceive speech,"
Nor does he perceive the mind.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the depravity of body, speech, and mind;
moreover, Śāriputra, if from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, the ten paths of wholesome action continue to follow for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, [he purifies them].
Furthermore, he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha;

rather, a mind of great compassion is constantly and continuously present toward all sentient beings. Śāriputra, it is in this way that I say the corruption of body, speech, and mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is pure.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom and purifying the path to enlightenment, course in the perfection of generosity, course in the perfection of ethical discipline,
and course in the perfection of patience.
They practice the perfection of vigor, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration,
and they practice the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, what is the path to enlightenment for bodhisattva mahāsattvas?"
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the body,
nor does he apprehend speech,"
One does not apprehend the mind,
nor does one apprehend the perfection of generosity, nor does one apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline.
He does not apprehend the perfection of patience,
he does not apprehend the perfection of vigor, and he does not apprehend the perfection of meditation.
One does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does one apprehend a śrāvaka,
nor does one apprehend a pratyekabuddha.

One does not apprehend a bodhisattva, nor does one apprehend a Buddha. Śāriputra, this is the path to enlightenment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, the non-apprehension of all dharmas; proceeding by means of this path, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [traverses] the six perfections.
"Practicing thus, he cannot be overcome.
This is the instruction on incapacity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections does not conceive of form.
He does not conceive of feeling, he does not conceive of perception, and he does not conceive of mental formations.
One does not conceive of consciousness,
nor does one conceive of the earth element, nor does one conceive of the water element.
He does not conceive of the fire element, he does not conceive of the wind element, and he does not conceive of the space element.
He does not conceive of the element of consciousness,
he does not conceive of the element of the eye, and he does not conceive of the element of form.
He does not conceive of the eye-consciousness element,
he does not conceive of the ear element, and he does not conceive of the sound element.
