He does not conceive of the ear-consciousness element, he does not conceive of the nose element,
and he does not conceive of the odor element.
He does not conceive of the nose-consciousness element, he does not conceive of the tongue element, and he does not conceive of the taste element.
He does not conceive of the tongue-consciousness element,
he does not conceive of the body element, and he does not conceive of the tangible-object element.
He does not conceive of the body-consciousness element, he does not conceive of the mind element, and he does not conceive of the phenomena element.
He does not conceive of the mind-consciousness element;
he does not conceive of the applications of mindfulness;
he does not conceive of the right efforts.
He does not conceive of the bases of psychic power, he does not conceive of the faculties, and he does not conceive of the powers.
He does not conceive of the factors of enlightenment,
he does not conceive of the path,
and he does not conceive of the perfection of generosity.
He does not conceive of the perfection of ethical discipline,
he does not conceive of the perfection of patience, and he does not conceive of the perfection of vigor.
He does not conceive of the perfection of meditation,
he does not conceive of the perfection of wisdom,
and he does not conceive of the grounds of self-confidence.
He does not conceive of the analytical knowledges, he does not conceive of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he conceive of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He does not conceive of the fruit of stream-entry, he does not conceive of the fruit of once-returning, and he does not conceive of the fruit of non-returning.
He does not conceive of arhatship, he does not conceive of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and he does not conceive of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

He does not conceive of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment as something to be attained. For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva increases by means of the six perfections and is not crushed by anything.
There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the knowledge of omniscience.
By being endowed with which knowledge all doors to the lower realms are closed,
they do not experience the misfortune of human poverty, nor do they take on such a physical form.
"By this they become objects of reproach for the world, including the gods.
Thus was the instruction on tirelessness given.
Śāriputra then said:
“What, Blessed One, is the omniscient knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:

“It is that knowledge endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives, in the eastern direction, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and [perceives] those of them...”
He attends upon the Saṅgha and beholds the purification of the Buddha-fields;
likewise, in the south, the west, the north, the intermediate directions, below, and above, he beholds Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
He hears their teaching of the Dharma,
attends upon the Saṅgha,
and beholds the purification of the Buddha-fields.
By means of that wisdom with which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are endowed, there arises no perception of a Buddha, no perception of enlightenment,
and no perception of a Śrāvaka.
There is no perception of a pratyekabuddha,
there is no perception of a self, and there is no perception of another.
There is no perception of a buddha-field for the bodhisattva mahāsattva who, endowed with that wisdom, practices the perfection of generosity and practices the perfection of ethical discipline.
He practices the perfection of patience,
he practices the perfection of vigor,
and he practices the perfection of meditative concentration.
He practices the perfection of wisdom,
yet does not apprehend that perfection;
endowed with which knowledge the bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the foundations of mindfulness.
He does not apprehend the foundations of mindfulness,
yet he cultivates the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
and he does not apprehend those right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, or the path.

He fully accomplishes the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, yet he does not perceive those powers, grounds of self-confidence, or unique qualities of a Buddha. Śāriputra, this is the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Endowed with which gnosis a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills all the qualities of a buddha, yet does not conceive of those qualities of a buddha as "mine. This is the instruction on the complete acquisition of the practice.
“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who obtain and purify the five eyes.
What are these five? Namely: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye.
Śāriputra said:
“What, Blessed One, is the perfectly pure flesh-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, there is a flesh-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that sees for a hundred yojanas; Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that sees for two hundred yojanas; Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that sees the entire Jambudvīpa.
Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva which sees a world-system of four continents;
Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva which sees a thousandfold world-system;
Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva which sees a two-thousandfold world-system.

"Śāriputra, there is the fleshly eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which sees the triple-thousand great-thousand world system. Śāriputra, this is the purified fleshly eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said:
“What, Blessed One, is the purified divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:
“Śāriputra, that which is the divine eye of the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings, that the bodhisattva fully knows.”
The divine eye of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, that the Bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Yāma gods, that the Bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Tuṣita gods, that the Bodhisattva understands.
The divine eye of the Nirmāṇarati devas, which the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, which the bodhisattva understands;
and the divine eye of the Brahmapārṣadya devas, which the bodhisattva understands.
The divine eye of the Brahmapurohita gods, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Mahābrahmā gods, that the bodhisattva understands.
The Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Parīttābha devas;
the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Apramāṇābha devas;
the Bodhisattva understands the divine eye of the Ābhāsvara devas.
The divine eye of the Śubhakṛtsna gods, that the Bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Anabhraka gods, that the Bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Puṇyaprasava gods, that the Bodhisattva understands.
The divine eye of the Bṛhatphala gods, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the asaṃjñisattva gods, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Śuddhābhāsa gods, that the bodhisattva understands.
The divine eye of the Asprha devas, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Atapa devas, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Sudrśa devas, that the bodhisattva understands.
The divine eye of the Sudarśana gods, that the bodhisattva understands;
the divine eye of the Akaniṣṭha gods, that the bodhisattva understands.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, which the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm do not understand—
The gods of the Thirty-three do not know it;
the Yāma gods do not know it;
the Tuṣita gods do not know it.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati heaven do not know it;
the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven do not know it;
the gods of the Brahmapārṣadya heaven do not know it.
The Brahmapurohita gods do not know it; the Mahābrahmā gods do not know it;
the Parīttābha gods do not know it.
The gods of the Immeasurable Light do not know it;
the gods of the Radiant Light do not know it;
the gods of Limited Purity do not know it.
The gods of the Apramāṇaśubha heaven do not know it;
the Śubhakṛtsna gods do not know it;
the Anabhraka gods do not know it.
The Puṇyaprasava gods do not know it; the Bṛhatphala gods do not know it;
the Āsaṃjñisattva gods do not know it.
The Śuddhāvāsa gods do not know it;
the Aspr̥ha gods do not know it;
the Atapa gods do not know it.
The Sudṛśa gods do not know it,
nor do the Sudarśana gods know it; that divine eye of the bodhisattva mahāsattva which the Akaniṣṭha gods do not know.

With that very same purified divine eye, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings in world systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā;

with that very same purified divine eye, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings in world systems in the southern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
With that very same purified divine eye, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all beings in world systems in the western direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
with that very same purified divine eye, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all beings in world systems in the northern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
likewise, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all beings in world systems in the northeastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
In the southeastern direction, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings;
in the southwestern direction, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings;
in the northwestern direction, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of all sentient beings.
In the downward direction, he knows, as it truly is, the death and rebirth of all sentient beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;

in the upward direction, he knows, as it truly is, the death and rebirth of all sentient beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges. Śāriputra, this is the purified divine eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, what is the completely pure eye of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
Śāriputra, by means of that eye of wisdom with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed, he does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever—
whether conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, with outflows or without outflows, afflicted or non-afflicted, mundane or supramundane, or defiled or purified.

By that eye of wisdom, Śāriputra, no phenomenon whatsoever has been seen, heard, thought, or cognized by the bodhisattva mahāsattva. This, Śāriputra, is the completely pure eye of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said:
“What, Blessed One, is the perfectly pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
“In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows by means of the Dharma-eye as follows:”
This person is a follower by faith;
this person is a follower by dharma;
this person dwells in emptiness.
This person dwells in the signless; this person dwells in the wishless;
this person dwells in emptiness.
For this person, the five faculties will arise by way of the door of liberation that is emptiness; by means of these five faculties, he will enter the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*);
and by means of the immediate concentration, he will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
By means of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will abandon the three fetters—
namely, the view of a self-identity, the adherence to rules and observances, and doubt—
and this person is called a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna).
Having attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because of the attenuation of sensual desire and ill-will, this person is called a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).
By means of that very path of cultivation when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, through the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will, this person is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

By means of that very path of cultivation when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, having abandoned attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), ignorance, pride, and restlessness, this person is called an arhat.
This person dwells in the signless;
for this person, through the gateway of liberation that is the signless, the five faculties will arise;

by means of these five faculties, he will enter the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*); and by means of the immediate concentration, he will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
Through the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will abandon the three fetters—
namely, the view of a self-identity, the adherence to rites and rituals, and doubt—
and such a person is called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Having attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because of the attenuation of sensual desire and ill-will, this person is called a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).
By means of that very path of cultivation when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, through the abandonment of sensual desire and ill-will, this person is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

By means of that very path of cultivation when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, having abandoned attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*), this person is called an arhat.
This person dwells in the wishless; for this person, the five faculties will arise by means of the wishless door of liberation,
and by means of these five faculties, they will enter the immediate concentration.
By means of the immediate concentration, he will produce the knowledge and vision of liberation;
by means of that knowledge and vision of liberation, he will abandon the three fetters:
the view of a self-identity, the adherence to rules and observances, and doubt.
This person is called a stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*).
Having attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because sensual desire and ill-will have become attenuated, this person is called a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).
Through that very same path of cultivation, now highly cultivated, because sensual desire and ill-will have been abandoned, this person is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). He... (PvsP1-1: 96)

By means of that very path of cultivation, when it has been cultivated to a superior degree, having abandoned attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness, this person is called an Arhat. Śāriputra, this is the completely pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way:
Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation; thus he understands.
Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he attains the five faculties. This, Śāriputra, is the perfectly pure Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way:
This bodhisattva, who has first resolved to attain awakening and who practices either the perfection of generosity or the perfection of ethical discipline,
thereby obtains pure faculties.
And as for the faculty of vigor, being endowed with skill in means, he intentionally assumes a physical existence and yet maintains the perception of the roots of virtue.
This bodhisattva will be reborn in families of great brahmins; this one will be reborn in families of great kṣatriyas;
this one will be reborn in families of great householders.
This one will be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings;
this one will be reborn among the gods of the Thirty-three;
this one will be reborn among the Yāma gods.
This one will be reborn among the Tuṣita gods;
this one will be reborn among the Nirmāṇarati gods;
this one will be reborn among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
He will be reborn as far as among the Akaniṣṭha gods; remaining there, he will bring sentient beings to maturity and attend to them with every provision for their happiness.
He will purify a buddha-field,
and he will please, honor, revere, respect, esteem, and worship the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Nor will he fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn back until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This, Śāriputra, is the purified [state] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows thus:
These bodhisattva mahāsattvas have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
these bodhisattvas have not been prophesied;
these bodhisattvas are irreversible.
"These bodhisattvas are not irreversible;
the supernormal knowledges of these bodhisattvas are perfected,
while those of these bodhisattvas are not perfected."

This bodhisattva, having perfected the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), goes to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, and so on up to the zenith, where he honors, reveres, respects, and worships the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; whereas this bodhisattva, until he has perfected the superknowledges and performed such worship, does not do so.
"This bodhisattva will obtain the superknowledges; this bodhisattva will not obtain the superknowledges;
the buddha-field of this bodhisattva mahāsattva will be completely pure."
"The buddha-field of this bodhisattva mahāsattva will be impure;
by this bodhisattva sentient beings have been purified;
by this bodhisattva sentient beings have not been purified."
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak in praise of this bodhisattva mahāsattva;
they do not speak in praise of that other bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and these bodhisattvas will become those who stand in the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
These bodhisattva mahāsattvas will not be those who remain in proximity;
the lifespan of this bodhisattva will be limited,
while the lifespan of that bodhisattva will be immeasurable.
The community of this bodhisattva will be limited; the community of this bodhisattva will be immeasurable;
and when this bodhisattva has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will be a community of bodhisattvas.
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, there will be no community of bodhisattvas;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva will practice difficult austerities;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not practice difficult austerities."
"This bodhisattva is in his final existence; this bodhisattva is not in his final existence;
this bodhisattva shall sit at the seat of awakening."
"This bodhisattva will not sit upon the seat of awakening;
this bodhisattva will have Māra;
this bodhisattva will not have Māra. In this way, Śāriputra, the Dharma-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is completely pure.
Śāriputra asked:
"Blessed One, what is the completely pure Buddha-eye of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, immediately after the thought of awakening, enters the diamond-like samādhi and, through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind, attains the knowledge of all aspects— being endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion— [he becomes a Buddha].

And with that eye, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has nothing whatsoever that is unseen, unheard, unthought, or unknown in all its aspects. For it is thus, Śāriputra, that the Buddha-eye of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is completely pure.
For it is thus, Śāriputra, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to purify the five eyes should apply himself to the six perfections. Why is that?

For it is thus, Śāriputra: within the six perfections are included all wholesome dharmas—namely, all the dharmas of the śrāvakas, all the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
Indeed, Śāriputra, those who would speak correctly of the "compendium of all wholesome dharmas" would speak correctly of the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For it is thus, Śāriputra: the perfection of wisdom is the mother of all the perfections.
And regarding these five eyes of the bodhisattvas,
Śāriputra, it is by training in these five eyes of the bodhisattvas that bodhisattva mahāsattvas fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus concludes the instruction on the five eyes.

In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the perfection of the superknowledges; he experiences various kinds of miraculous powers and even causes the earth to tremble.
Having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one;
he experiences both manifestation and disappearance.
He passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains, just as if he were moving through space; he walks upon the earth as if he were a winged bird;
he performs the act of diving and surfacing in the earth as if it were water;
and he moves upon water without breaking the surface, just as if he were walking upon the earth.
It smokes and it blazes like a great mass of fire;
it also releases water from its body like a great cloud;
it touches and strokes with its hand even these two, the sun and the moon, who possess such great psychic power and majesty; and it exercises mastery over its body as far as the Brahma-world.

And by means of that supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he does not conceive [of it as real], because he does not apprehend the supernatural power of the noble ones; he does not conceive even that by which he might conceive, nor that by which he conceives, based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the isolation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viviktatā*).
Based on the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature,

he does not even give rise to the thought of supernatural power, nor the thought of accomplishing supernatural power, except for the mental attention directed toward omniscience. It is in this way, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom realizes the knowledge of the supernormal power of the modes of supernatural power.
He brings this about.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears sounds— both divine and human—
and yet he does not conceive pride because of that divine ear.
"I hear sounds," yet, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, because they are secluded from intrinsic nature, and because their intrinsic nature is unapprehendable,
he does not even give rise to the mental intention regarding the divine ear.

Nor does he have the intention to produce the divine ear, except for the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom produces the knowledge of the direct realization of the superknowledge of the divine ear.
He knows, as it truly is, the minds of other beings and other persons by means of his own mind.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" according to reality; he understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" according to reality;
he understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred" according to reality.
He understands, as it truly is, a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred";
he understands, as it truly is, a deluded mind as "a deluded mind"; and he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion."
One knows a mind with craving as a mind with craving, according to reality; one knows a mind free from craving as a mind free from craving, according to reality;
one knows a mind with clinging as a mind with clinging, according to reality.
He understands, as it truly is, "the mind is without grasping, the mind is without grasping";
he understands, as it truly is, "the mind is contracted, the mind is contracted"; he understands, as it truly is, "the mind is distracted, the mind is distracted."
He understands as it really is a limited mind as "a limited mind"; he understands as it really is an expansive mind as "an expansive mind";
he understands as it really is a vast mind as "a vast mind."
He understands, as it truly is, a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind"; he understands, as it truly is, an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind";
he understands, as it truly is, a secluded mind as "a secluded mind."
He understands as it really is an undiscriminated mind as "an undiscriminated mind";
he understands as it really is an out-flowing mind as "an out-flowing mind";
he understands as it really is an out-flow-free mind as "an out-flow-free mind."
He understands, as it truly is, a mind with blemish as "a mind with blemish," and he understands,
as it truly is, a mind without blemish as "a mind without blemish"; [he understands] a surpassable mind...
He understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, as it truly is;
he understands an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind, as it truly is; and he does not conceive himself on account of that.
For that mind is no-mind, by virtue of its inconceivability;
it does not conceive "I am one who understands," because that very mind is not apprehended, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Based on the fact that intrinsic nature is secluded and based on the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature,

he does not even produce a volition toward the mind of another, nor a volition for the accomplishment of another's mind, except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, Śāriputra, it is so.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, brings forth the knowledge that realizes the supernormal cognition of the mental conduct of all sentient beings. By means of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes, he recollects even a single birth, two, three, and so on, up to hundreds of thousands of births.
He recollects even a single state of mind, up to a hundred states of mind; he recollects even a single day, up to a hundred days; he recollects even a single month, up to a hundred months.

He recollects even one year or even a hundred years, even one eon or even a hundred eons, even many hundreds of eons, many thousands of eons, many hundreds of thousands of eons, and even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, as far back as—
He recollects even the furthest limit of the past:
"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"Having passed away from there, he was reborn there;
having passed away from there, I have been reborn here"— in this way,
he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes, details, and specific circumstances.
And by means of that supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes, he does not conceive [a sense of self];
for that knowledge is non-knowledge, by virtue of its inconceivability;
thus he does not conceive, "I am the one who knows."
Relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, relying on the isolation from intrinsic nature, and relying on the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature, he does not perceive that very knowledge;

nor does he even give rise to the volition for recollecting former abodes, nor the volition for the accomplishment of recollecting former abodes, except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus...
For, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings forth the knowledge that realizes the recollection of former abodes.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— fair and ugly, lowly and exalted— and he understands how beings fare according to their karma, whether in a happy destiny or a miserable one.
These venerable beings are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind;
they do not revile the noble ones and possess right view. By reason of that good conduct of body, speech, and mind, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.
Furthermore, these beings, sirs, are possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech,
and possessed of misconduct of mind.

Those who revile the noble ones and hold wrong views, because of their undertaking of actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in states of woe, in evil destinies, in perdition, in the hells. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he knows as it really is the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to the six destinies throughout the worlds in the ten directions— in all world-systems reaching to the limit of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and ending at the limit of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu).
And he does not conceive [an identity] because that eye is a non-eye, by virtue of its inconceivability;
he does not conceive "I see" because he does not apprehend that very eye, by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Based on the fact that intrinsic nature is isolated and based on the fact that intrinsic nature is unapprehendable,
he does not even give rise to the thought of the divine eye.
Nor does he have the intention to produce the divine eye, except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom produces the knowledge of the realization of the supernormal power of the divine eye;
he produces the knowledge of the supernormal power of the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

He does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he aspire to any other dharma except for the thought, "I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because of his skill in accomplishing the knowledge of the supernormal power of realizing the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), he does not conceive pride; for that knowledge is non-knowledge, by virtue of its inconceivability.

Thus, he does not conceive the thought "I know," nor does he apprehend that very knowledge, by reason of its emptiness of intrinsic nature, its isolation from intrinsic nature, and the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature; furthermore,

he does not even give rise to the volition for the destruction of the outflows, nor the volition for the actualization of the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, except in other cases.

Because of the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes. For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings forth the knowledge that realizes the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom in this manner, the six superknowledges are fulfilled and purified.

Śāriputra, the supernormal knowledges, when completely purified, lead to all-aspect omniscience. Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in the perfection of generosity and purify the path to all-aspect omniscience.
And because of the non-apprehension of even absolute emptiness,

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience, by virtue of the fact that through absolute emptiness there is neither transgression nor non-transgression.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of patience, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, on account of its unshakeability. There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of vigor, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects.
By means of absolute emptiness, they maintain the non-laxity of physical and mental vigor.

Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness, through the state of an undistracted mind.

“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of wisdom, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience by means of the absolute emptiness that consists in the complete avoidance of the mind of faulty wisdom.
It is in this way, Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the six perfections, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience.”
Based on absolute emptiness, generosity is designated in dependence upon grasping; based on absolute emptiness, ethical discipline is designated in dependence upon immorality.
Patience is designated in dependence upon impatience; vigor is designated in dependence upon laziness;
meditative concentration is designated in dependence upon lack of concentration.
Wisdom is designated in dependence upon faulty wisdom;
he does not think "I have crossed over," nor does he think "I have not crossed over."
He does not conceive of giving as grasping; he does not conceive of ethical discipline as immorality;
he does not conceive of patience as agitation.
One does not conceive of vigor as laziness; one does not conceive of meditative concentration as non-concentration;
one does not conceive of wisdom as lack of wisdom.
He does not think, "I have been reviled," nor does he think, "I have been praised," nor does he think, "I have been honored."
He does not think, "I have been treated with disrespect. For what reason?
Śāriputra, it is because non-arising does not think, "I have been reviled," nor does it think, "I have been honored."
He thinks, "I am honored," and he thinks, "I am dishonored. Why is that?
Because the perfection of wisdom completely cuts off all such conceits.
In this regard, Śāriputra, whatever qualities belong to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom do not exist at all for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Fulfiling these qualities, he brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies a buddha-field, and attains the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom generates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Having generated a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, he attains the equality of all phenomena;
having attained the equality of all phenomena, he establishes all sentient beings in the equality of all phenomena.
In this very life, he becomes dear and pleasing to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He becomes beloved and pleasing to all bodhisattvas, as well as to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
wherever he is reborn, there he never sees with his eyes forms that are unpleasant,
nor does he hear with his ears sounds that are unpleasant.
He does not smell unpleasant odors with the nose, he does not taste unpleasant flavors with the tongue,
and he does not touch unpleasant tangibles with the body.
He does not perceive disagreeable phenomena with the mind,
nor does he fall away from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, while this teaching on the perfection of wisdom was being expounded, three hundred bhikṣuṇīs [addressed] the Blessed One.
They covered themselves with their robes as they had been worn and generated the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, at that moment, the Blessed One smiled.
Thereupon, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One.
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, he said this:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?
For Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition."
The Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, these three hundred bhikṣuṇīs, after passing away from here in the Tārakopama kalpa, will arise in the sixty-first kalpa as Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Mahāketu in the world; they will be reborn in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya."
And sixty thousand sons of gods,

whoever were ripened by this teaching of the Dharma, will attain final nirvana in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya. Then, indeed, through the power of the Blessed One, at that very moment they beheld a thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction.
From the assembly circle of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the fourfold assemblies likewise saw a thousand Buddhas in the southern direction and a thousand Buddhas in the western direction.
In the northern direction they see a thousand Buddhas;
in the northeastern direction they see a thousand Buddhas;
in the southeastern direction they see a thousand Buddhas.
In the southwestern direction they see a thousand Buddhas;
in the northwestern direction they see a thousand Buddhas;
below and above, in each direction, they see a thousand Buddhas.

They behold the magnificent arrays of qualities of great buddha-fields, yet they do not behold such arrays of qualities of buddha-fields here in this Sahā world-system as they behold those arrays of qualities of the buddha-fields of those Blessed Buddhas in the ten directions.
Then, from the assembly circle of the Blessed Śākyamuni, ten thousand living beings made these vows: "We shall perform those meritorious deeds by which [we may attain] these..."
"We shall be reborn in the Buddha-fields.
Then, the Blessed One, having understood the intention of those sons of good family, at that moment smiled.
Ānanda said: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?"
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, do you see these ten thousand living beings?
Ānanda replied: "I see them, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, these ten thousand living beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in thousands of Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions,
and they shall never be separated from the Tathāgatas."
Thereafter, Tathāgatas named Vyūharāja will appear in the world.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Subhūti, and the venerable Mahākāśyapa—
these and many other well-known monks, as well as bodhisattvas, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, said this to the Blessed One:
“O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the great perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; it is the foremost perfection, the distinguished perfection,
the excellent perfection, the unsurpassed perfection, the peerless perfection, the unequaled perfection, the space-like perfection, and the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics.”
“Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is the invincible perfection of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.

For herein, Blessed One, by those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom, incomparable gifts have been given, and by them the incomparable perfection of giving has been fulfilled; by them an incomparable personal existence has been attained.”
They will become attainers of the unequaled Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
By them the unequaled ethical discipline has been guarded;
by them the unequaled perfection of ethical discipline has been fulfilled.
By them, a peerless physical form has been attained; they will become recipients of the peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. By them, peerless patience has been cultivated.

By them the peerless perfection of patience has been fulfilled; by them a peerless physical form has been attained; they shall become possessors of the peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
By them, incomparable vigor was undertaken;
by them, the incomparable perfection of vigor was fulfilled; by them, an incomparable physical form was attained.
They will become attainers of the unequaled Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
By them, the unequaled meditative concentration has been produced; by them, the unequaled perfection of meditative concentration has been fulfilled.
By them has been attained a physical existence that is peerless; they shall become possessors of the peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
by them has been cultivated peerless wisdom.

By them the peerless perfection of wisdom has been fulfilled; by them a peerless physical form has been attained; they shall become possessors of the peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

And it was precisely by practicing this very perfection of wisdom, O Blessed One, that you became an obtainer of form that is unequaled; you became an obtainer of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are unequaled; you fully awakened to an unequaled enlightenment; and you set in motion an unequaled wheel of Dharma.

In this very way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, while coursing in this very perfection of wisdom, have perfectly awakened, will perfectly awaken, and are perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, O Blessed One, [this is the source] of all dharmas.
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to go to the further shore should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who course in this perfection of wisdom are to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those many Śrāvakas and those Bodhisattvas:
"So it is, noble son; so it is.
Those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who course in this perfection of wisdom are worthy of being honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. For what reason?
It is because, Śāriputra, it is by depending on the bodhisattva that the appearance of the world in the world occurs."
Of the human world and the divine world; of the great noble kṣatriya families, the great noble brahmin families, and the great noble householder families;
and of the universal monarchs, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.

Of the gods of the Brahma-parṣadyas, the gods of the Brahma-purohitas, the gods of the Mahābrahmans, the gods of the Parīttābhas, the gods of the Apramāṇābhas, the gods of the Ābhāsvaras, the gods of the Parīttaśubhas, the gods of the Apramāṇaśubhas,
the gods of the Śubhakṛtsnas, the gods of the Anabhrakas, the gods of the Puṇyaprasavas, and the gods of the Bṛhatphalas.
of the gods who are non-percipient beings; of the Śuddhābhāsa gods; of the Aspr̥ha gods; of the Atapa gods;
of the Sudr̥śa gods; of the Sudarśana gods; of the Akaniṣṭha gods; of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space;

of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness; of the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness; and of the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The manifestation of gods occurs in the world;
the manifestation of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas occurs in the world.
For it is by depending on the Bodhisattva, Śāriputra, that the appearance of the Three Jewels occurs in the world;

and the appearance of all worldly means of livelihood occurs in the world— namely, food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, medicinal requisites for the sick, and various articles such as gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver.

To whatever extent, Śāriputra, there is the appearance in the world of all sources of happiness— whether divine or human, the happiness of existence or the happiness of nirvāṇa— it is entirely due to the Bodhisattva, Śāriputra. For what reason?
For, Śāriputra, while practicing the conduct of the six perfections, a bodhisattva enjoins sentient beings [to them]:

he causes them to give gifts, encourages them to undertake ethical discipline, establishes them in patience, enjoins them to vigor, establishes them in meditative concentration, and enjoins them to wisdom.
And all sentient beings, having relied upon the bodhisattva, practice the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One extended his tongue-faculty and covered this great trichiliocosm with it.
Then, from that tongue-faculty, rays of light of many colors and various hues issued forth.

Having emerged, they illuminated world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance. Likewise, they illuminated world-systems in the southern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance;

they illuminated world-systems in the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance; and they illuminated world-systems in the northern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, with their radiance.

In the northeastern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance; in the southeastern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance;
in the southwestern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance.

In the northwestern direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance; in the downward direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance;
and in the upward direction, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with their radiance.
Then, indeed, from as many Buddha-fields in the eastern direction— and likewise up to the zenith— as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,
immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas, having seen those arrays of light, questioned the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their respective Buddha-fields:
"Blessed One, whose power is this, by which this radiance of majesty is seen?
Those Blessed Buddhas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas:
"Noble sons, in the western direction, as far as the downward quarter, in the Sahā world-system, there dwells, remains, and sustains himself a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."

Extending his tongue-faculty, he illuminated with radiance world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, and likewise up to the zenith; thus, in all ten directions, he illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with radiance, namely for the teaching and the proclamation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to the bodhisattvas, the great beings (*mahāsattvas*).
Those bodhisattvas said to those Tathāgatas:

"O Blessed One, we shall go to that Sahā world-system to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata; and we shall go to hear that Perfection of Wisdom and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas assembled from the ten directions."
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, said:
"Go, sons of good family, at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas [brought] from the ten directions flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory banners.
Taking baskets of flowers made of various jewels, gold, and silver, and accompanied by a great concert of musical instruments and vocal performances,
they approached the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Then indeed the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods [approached].

the gods who wield power over the creations of others, the gods who are ministers of Brahmā, the gods who are the Great Brahmās, the gods of Limited Radiance, the gods of Immeasurable Radiance, the gods of Utmost Radiance, the gods of Limited Purity,
the gods of Immeasurable Purity, the gods of Universal Purity, the Cloudless gods, the gods of Merit-Born, the gods of Vast Fruit, the gods of Non-percipient Beings, and the gods of Pure Luster.

The Asprha gods, the Atapa gods, the Sudrśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods took divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags— blue lotuses, white lotuses, pink lotuses, māndārava flowers, kesara flowers, and tamāla leaves— and approached the Blessed One.
Then those bodhisattvas and those gods scattered those flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.

Then indeed, those flowers, having risen into the air, formed above this great trichiliocosm a flower-pavilion; it was four-pillared, square in its proportions, well-proportioned, delightful, and enchanting.

Then, from that assembly, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and placed their right knees upon the ground.
Having established himself, he bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Blessed One, may we in a future time become recipients of such qualities as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; may we likewise lead a community of disciples and teach the Dharma in an assembly just as the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, teaches the Dharma now.”

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition of those sons of good family and having recognized their patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the non-arising, non-cessation, non-conditioning, and non-manifestation of all phenomena, smiled. Thereupon, rays of light of many colors issued from the Blessed One’s mouth;
they circled the entire world to the right and returned to vanish into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.
Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?"
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, after sixty-eight hundred thousand million billion eons, these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings shall appear in the world as Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa.
This is the instruction on the six supernormal knowledges.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"May it be inspired in you, Subhūti, concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—how the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, should set forth in the perfection of wisdom.
Then, this thought occurred to those bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, to those great śrāvakas, and to those sons of the gods:

"Will the Venerable Subhūti indeed teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas by means of the power of his own wisdom and eloquence, or rather through the majesty of the Buddha? Then the Venerable Subhūti, having understood with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, those great śrāvakas, and those sons of the gods, [addressed] the Venerable...
He said this to Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, whatever the disciples of the Blessed One speak, teach, or explain, all that should be known as the personal power (*puruṣakāra*) of the Tathāgata. For what reason?"

For whatever dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata, those training in that teaching of the dharma realize that very nature of phenomena (dharmatā); having realized that nature of phenomena, whatever they speak, teach, or instruct, all of it is not in contradiction with that nature of phenomena.
"Śāriputra, it is the Tathāgata himself who, through the application of skillful means, will teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Śāriputra, this is not within the domain of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Thus ends the introduction to the instruction on the path of seeing.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when it is said 'bodhisattva,' of what dharma, Blessed One, is this the designation, namely 'bodhisattva'?"
“Blessed One, I do not perceive any phenomenon that is called ‘bodhisattva.
Therefore, Blessed One, since I do not perceive a bodhisattva and do not apprehend even the perfection of wisdom, which bodhisattva shall I speak of, and in which perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, this is merely a name—namely, "perfection of wisdom" and "bodhisattva.
Furthermore, that name "bodhisattva" is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a "sentient being" is spoken of as a "sentient being."
And there is no apprehension of any sentient being whatsoever; that which is called a "name" is merely a designation, a designated phenomenon, existing only as a designation.
This is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
And for that designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely designated by way of names and conventions.

In the same way, all these—self, sentient being, life-force, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer—are all designated phenomena; they are all without arising and without cessation, being designated by way of name alone.
In the same way, Subhūti, both the perfection of wisdom,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva,
and the name "bodhisattva"— all these are merely designated phenomena.
All these are without arising and without cessation; they are merely designated by way of names.
Subhūti, it is just as if this were "internal form"—it is a mere conceptual designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*).
And for that conceptual designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by way of mere names and symbols.
"Feeling," Subhūti, is merely a designation for a phenomenon;
and of that designation for a phenomenon, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed as a mere name and conventional symbol.
"Perception," Subhūti, is merely a designation for a phenomenon.
And for that designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely designated by way of a name and convention.
Subhūti, "formations" (*saṃskāra*) are merely a designation of phenomena;
and for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely designated by way of a name and convention.
"Subhūti, 'consciousness' is merely a designation for a phenomenon;
and of that designation for a phenomenon there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions.
In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva, and the name 'bodhisattva'—all these are phenomena that are mere designations."
And for those phenomena that are mere designations, there is neither arising nor cessation; they are designated by means of nothing other than mere names and conventions.
Subhūti, "the eye" is merely a designation of a phenomenon;
and for that designation of a phenomenon, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by the mere name and convention, namely, "the eye."
And that eye is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "ear" is merely a designation for a phenomenon;
and of that designation for a phenomenon there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of a mere name and sign, namely, "ear."
And that ear is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "nose" is merely a designation for a dharma;
and of that designation for a dharma there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by a mere name and sign, namely, "nose."
And that nose is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "tongue" is a mere designation of phenomena;
for that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor ceasing, except that it is conventionally expressed by the mere name and convention, namely, "tongue."
And that tongue is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "body" is merely a designation for phenomena; and of that designation for phenomena—

There is neither arising nor ceasing; it is merely by way of a name and a conventional designation that it is expressed as "the body," yet that body is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, "mind" is likewise a mere designation for phenomena.
And for that [mind], there is neither arising nor cessation by way of designations of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), except that it is conventionally expressed by mere name and designation as "mind.
That mind is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "form" is merely a designation of phenomena.
And for that designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely by way of name and convention that it is expressed as "form.
Subhūti, this "sound" is also merely a designation of phenomena;
for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely by way of name and convention that it is expressed as "sound."
"O Subhūti, 'odor' is merely a designation for a phenomenon;
and regarding that designation for a phenomenon, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed as 'odor' by means of a mere name and convention.
O Subhūti, 'taste' is merely a designation for a phenomenon."
And for that [designation], there is neither arising nor ceasing through the designations of phenomena; it is merely by way of name and convention that it is expressed as "taste.
Subhūti, "contact" is also merely a designation of phenomena;
and for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing; it is merely by way of name and convention that it is expressed as "contact."

"Subhūti, 'dharma' is merely a designation for a dharma; and of that designation for a dharma, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols as 'dharma.
Subhūti, the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element are likewise merely designations for dharmas."

And for that [designation], there is neither arising nor cessation through the designations of phenomena (dharmaprajñapti), except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions;
and these are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, "the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element"—this is merely a designation of phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding this designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is merely expressed by way of names and conventions.
Moreover, these are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
"Subhūti, the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element—these are merely designations for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*).
And of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed as mere names and symbols;
furthermore, they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."
"Subhūti, the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element—these are merely designations for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*).
And of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of names and conventions that they are expressed in common usage.
Furthermore, they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."
Subhūti, the body element, the tangible element, and the body-consciousness element—these are merely designations for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*).
Of these designations for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that they are conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols;
and they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, the mind element, the dharma element, and the mind-consciousness element—these are merely designations for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*).
Of these designations for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that they are conventionally expressed by means of mere names and conventions;
and they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," and "the name of a bodhisattva" is merely a designation for phenomena (dharmaprajñaptimātra).
And of that designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor ceasing; it is merely expressed by way of a name and convention.
Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, this internal body is conventionally expressed as "body."
The head, neck, abdomen, shoulders, two arms, back, ribs, waist, thighs, shanks, and feet are designated as "bones";
yet these are phenomena existing only as conceptual designations (*prajñapti-dharma*), for they have neither arising nor cessation, being designated by nothing other than mere names and conventions.
Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," and "the name of a bodhisattva"—all these are merely designated phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*). They have neither arising nor cessation; they are conventionally expressed as nothing other than mere names and conventions.
And that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Subhūti, it is just as if all external grass, wood, branches, leaves, and foliage were designated by various names;
yet those names have neither arising nor ceasing, except that they are conventionally expressed as mere names and signs.
And those names are not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," and "the name of a bodhisattva"—all these are merely designated phenomena (prajñaptidharma). They are designated by various names, yet for those names there is neither arising nor cessation; they are used in conventional discourse as nothing other than mere names and conventions.
Furthermore, those names are not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with those things that are like a dream, an echo, a mirage, a reflection, or an illusion, and with the emanations of a Tathāgata—all these are merely designations of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). They have neither arising nor cessation, except that they are conventionally expressed by means of mere names and signs;
and yet that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," and "the name of a bodhisattva"—

all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols.
And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom should train in the designation of names and conventions, the designation of instruction, and the designation of phenomena.
This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as permanent,
nor does he perceive form as impermanent;
nor does he perceive form as pleasant.
He does not perceive form as suffering;
he does not perceive form as self;
he does not perceive form as non-self.
He does not perceive form as peaceful, he does not perceive form as unpeaceful,
and he does not perceive form as empty.
He does not perceive form as empty;
he does not perceive form as having signs;
he does not perceive form as signless.
He does not perceive form as being with aspiration, nor does he perceive form as being without aspiration.
One does not perceive form as conditioned,
nor does one perceive form as unconditioned,
nor does one perceive form as arisen.
He does not perceive form as unarisen; he does not perceive form as ceased;
he does not perceive form as unceased.
One does not perceive form as secluded, nor does one perceive form as non-secluded;
one does not perceive form as wholesome.
He does not perceive form as unwholesome; he does not perceive form as blameworthy; he does not perceive form as blameless.
He does not perceive form as being with outflows, he does not perceive form as being without outflows,
and he does not perceive form as being defilement.
He does not perceive form as being free from affliction; he does not perceive form as mundane;
he does not perceive form as supramundane.
He does not perceive form as defilement; he does not perceive form as purification;
he does not perceive form as saṃsāra.
He does not perceive form as nirvāṇa.
He does not perceive feeling as permanent,
nor does he perceive feeling as impermanent.
He does not perceive it as pleasant, nor does he perceive it as painful; he does not perceive it as self, nor as non-self; he does not perceive it as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful.
One does not perceive feeling as empty, nor as non-empty; as having signs, nor as signless; as with aspiration, nor as without aspiration.
Neither conditioned nor unconditioned,
neither arisen nor unarisen,
neither ceased nor unceased.
It is neither secluded nor unsecluded; neither wholesome nor unwholesome; neither faulty nor faultless;
neither with outflows nor without outflows.
It is neither afflicted nor free from affliction; neither mundane nor supramundane; neither affliction nor purification.
He does not perceive sensation as "saṃsāra" nor as "nirvāṇa.
He does not perceive perception as permanent.
One does not perceive perception as permanent, nor as pleasant, nor as painful, nor as self, nor as non-self;
nor as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful; nor as empty, nor as non-empty; nor as having signs, nor as signless.
He does not perceive the notion that it is "with aspiration" nor "without aspiration";
he does not perceive it as "conditioned" nor "unconditioned," as "arisen" nor "unarisen," as "ceased" nor "unceasing," nor as "secluded" nor "unsecluded."

One does not perceive the notion that [anything] is wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless, with outflows or without outflows; one does not perceive it as defilement or freedom from defilement, mundane or supramundane, nor as affliction or purification, nor as saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
One does not perceive conditioned phenomena as being permanent.

He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as impermanent; he does not perceive them as pleasant or as painful, as self or as non-self, as peaceful or as unpeaceful, as empty or as non-empty, as having signs or as signless, or as being with aspiration or as being without aspiration.
He contemplates conditioned phenomena as neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither arisen nor unarisen, neither ceased nor unceased, neither secluded nor unsecluded,
and neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
They are neither blameworthy nor blameless; neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither afflictions nor free from afflictions.
He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as mundane, nor as supramundane; as affliction, nor as purification; as saṃsāra, nor as nirvāṇa.
He does not perceive consciousness as permanent, nor does he perceive consciousness as impermanent.

One does not perceive consciousness as "it is pleasure" or "it is suffering," nor as "self" or "not-self," nor as "peaceful" or "not peaceful," nor as "empty" or "not empty," nor as "signless" or "not signless," nor as "wishless" or "not wishless."

It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither arisen nor unarisen; neither ceased nor unceased; neither secluded nor non-secluded; neither wholesome nor unwholesome; neither faulty nor faultless; neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither afflicted nor free from affliction.
One does not perceive consciousness as being mundane or supramundane, as defilement or purification, or as saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Thus, he does not perceive the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent; he does not perceive the form-element as either permanent or impermanent;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not perceive the eye-element as either pleasant or painful;
one does not perceive the form-element as either pleasant or painful;
one does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either pleasant or painful.
One does not perceive the eye-element as self or as non-self;
one does not perceive the form-element as self or as non-self;
one does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as self or as non-self.
He does not perceive the eye-element as either peaceful or not peaceful;
he does not perceive the form-element as either peaceful or not peaceful;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either peaceful or not peaceful.
He does not perceive the eye-element as either empty or non-empty;
he does not perceive the form-element as either empty or non-empty;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either empty or non-empty.
He does not perceive the eye-element as having signs or as being signless; he does not perceive the form-element as having signs or as being signless;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as having signs or as being signless.
He does not perceive the eye-element as being with aspiration or without aspiration;
he does not perceive the form-element as being with aspiration or without aspiration;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as being with aspiration or without aspiration.
He does not perceive the eye-element as conditioned or as unconditioned;
he does not perceive the form-element as conditioned or as unconditioned;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as conditioned or as unconditioned.
He does not perceive the eye-element as arisen or as unarisen; he does not perceive the form-element as arisen or as unarisen;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as arisen or as unarisen.
He does not perceive the eye-element as ceased or as unceased;
he does not perceive the form-element as ceased or as unceased;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as ceased or as unceased.
He does not perceive the eye-element as either secluded or not secluded; he does not perceive the form-element as either secluded or not secluded;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either secluded or not secluded.
He does not perceive the eye-element as either wholesome or unwholesome;
he does not perceive the form-element as either wholesome or unwholesome;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either wholesome or unwholesome.
One does not perceive the eye-element as either faulty or faultless;
one does not perceive the form-element as either faulty or faultless;
one does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either faulty or faultless.
He does not perceive the eye-element as either with outflows or without outflows;
he does not perceive the form-element as either with outflows or without outflows;
he does not perceive the eye-consciousness-element as either with outflows or without outflows.
He does not perceive the eye-element as being either afflicted or free from affliction;
he does not perceive the form-element as being either afflicted or free from affliction; nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness-element [as being either afflicted or free from affliction].
He does not perceive it as "with affliction" or "without affliction.
He does not perceive the eye-element as mundane or supramundane;
he does not perceive the form-element as mundane or supramundane.
He does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as either mundane or supramundane.
He does not perceive the eye element as either defilement or purification,
nor does he perceive the form element as either defilement or purification.
He does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as either defilement or purification.
He does not perceive the eye element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
he does not perceive the form element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
One does not perceive the eye-consciousness element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Likewise, one does not perceive the ear element, the sound element, or the ear-consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not perceive the ear element, the sound element, or the ear-consciousness element as either pleasant or painful.
He does not perceive the ear-element, the sound-element, or the ear-consciousness-element as either self or non-self.
He does not perceive the ear-element, the sound-element, or the ear-consciousness-element as either peaceful or unpeaceful.

He does not perceive the nose element, the odor element, or the nose-consciousness element as either defilement or purification.
One does not perceive the nose element, the odor element, or the nose-consciousness element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
One does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either pleasure or suffering.
One does not perceive the tongue-element, the taste-element, or the tongue-consciousness-element as either self or non-self.
One does not perceive the tongue-element, the taste-element, or the tongue-consciousness-element as either peaceful or unpeaceful.
One does not perceive the tongue-element, the taste-element, or the tongue-consciousness-element as either empty or non-empty.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as having signs or as being signless.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as being with wish or as being wishless.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as being conditioned or as being unconditioned.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either arisen or unarisen.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either ceased or unceased.
He does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either secluded or non-secluded.

One does not perceive the tongue element, the taste element, or the tongue-consciousness element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
One does not perceive the body element, the tangible object element, or the body-consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not perceive the body element, the tangible object element, or the body-consciousness element as either pleasant or painful.

He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as having signs or as being signless.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as being with wish or as being wishless.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as being conditioned or as being unconditioned.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either arisen or unarisen.

He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either secluded or non-secluded.

He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either with-outflows or without-outflows.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either defiled or free from defilement.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either mundane or supramundane.
He does not perceive the body-element, the tangible-object-element, or the body-consciousness-element as either affliction or purification.
