One does not perceive the mind-element, the mental-object-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the mental-object-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either pleasant or painful.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either self or non-self.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either peaceful or unpeaceful.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either empty or non-empty.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as having signs or as being signless.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as being with wish or as being wishless.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as being conditioned or as being unconditioned.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either arisen or unarisen.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either ceased or unceased.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either secluded or unsecluded.
He does not perceive the mind element, the phenomena element, or the mind-consciousness element as either wholesome or unwholesome.
He does not perceive the mind element, the phenomena element, or the mind-consciousness element as either blameworthy or blameless.
He does not perceive the mind element, the phenomena element, or the mind-consciousness element as either with outflows or without outflows.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either afflicted or free from affliction.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either mundane or supramundane.
One does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either defilement or purification.
He does not perceive the mind-element, the phenomena-element, or the mind-consciousness-element as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by eye, forms, and eye-consciousness-contact,
he does not perceive that either as permanent or as impermanent.
Thus, he does not perceive it as either pleasure or pain;
he does not perceive it as either self or non-self;
he does not perceive it as either peaceful or unpeaceful.
He does not perceive it as empty or as non-empty;
he does not perceive it as having signs or as signless; he does not perceive it as having a wish or as wishless.
He does not perceive it as conditioned or as unconditioned;
he does not perceive it as arisen or as unarisen;
he does not perceive it as ceased or as unceased.
He does not perceive it as secluded or as non-secluded; he does not perceive it as wholesome or as unwholesome;
he does not perceive it as faulty or as faultless.
He does not perceive it as either with outflows or without outflows;
he does not perceive it as either afflicted or free from affliction;
he does not perceive it as either mundane or supramundane.
He does not perceive it as defilement, nor does he perceive it as purification.

Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by eye-contact, visual consciousness, and the eye, that too he does not perceive as saṃsāra, nor does he perceive it as nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness,
he does not regard that as either permanent or impermanent;
likewise, he does not regard it as either pleasant or painful.
He does not perceive it as "self" or as "not-self," nor as "peaceful" or as "not peaceful," nor as "empty" or as "not empty."

He does not perceive it as having signs, nor as being signless; he does not perceive it as being with aspiration, nor as being without aspiration; he does not perceive it as conditioned, nor as being unconditioned.
Neither as "arisen" nor as "unarisen," neither as "ceased" nor as "unceased," neither as "secluded" nor as "unsecluded."
Neither as "wholesome" nor as "unwholesome," neither as "blameworthy" nor as "blameless," neither as "with outflows" nor as "without outflows."
He does not perceive it as either afflicted or free from affliction, nor as either mundane or supramundane, nor as either defilement or purification.

Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness, he does not perceive that as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Moreover, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the nose, odors, and olfactory consciousness...
He does not perceive even that as either permanent or impermanent;
nor as pleasant or painful;
nor as self or non-self.
One does not perceive it as "peaceful" nor as "not peaceful," nor as "empty" nor as "not empty," nor as "sign" nor as "signless."
One does not perceive it as "with aspiration" nor as "without aspiration," nor as "conditioned" nor as "unconditioned," nor as "arisen" nor as "unarisen."
It is not ceased, nor is it unceased; it is not secluded, nor is it unsecluded;
it is not wholesome, nor is it unwholesome.
Neither as "faulty" nor as "faultless," neither as "with outflows" nor as "without outflows," neither as "affliction" nor as "free from affliction."
He does not perceive it as mundane nor as supramundane; nor does he perceive it as affliction or as purification.
Whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by the contact of the nose, odor, and olfactory consciousness, [he does not perceive that either].
Even that he does not perceive as either "saṃsāra" or "nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness,
even that he does not perceive as either "permanent" or "impermanent."
He does not perceive it as "pleasure" or "suffering," nor as "self" or "non-self," nor as "peaceful" or "not peaceful."
He does not perceive it as "empty" nor as "not empty," nor as "with signs" nor as "signless," nor as "with aspiration" nor as "without aspiration."
Neither as conditioned nor as unconditioned, neither as arisen nor as unarisen, neither as ceased nor as unceased.
Neither as "secluded" nor as "not secluded," neither as "wholesome" nor as "unwholesome," neither as "blameworthy" nor as "blameless."
It is neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither defilement nor freedom from defilement; neither mundane nor supramundane.
He does not perceive it as defilement nor as purification.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness,
he likewise does not perceive that as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of the body, the tangible object, and body-consciousness,
he does not regard that as either permanent or impermanent,
nor as pleasant or painful.
Neither as "self" nor as "non-self," neither as "peaceful" nor as "not peaceful," neither as "empty" nor as "not empty."
He does not perceive it as having signs, nor as signless; he does not perceive it as having a wish, nor as wishless; he does not perceive it as conditioned, nor as unconditioned.
Neither arisen nor unarisen, neither ceased nor unceased, neither secluded nor unsecluded.
Neither as wholesome nor as unwholesome; neither as faulty nor as faultless;
neither as with-outflows nor as without-outflows.
He does not perceive it as defilement nor as freedom from defilement; he does not perceive it as mundane nor as supramundane; he does not perceive it as defilement nor as purification.

Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of body, tangibles, and body-consciousness, he does not regard that as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by the contact of mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness, [he likewise does not regard it as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa].
Whether it be pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure,
he does not regard even that as either permanent or impermanent;
nor does he regard it as pleasure or as pain.
He does not perceive it as "self" or "not-self," nor as "peaceful" or "not peaceful," nor as "empty" or "not empty."
He does not perceive it as having signs, nor as signless; he does not perceive it as with aspiration, nor as without aspiration; he does not perceive it as conditioned, nor as unconditioned.
It is neither arisen nor unarisen; neither ceased nor unceased;
neither secluded nor non-secluded.
Neither as wholesome nor as unwholesome; neither as faulty nor as faultless;
neither as with-outflows nor as without-outflows.
He does not perceive it as defilement nor as freedom from defilement; he does not perceive it as mundane nor as supramundane; he does not perceive it as defilement nor as purification.
Furthermore, whatever feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— arises conditioned by the contact of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness,
one does not regard even that as either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
This is the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣāntiḥ*).
For what reason?

Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor the name "perfection of wisdom," nor that bodhisattva, nor the name "bodhisattva," whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm. For in this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not conceptualize or discriminate these all dharmas.
Abiding in the non-conceptual dharma, he cultivates the foundations of mindfulness;
practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name "perfection of wisdom";
he does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the name "bodhisattva."

In this way, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the perfections, the powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor the name "perfection of wisdom," nor the Bodhisattva, nor even the name "Bodhisattva."
Except for the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*);
for by him who courses in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) has been penetrated.

And that which is the characteristic of phenomena neither becomes defiled nor purified. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should understand the designation of phenomena as being merely conventional and nominal.
This is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding origination (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣāntiḥ*).
Having understood the conventional designation of phenomena through its mere name, he will not adhere to form,
he will not adhere to feeling, and he will not adhere to perception.
One will not adhere to volitional formations,
nor will one adhere to consciousness;
one will not adhere to the eye.
One will not adhere to form, one will not adhere to visual consciousness,
and one will not adhere to visual contact.
Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too will not be adhered to.
One will not adhere to the ear, nor to sound, nor to ear-consciousness, nor to ear-contact;
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by ear-contact, that too will not be adhered to.
One will not adhere to the nose, nor to odor, nor to nose-consciousness, nor to nose-contact;
furthermore, one will not adhere even to that feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by nose-contact.
One will not adhere to the tongue, nor to taste, nor to tongue-consciousness, nor to tongue-contact.
Furthermore, whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by tongue-contact, that too will not be adhered to.
One will not adhere to the body, nor to tangible objects, nor to body-consciousness, nor to body-contact;
and as for whatever feeling arises conditioned by body-contact...
Whether it be pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain, one will not adhere to that.
One will not adhere to the mind, nor to mental phenomena, nor to mental consciousness, nor to mental contact;
and even as for the feeling arisen conditioned by mental contact—whether it be pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—one will not adhere to that either.
Nor will one adhere to the conditioned realm, nor will one adhere to the unconditioned realm.
This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding origination.
He will not be attached to the perfection of generosity, he will not be attached to the perfection of ethical discipline,
and he will not be attached to the perfection of patience.
He will not adhere to the perfection of vigor, he will not adhere to the perfection of meditation,
and he will not adhere to the perfection of wisdom.
One will not adhere even to their names or their characteristics,
nor will one adhere to the body;
one will not adhere to the fleshly eye.
One does not become attached to the divine eye,
one does not become attached to the wisdom eye, and one does not become attached to the Dharma eye.
One will not be attached to the Buddha-eye,
nor will one be attached to the superknowledges;
one will not be attached to internal emptiness.
One will not be attached to external emptiness,
nor will one be attached to internal-external emptiness,
nor to the emptiness of emptiness, nor to great emptiness, nor to the emptiness of the ultimate, nor to the emptiness of the conditioned.

Neither in the emptiness of the unconditioned, nor in ultimate emptiness, nor in the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, nor in the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor in the emptiness of all phenomena, nor in the emptiness of specific characteristics, nor in the emptiness of non-apprehension, nor in the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, nor in the emptiness of existence, nor in the emptiness of non-existence, nor in the emptiness of self-nature.
One will not adhere to the emptiness of other-nature.

One will not adhere to suchness, nor to the limit of reality, nor to the realm of phenomena, nor to the maturation of sentient beings, nor to the purification of the Buddha-field, nor to skill in means. Why is that?
Because all those phenomena do not exist—the one who would adhere, that by which one would adhere, and that wherein one would adhere.
Thus is the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering].

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, being unattached to all phenomena, increases through the perfection of giving and the perfection of ethical discipline.
It increases;
it increases through the perfection of patience;
it increases through the perfection of vigor.
He increases through the perfection of meditative concentration,
he increases through the perfection of wisdom,
and he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
Thus is the subsequent knowledge regarding origination.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom enters the stage of non-retrogression.
Thus is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation.
Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the superknowledges;
having fulfilled the superknowledges, he travels from buddhafield to buddhafield and brings sentient beings to maturity.

He honors, reveres, respects, and worships the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; by that very root of merit, he is reborn in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and hears the Dharma. The teachings heard by him shall never be lost until he reaches the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*); thus he will attain the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*) and the gateways of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train].
One practicing the perfection of wisdom should understand that the designation of phenomena is merely conventional and nominal.
This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation.
What do you think, Subhūti: is that which is called a "bodhisattva, a mahāsattva" actually form (rūpa) that is the bodhisattva?
"Feeling is the bodhisattva," "perception is the bodhisattva," "formative factors are the bodhisattva."
"Is consciousness the bodhisattva?
"What do you think, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva something other than form, or is the bodhisattva something other than feeling?"
Is there a "bodhisattva" apart from perception, a "bodhisattva" apart from mental formations, or a "bodhisattva" apart from consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva [to be found] in form? Is a bodhisattva [to be found] in feeling? Is a bodhisattva [to be found] in perception?
"In the formative forces (saṃskāra) there is a bodhisattva," or "in consciousness (vijñāna) there is a bodhisattva"?
What do you think, Subhūti, is there "form" (rūpa) in a bodhisattva?
"Feeling in the Bodhisattva," "perception in the Bodhisattva," "formative factors in the Bodhisattva."
Regarding the "consciousness" in a bodhisattva:
what do you think, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva formless, is a bodhisattva without feeling?
Is it thus: "the bodhisattva is without perception," "the bodhisattva is without conditioned formation," or "the bodhisattva is without consciousness"?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the eye the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than the eye; is the Bodhisattva in the eye, or is the eye in the Bodhisattva; is the Bodhisattva one who is without an eye? Is the ear the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than the ear; is the Bodhisattva in the ear, or is the ear in the Bodhisattva; is the Bodhisattva one who is without an ear? Is the nose the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than the nose; is the Bodhisattva in the nose, or is the nose in the Bodhisattva; is the Bodhisattva one who is without a nose?
Is the tongue the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva is other than the tongue; is the Bodhisattva in the tongue, and the Bodhisattva is one whose tongue is not the tongue?
Is the body the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva is other than the body; is the Bodhisattva in the body, and the Bodhisattva is one whose body is not a body?
Is the mind the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva is other than the mind; is the Bodhisattva in the mind, and the Bodhisattva is one who is without mind?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti: is form the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than form, or is the Bodhisattva in form, or is form in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva formless?
What do you think, Subhūti: is sound the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than sound, or is the Bodhisattva in sound, or is sound in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva soundless?
What do you think, Subhūti: is odor the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than odor, or is the Bodhisattva in odor, or is odor in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva odorless?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the taste the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the taste? Is the bodhisattva in the taste, or is the taste in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva without taste? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the tangible the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the tangible? Is the bodhisattva in the tangible, or is the tangible in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva without the tangible? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the phenomenon (dharma) the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the phenomenon? Is the bodhisattva in the phenomenon, or is the phenomenon in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva without the phenomenon?"
What do you think, Subhūti? Is the bodhisattva other than the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness; or is he in them; or is there a bodhisattva apart from the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva other than the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness, or is he within them?
Is he a bodhisattva apart from the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva other than the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness, or is he within them?
Are these—the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness—apart from the Bodhisattva?

What do you think, Subhūti: are the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness the Bodhisattva, or is he elsewhere than in them, or is he the Bodhisattva apart from the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva apart from body, tangibles, and body-consciousness, or is he in them; or is there a bodhisattva without body, tangibles, and body-consciousness?
What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva apart from mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness, or is he in them?
"Are these, in the absence of mind, mental phenomena, and mental consciousness, what is called a 'bodhisattva'?
Subhūti replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is the earth element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the earth element? In that case, is the bodhisattva within the bodhisattva the earth element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the earth element?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the water element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the water element? In that case, is the bodhisattva within the bodhisattva the water element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the water element?"

What do you think, Subhūti? Is the fire element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the fire element? In that case, is the bodhisattva within the bodhisattva the fire element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the fire element? What do you think, Subhūti? Is the wind element the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from the wind element? In that case, is the bodhisattva within the bodhisattva the wind element, or is the bodhisattva one who is not the wind element?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is space the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva elsewhere than space? In that regard, is the bodhisattva in the bodhisattva [identical to] space, or is the bodhisattva one who is not space? What do you think, Subhūti? Is consciousness the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva elsewhere than consciousness? In that regard, is the bodhisattva in the bodhisattva [identical to] consciousness, or is the bodhisattva one who is not consciousness? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva ignorance, or is a bodhisattva apart from ignorance? Is a bodhisattva in ignorance, or is ignorance in the bodhisattva? Or is it that 'a bodhisattva is one who is without ignorance'?"

What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), or is a bodhisattva apart from the formative forces, or is a bodhisattva within the formative forces, or are the formative forces within a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is without formative forces?

What do you think, Subhūti: is consciousness (*vijñāna*) a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva apart from consciousness, or is a bodhisattva within consciousness, or is consciousness within a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is without consciousness?

What do you think, Subhūti: is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva apart from name-and-form, or is a bodhisattva within name-and-form, or is name-and-form within a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is without name-and-form?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is a bodhisattva the six sense-bases, or is a bodhisattva apart from the six sense-bases; is the bodhisattva in the six sense-bases, or are the six sense-bases in the bodhisattva; or is the bodhisattva one who does not have the six sense-bases? What do you think, Subhūti? Is contact the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from contact; is the bodhisattva in contact, or is contact in the bodhisattva; or is the bodhisattva one who does not have contact? What do you think, Subhūti? Is feeling the bodhisattva, or is the bodhisattva apart from feeling; is the bodhisattva in feeling, or is feeling in the bodhisattva; or is the bodhisattva one who does not have feeling?"

What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva craving, or is a bodhisattva apart from craving; is a bodhisattva in craving, or is craving in a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is neither craving nor non-craving?

What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva grasping, or is a bodhisattva apart from grasping; is a bodhisattva in grasping, or is grasping in a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is without grasping?

What do you think, Subhūti: is a bodhisattva becoming, or is a bodhisattva apart from becoming; is a bodhisattva in becoming, or is a bodhisattva in a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva a bodhisattva who is both becoming and non-becoming?

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is birth the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than birth? Is the Bodhisattva in birth, or is birth in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva non-birth? "What do you think, Subhūti? Is aging-and-death the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than aging-and-death? Is the Bodhisattva in aging-and-death, or is aging-and-death in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva free from aging-and-death? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of form the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of form? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of form? Is the suchness of form in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva the suchness of non-form? What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of feeling the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of feeling? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of feeling? Is the suchness of feeling in the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva the suchness of non-feeling?

Regarding "bodhisattva": what do you think, Subhūti, is that which is the suchness of perception the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of perception? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of perception? Is the suchness of perception in the bodhisattva? Or is the bodhisattva the suchness of non-perception? Is he the bodhisattva?

What do you think, Subhūti: is that which is the suchness of formations (*saṃskāra-tathatā*) the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of formations? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of formations, or is the suchness of formations in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of formations, or is the suchness of formations the Bodhisattva? What do you think, Subhūti: is that which is the suchness of consciousness (*vijñāna-tathatā*) the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of consciousness? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of consciousness, or is the suchness of consciousness in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of consciousness...
“Is a bodhisattva one who does not cognize suchness?
Subhūti replied, “Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? If there is no bodhisattva in the individual aggregates, nor in them taken together, then is that which is the suchness of the aggregates the bodhisattva? Or is the bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the aggregates, or within the suchness of the aggregates?"
"Is the suchness of the aggregates in a bodhisattva the suchness of non-aggregates, [such that] he is called a 'bodhisattva'?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness? Or is the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness within the Bodhisattva, or the Bodhisattva within the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness?"
Is it that the suchness of the eye, forms, and visual consciousness is the Bodhisattva?

Likewise, is it that the suchness of the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness; the suchness of the nose, odors, and olfactory consciousness; the suchness of the tongue, tastes, and gustatory consciousness;
the suchness of the body, tangibles, and tactile consciousness; and the suchness of the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness—that is the Bodhisattva, and nothing other than that?

"Is the suchness of mind, phenomena, and mental consciousness, within the suchness of mind, phenomena, and mental consciousness, the Bodhisattva; and is the Bodhisattva, within the Bodhisattva, the suchness of mind, phenomena, and mental consciousness, yet not the suchness of mind, phenomena, and mental consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the earth element the Bodhisattva, apart from the suchness of the earth element?"
"In the suchness of the earth element, is there a bodhisattva, or is the suchness of the earth element not the suchness of a bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the water element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than in the suchness of the water element? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the water element? Is the suchness of the water element in the Bodhisattva? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the water element?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the fire element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the fire element? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the fire element? Is the suchness of the fire element in the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva the suchness of the fire element, or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the fire element? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the wind-element the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the wind-element?"
"In the suchness of the wind element, is there a bodhisattva, or is a bodhisattva the suchness of the wind element, or is a bodhisattva not the suchness of the wind element?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the element of space the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of the element of space?
Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of the element of space? Is the suchness of the element of space in the bodhisattva? Or is the bodhisattva not the suchness of the element of space?"
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the consciousness-element the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the consciousness-element?

Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the consciousness-element? Is the suchness of the consciousness-element in the Bodhisattva? Or is it that the suchness of the consciousness-element is the Bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"

Subhūti, if the Bodhisattva does not exist in the elements taken individually, nor in them taken collectively—then what is the suchness of the elements, that is the Bodhisattva; is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the elements, or is the suchness of the elements other than the suchness of the elements, or is the Bodhisattva other than the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of the elements? Or is the suchness of the elements other than the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements?

Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Is the Bodhisattva [merely] the suchness of the elements? Or is the Bodhisattva not the suchness of the elements? Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of the eye the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of the eye? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the eye, or is the suchness of the eye in the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva without the suchness of the eye? In the same way, [consider] that which is the suchness of the ear, the suchness of the nose, the suchness of the tongue, and the suchness of the body.

"What do you think, Subhūti: is that which is the suchness of the mind the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the mind? Is the Bodhisattva in the suchness of the mind, or is the suchness of the mind in the Bodhisattva? Or is the Bodhisattva the suchness of the mind, or the suchness of the mind the Bodhisattva? Subhūti said:

"Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of form (rūpa-tathatā) the bodhisattva? Is the bodhisattva other than the suchness of form? Is the bodhisattva in the suchness of form? Or is the suchness of form in the bodhisattva? Is it the suchness of non-form (arūpa-tathatā)?"

What is a "bodhisattva"? That which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena is the bodhisattva; apart from the suchness of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena, there is no bodhisattva.
Within the suchness of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena is the bodhisattva, and within the bodhisattva is the suchness of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena.
“Is a bodhisattva the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena?
Subhūti replied,
“Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, if the Bodhisattva does not exist in the sense-bases taken individually, nor in them taken collectively—then, Subhūti, that which is the suchness of the sense-bases is the Bodhisattva; apart from the suchness of the sense-bases there is no Bodhisattva, and within the suchness of the sense-bases there is the Bodhisattva."
"Is a bodhisattva the suchness of non-bases?
Subhūti replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the suchness of ignorance the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva elsewhere than the suchness of ignorance? Is the suchness of ignorance within the suchness of ignorance, or is the Bodhisattva within the Bodhisattva, or is the suchness of ignorance not the suchness of ignorance, or is the Bodhisattva not the Bodhisattva?"

In this way, that which is the suchness of formative forces (*saṃskāra-tathatā*), the suchness of consciousness (*vijñāna-tathatā*), the suchness of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-tathatā*), the suchness of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana-tathatā*), the suchness of contact (*sparśa-tathatā*), the suchness of feeling (*vedanā-tathatā*), the suchness of craving (*tṛṣṇā-tathatā*), the suchness of grasping (*upādāna-tathatā*), and the suchness of becoming (*bhava-tathatā*)—what do you think, Subhūti, is that which is the suchness of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa-tathatā*) the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of aging-and-death? Is the Bodhisattva within the suchness of aging-and-death? Or is the suchness of aging-and-death the Bodhisattva?
Or is the Bodhisattva the suchness of aging-and-death, or the absence of the suchness of aging-and-death?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti: if there is no Bodhisattva in the individual members of dependent origination, nor in them collectively, then is that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of dependent origination the Bodhisattva? Is the Bodhisattva other than the suchness of dependent origination?
Is the Bodhisattva within the suchness of dependent origination? Or is the suchness of dependent origination the Bodhisattva, or is the Bodhisattva the suchness of non-dependent origination?
Subhūti said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, Subhūti, for what reason do you say this:
that "form is not a bodhisattva," nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; nor the earth element, nor the water element, nor the fire element?

Neither the wind element, nor the space element, nor the consciousness element; neither forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental phenomena; neither the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind.

There is no eye, no form, no eye-consciousness; no ear, no sound, no ear-consciousness; no nose, no odor, no nose-consciousness; no tongue, no taste, no tongue-consciousness; no body, no tangible object, no body-consciousness; no mind, no mental phenomenon, no mind-consciousness.

Likewise, there is no ignorance, and thus no volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, aging, and death—nor is there a "bodhisattva."
As long as it is not the case that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination are the bodhisattva;
nor is the suchness of form the bodhisattva; nor is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, nor the suchness of mental formations [the bodhisattva].

The suchness of consciousness, up to and including the suchness of the earth element, the suchness of the water element, the suchness of the fire element, the suchness of the wind element, the suchness of the space element, and the suchness of the consciousness element;
the suchness of the eye, the suchness of the ear, the suchness of the nose, the suchness of the tongue, the suchness of the body, and the suchness of the mind;
the suchness of form, the suchness of sound, the suchness of odor, the suchness of taste, the suchness of the tangible, and the suchness of mental phenomena.

There is no such thing as the suchness of the eye, forms, or eye-consciousness; no such thing as the suchness of the ear, sounds, or ear-consciousness; no such thing as the suchness of the nose, odors, or nose-consciousness; no such thing as the suchness of the tongue, tastes, or tongue-consciousness; no such thing as the suchness of the body, tangibles, or body-consciousness; no such thing as the suchness of the mind, mental phenomena, or mind-consciousness.

There is no such thing as the suchness of ignorance, no such thing as the suchness of formative predispositions, no such thing as the suchness of consciousness, no such thing as the suchness of name-and-form, and no such thing as the suchness of the six sense bases.

There is no such thing as the suchness of contact, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of craving, the suchness of grasping, the suchness of becoming, the suchness of birth, or the suchness of old age and death; nor is there the suchness of the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields, nor the suchness of dependent origination that is called a "bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
Blessed One, since a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended,
how could form be a bodhisattva? How could feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be a bodhisattva?
Ultimately, Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended. How then could the earth element be a bodhisattva?
Likewise, how could the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element be a bodhisattva?
Ultimately, Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended.
How then could form be a bodhisattva? Likewise, how could sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena be a bodhisattva?
Likewise, how could the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind be a bodhisattva?
Blessed One, since a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended, how could the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness be a bodhisattva?
Likewise, how could the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness; the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; or the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness be a bodhisattva?
The body, tangibles, and body-consciousness,
as well as the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness— these will be the Bodhisattva.
Yet, O Blessed One, a Bodhisattva is ultimately neither found nor perceived.

How then could ignorance be a bodhisattva? Likewise, how could volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death be a bodhisattva?
Blessed One, since a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended, how then could the suchness of form be apprehended for him?
The suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness will be apprehended.
Yet, Blessed One, since a bodhisattva ultimately does not exist and is not apprehended,
how could the suchness of his earth element be apprehended?
In this way, the water element, fire element, air element, space element, consciousness element, and the suchness of these will not be apprehended.
Since, Blessed One, a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended, how could his suchness of form be apprehended?
In this way, the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena will be apprehended;
in this way, the suchness of the eye, the suchness of the ear, the suchness of the nose, the suchness of the tongue, the suchness of the body, and the suchness of the mind will be apprehended;
in this way, the suchness of the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness will be apprehended.

In this way, the suchness of the ear, sound, and ear-consciousness; the suchness of the nose, odor, and nose-consciousness; the suchness of the tongue, taste, and tongue-consciousness; the suchness of the body, tangible objects, and body-consciousness; and the suchness of the mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness will not be apprehended.
Since, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense, how could the suchness of ignorance be apprehended for him?

In this way, O Blessed One, the suchness of volitional formations, the suchness of consciousness, the suchness of name-and-form, the suchness of the six sense bases, the suchness of contact, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of craving, the suchness of grasping, and the suchness of becoming— thus, in each individual case among the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, whether taken separately or collectively, a bodhisattva absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended. How then could the suchness of these aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination be apprehended?
This is not possible.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom through the non-apprehension of sentient beings.
Thus the Blessed One spoke regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
"What do you think, Subhūti, is 'bodhisattva' a designation for form?
Is 'bodhisattva' a designation for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is it a designation for the permanence of form or for the impermanence of form that one says 'bodhisattva'?"
Is "bodhisattva" a designation for the pleasantness of form, the painfulness of form, the selfhood of form, the non-selfhood of form, the peacefulness of form, or the non-peacefulness of form?

What do you think, Subhūti—is "bodhisattva" a designation for the impermanence of feeling, the impermanence of feeling; is it a designation for the pleasantness of feeling, the painfulness of feeling, the selfhood of feeling, the non-selfhood of feeling, the peacefulness of feeling, or the non-peacefulness of feeling?

What do you think, Subhūti, is "bodhisattva" a designation for the permanence of perception, or for the impermanence of perception; is "bodhisattva" a designation for the pleasure of perception, the suffering of perception, the selfhood of perception, the selflessness of perception, the peace of perception, or the non-peace of perception?
What do you think, Subhūti, is "bodhisattva" a designation for the permanence of volitional formations, or for the impermanence of volitional formations?

"Bodhisattva" is a designation for the pleasantness of conditioned phenomena, the suffering of conditioned phenomena, the selfhood of conditioned phenomena, the non-selfhood of conditioned phenomena, the peace of conditioned phenomena, and the lack of peace of conditioned phenomena.
What do you think, Subhūti—is "Bodhisattva" a designation for the permanence of consciousness, or for the impermanence of consciousness?

Is "Bodhisattva" a designation for the pleasantness of consciousness, the suffering of consciousness, the selfhood of consciousness, the non-selfhood of consciousness, the peace of consciousness, or the lack of peace of consciousness?

What do you think, Subhūti? Is this a designation for the emptiness of form, the non-emptiness of form, the sign-ness of form, the signlessness of form, the wishlessness of form, or the wishlessness of form? And likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations?
What do you think, Subhūti? Is this a designation for the emptiness of consciousness, the non-emptiness of consciousness, or the sign-ness of consciousness?
“Is ‘bodhisattva’ a designation for the signlessness of consciousness, the wishlessness of consciousness, and the absence of aspiration regarding consciousness? Subhūti replied,
“Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"But, Subhūti, for what reason do you say this: that 'Bodhisattva' is neither a designation for the permanence of form nor a designation for its impermanence?"

Thus, "Bodhisattva" is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; it is not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self; it is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for lack of peace; it is not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; and it is not a designation for the aspiration regarding form, nor a designation for the absence of aspiration.
A bodhisattva is not a designation for the permanence of feeling, nor is he a designation for its impermanence;
likewise, he is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self;
not a designation for peace, nor a designation for lack of peace; not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; nor is he a designation for signs.

A "bodhisattva" is not a designation for the signless, nor is it a designation for the absence of aspiration regarding feeling, nor is it a designation for the absence of aspiration regarding perception; likewise, it is not a designation for permanence, nor is it a designation for impermanence regarding perception;
in the same way, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor is it a designation for suffering, nor is it a designation for self, nor is it a designation for non-self.

"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for non-peace; it is not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; it is not a designation for the willed of perception, nor a designation for the unwilled.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the permanence of conditioned phenomena, nor a designation for their impermanence.
Thus, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering; not a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self;

not a designation for peace, nor a designation for non-peace; not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; and not a designation for the conditioned as being with wish, nor a designation for the conditioned as being without wish.
"Bodhisattva" is not a designation for the permanence of consciousness, nor is "bodhisattva" a designation for its impermanence;
likewise, it is not a designation for pleasure, nor a designation for suffering, nor a designation for self, nor a designation for non-self.

"A Bodhisattva" is not a designation for peace, nor a designation for non-peace; it is not a designation for emptiness, nor a designation for non-emptiness; it is not a designation for signs, nor a designation for signlessness; it is not a designation for the directedness of consciousness, nor a designation for the lack of directedness.
Subhūti said:
Blessed One, form does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be a bodhisattva who is a designation for form?
Blessed One, feeling does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
How could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for feeling?
Blessed One, since perception does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense,
how could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for perception?
O Blessed One, conditioned phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be a "bodhisattva" as a designation for conditioned phenomena?
O Blessed One, consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
How could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for consciousness?
Blessed One, since it absolutely and eternally does not exist and is not apprehended,
how could there be the designation "bodhisattva" for the permanence of form?
“Blessed One, that which is ultimately impermanent does not exist and is not apprehended;
how then could a bodhisattva be a designation for the impermanence of form?
Likewise, there is no designation for pleasure, no designation for suffering, no designation for self, and no designation for non-self.”

A bodhisattva will not be one who has the designation "peace," nor one who has the designation "non-peace"; not one who has the designation "emptiness," nor one who has the designation "non-emptiness"; not one who has the designation "sign," nor one who has the designation "signless"; not one who has the designation "wishless," nor one who has the designation "non-wishless.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Blessed One, since permanence does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense,

how could there be a designation for the permanence of consciousness that would constitute a bodhisattva? Blessed One, since impermanence does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense, [how could there be a designation for the impermanence of consciousness that would constitute a bodhisattva?]
From where could there be a designation for the impermanence of consciousness that would be a bodhisattva?
Likewise, there is no designation for pleasure, no designation for suffering, no designation for self, no designation for non-self, no designation for peace, no designation for non-peace,
no designation for emptiness, no designation for non-emptiness, no designation for signs, no designation for signlessness, no designation for the wishless, and no designation for the non-wishless.
"He will become a bodhisattva.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend the designation of form, does not apprehend the designation of feeling, does not apprehend the designation of perception, does not apprehend the designation of formations, and does not apprehend the designation of consciousness.

By one who does not perceive the designation of form as permanent or impermanent; by one who does not perceive the designation of pleasure or pain; by one who does not perceive the designation of self or non-self; by one who does not perceive the designation of peace or lack of peace; by one who does not perceive the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness; by one who does not perceive the designation of sign or signlessness; by one who does not perceive the designation of the wishless or the non-wishless.

By one who does not perceive the designation of feeling as permanent or impermanent; by one who does not perceive the designation of pleasure or pain; by one who does not perceive the designation of self or non-self; by one who does not perceive the designation of peace or non-peace; by one who does not perceive the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness; by one who does not perceive the designation of sign or signlessness; and by one who does not perceive the designation of the wishless or the non-wishless.

Not perceiving the designation of permanence or impermanence regarding perception; not perceiving the designation of pleasure or pain; not perceiving the designation of self or non-self; not perceiving the designation of peace or non-peace; not perceiving the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness; not perceiving the designation of the signless or non-signless; and not perceiving the designation of the wishless or non-wishless.

By one who does not perceive the designation of formations as permanent or impermanent; by one who does not perceive the designation of pleasure or pain; by one who does not perceive the designation of self or non-self; by one who does not perceive the designation of peace or non-peace; by one who does not perceive the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness; by one who does not perceive the designation of the marked or the unmarked; by one who does not perceive the designation of the wishless or the non-wishless.

One should train in the perfection of wisdom by not apprehending the designation of consciousness as permanent or impermanent; by not apprehending the designation of pleasure or pain; by not apprehending the designation of self or non-self; by not apprehending the designation of peace or non-peace; by not apprehending the designation of emptiness or non-emptiness; by not apprehending the designation of the signless or non-signless; and by not apprehending the designation of the wishless or non-wishless.
Thus is the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as to what you said: "I do not perceive that dharma which is called a 'bodhisattva,'" [it is so].
For indeed, Subhūti, a phenomenon does not perceive the realm of phenomena,
nor does the realm of phenomena perceive a phenomenon.
This is the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
Subhūti, the form-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the form-element;
Subhūti, the feeling-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the feeling-element;
nor, Subhūti, does the perception-element perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the perception-element.
Subhūti, the element of formations does not perceive the element of phenomena, nor does the element of phenomena perceive the element of formations;
Subhūti, the element of consciousness does not perceive the element of phenomena.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the consciousness-element;
nor does the eye-element perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the eye-element.
The ear-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the ear-element;
the nose-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the nose-element;
nor does the tongue-element perceive the dharma-element;
nor does the dharma-element perceive the tongue-element.
The body-element does not perceive the dharma-element,
nor does the dharma-element perceive the body-element;
the mind-element does not perceive the dharma-element.
Nor does the dharma-element perceive the mind-element.
This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
Subhūti, the conditioned realm does not perceive the unconditioned realm, nor does the unconditioned realm perceive the conditioned realm.
This is the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
Thus concludes the instruction on the path of seeing.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is not possible to designate the unconditioned apart from the conditioned, nor is it possible to designate the conditioned apart from the unconditioned.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever;
not perceiving them, he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror,
nor does his mind retreat from any dharma.
His mind does not become remorseful. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling.
He does not perceive perception; he does not perceive volitional formations; he does not perceive consciousness.
He does not perceive the eye; he does not perceive the ear;
he does not perceive the nose.
He does not perceive the tongue;
he does not perceive the body; he does not perceive the mind.
He does not perceive forms, he does not perceive sounds,
he does not perceive odors.
He does not perceive tastes, he does not perceive tangibles, and he does not perceive mental phenomena.
He does not perceive the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element.
He does not perceive ignorance;

he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
He does not perceive passion,
he does not perceive hatred,
and he does not perceive delusion.
He does not perceive a self;
he does not perceive a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a progenitor, or a beholder.
He does not perceive the realm of desire.
He does not perceive the realm of form,
he does not perceive the formless realm,
and he does not perceive the realm of space.
He does not perceive a śrāvaka, he does not perceive a pratyekabuddha,
and he does not perceive a bodhisattva.
He does not perceive the dharmas of the śrāvakas; he does not perceive the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas;
he does not perceive the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
One does not perceive a Buddha,
one does not perceive the qualities of a Buddha,
and one does not perceive awakening.
As long as one does not perceive any phenomena,
by not perceiving any phenomena,
one is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become cowed or dejected?
The Blessed One replied:

For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend and does not perceive mental states and mental factors. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva neither shrinks back nor becomes despondent.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how is it that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble?
The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva neither perceives nor observes the mind or the mind-element.”

For in this way, Subhūti, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble. For in this way, Subhūti, having realized that all dharmas are unapprehendable, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend that perfection of wisdom nor perceive it, nor does he perceive that bodhisattva—
And one does not apprehend nor perceive that name "bodhisattva" nor that thought of awakening;
this indeed is the instruction for a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom, this indeed is the admonition.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand form must train in the perfection of wisdom;
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand feeling must train in the perfection of wisdom."
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand perception (*saṃjñā*) should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva who wishes to fully understand consciousness (*vijñāna*) [should train in the perfection of wisdom].
A great being should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the eye should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the ear should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the nose should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the tongue should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavān, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the body should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand the mind should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand form should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand sound should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand odor should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand taste should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand touch should train in the perfection of wisdom.
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand phenomena (dharma) should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand eye-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom;
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand ear-consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand olfactory consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand gustatory consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom;
O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand tactile consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand mental consciousness should train in the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand visual contact and the feeling born of visual contact should train in the perfection of wisdom;
[likewise] auditory contact and the feeling born of auditory contact.
nose-contact and the feeling born of nose-contact; tongue-contact and the feeling born of tongue-contact;
body-contact and the feeling born of body-contact;
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully understand mental contact and the feeling born of mental contact should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon passion, hatred, and delusion should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

Thus, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*)— as well as the fetters (*saṃyojana*), underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and outbursts (*paryutthāna*)— should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon the four bonds (*yoga*), the floods (*ogha*), the knots (*grantha*), the clingings (*upādāna*), and the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) should train in the perfection of wisdom.

O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon the ten unwholesome paths of action and who wishes to fully understand the ten wholesome paths of action should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Likewise, they should train] in the four meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness.

O Blessed One, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four analytical knowledges, the four grounds of self-confidence, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the samādhi called the limb of enlightenment should train in the perfection of wisdom.
[Likewise, one who wishes to attain] the Lion’s Play samādhi...
the lion’s sport samādhi, the samādhi of the gateway to all dhāraṇīs, and the śūraṅgama samādhi;
the Ratnamudrā samādhi,
the Candraprabha samādhi, and the Candradhvajaketu samādhi;
the samādhi that has reached the seal of all phenomena, the samādhi of the Avalokita-seal,
and the samādhi fixed in the realm of phenomena;
the concentration called Fixed Banner and Crest,
the diamond-like concentration,
and the concentration called the Entrance Door to All Dharmas;
the Samādhirāja concentration,
the Gaganagañjamudrā concentration, and the Balaviśuddha concentration;
the Samudgata concentration, the Sarvadharmaniruktiniyatapraveśa concentration,
and the Sarvadharmajñānamudrāpraveśa concentration;

the concentration on the entrance to the dhāraṇī of the seal of all dharmas, the concentration on the non-forgetfulness of all dharmas, and the concentration on the seal of the aspect of the convergence of all dharmas; (PvsP1-1: 150)
the concentration, the space-abiding concentration, the concentration of the purity of the three spheres,
and the concentration of the superknowledge that follows the non-falling [state].
the samādhi called Receptacle-Attained, the samādhi called Crest-Jewel of the Banner,
and the samādhi called Incinerator of All Afflictions;
the concentration that shatters the power of the four Māras,
the concentration of the torch of wisdom,
and the concentration arisen from the ten powers;

“O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the samādhi named ‘The Unstained Explanation of the Non-attachment of Space,’ as well as these and other gateways to samādhi, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the intentions of all sentient beings should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fulfill all roots of goodness— by means of which fulfilled roots of goodness one is not reborn in the miserable states, nor reborn in low families, and does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha— [should train in this perfection of wisdom].
Furthermore, one should train in the perfection of wisdom so as not to fall from the summit of the bodhisattva’s path.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fall from the summit?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being unskilled in means while practicing the six perfections and not knowing skill in means, relies upon the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he does not [fall] to the level of a śrāvaka..."
He neither falls to the level of a pratyekabuddha nor does he enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
this is called the "summit" of the bodhisattva.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, is this called the 'rawness' (āma) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, 'rawness' refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva's craving for dharmas."
Thus ends the instruction on the path of cultivation.
Having thus spoken regarding the instructions, Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*)?
Subhūti replied:

"In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not become attached to, does not rely upon, and does not adhere to [the notion] that 'form is impermanent.'"
He perceives that suffering is empty and selfless, yet he does not become attached to it, does not dwell upon it, and does not perceive it as such;
he does not become attached to the idea that form is empty or wishless, nor does he dwell upon it or perceive it as such;
[likewise] regarding feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He does not adhere to, does not dwell upon, and does not perceive that "consciousness is impermanent";
he does not adhere to, does not dwell upon, and does not perceive that "it is suffering, empty, and selfless";
he does not adhere to, does not dwell upon, and does not perceive that "consciousness is empty" or "it is wishless. This, venerable Śāriputra, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s conformable [wisdom].
Craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is "raw.
Thus, within the context of the Truth of Suffering, this is the specific distinction of the object and aspect of the "mild heat" (*mṛdu-uṣmagata*) stage:
one does not become attached, does not persist in, and does not perceive [the thought] that "form is to be abandoned" or "by this [means], form is to be abandoned."
In this way feeling is to be abandoned; by this means feeling is to be abandoned.
In this way perception is to be abandoned; by this means perception is to be abandoned.
In this way formations are to be abandoned; by this means formations are to be abandoned.

Thus, one does not become attached to, does not rely upon, and does not perceive [the notion]: "consciousness is to be abandoned; by this means consciousness is to be abandoned. Likewise, one does not become attached to, does not rely upon, and does not perceive [the notion]: "suffering is to be fully understood; by this means suffering is to be fully understood.
Similarly, one does not become attached to, does not rely upon, and does not perceive [the notion]: "origination is to be abandoned; by this means origination is to be abandoned."

Thus, within the section concerning the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), there is the specific distinction of the object and aspect for one who has attained the "mild" stage of heat (*mṛdu-uṣmagata*):
"In this way cessation is to be realized; by this [path] cessation is to be realized";
"In this way the path is to be cultivated; by this [path] the path is to be cultivated."
"This is affliction, this is purification";
"these phenomena are to be cultivated, these phenomena are not to be cultivated";
"one should practice here, one should not practice there."
"This path is to be cultivated; this is not to be cultivated.
This is the training of a bodhisattva; this is non-training.
This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva."
This is the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience;
this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor.
This is the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation;
this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom;
this is not the bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity.
This is not the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline;
this is not the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience;
this is not the bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor.

He does not become attached to, does not dwell upon, and does not perceive [the thought]: "This is the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom; this is the bodhisattva’s skill in means; this is a lack of skill in means. This is the bodhisattva’s summit.

"Venerable Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not thus adhere to, dwell upon, or perceive these phenomena, this is the bodhisattva’s conformable craving for the Dharma; it is raw. Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, what is the 'entry into the certainty' (*nyāma*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Subhūti replied:
"In this regard, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive external emptiness by means of internal emptiness."
One does not perceive internal emptiness by means of external emptiness;
one does not perceive internal-external emptiness by means of external emptiness;
nor does one perceive external emptiness by means of internal-external emptiness.
He does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness by means of internal-and-external emptiness;
he does not perceive internal-and-external emptiness by means of the emptiness of emptiness;
he does not perceive great emptiness by means of the emptiness of emptiness.
One does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness by means of the great emptiness;
one does not perceive the emptiness of the ultimate by means of the great emptiness; nor does one perceive the great emptiness by means of the emptiness of the ultimate.
He does not perceive conditioned emptiness by means of ultimate emptiness;
he does not perceive ultimate emptiness by means of conditioned emptiness;
he does not perceive unconditioned emptiness by means of conditioned emptiness.
One does not perceive conditioned emptiness by means of unconditioned emptiness;
one does not perceive ultimate emptiness by means of unconditioned emptiness;
nor does one perceive unconditioned emptiness by means of ultimate emptiness.

One does not perceive the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end through the emptiness of the absolute; one does not perceive the emptiness of the absolute through the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end;
