He will teach, proclaim, analyze, clarify, and fully illuminate these very kinds of discourses: the *geya*, the *vyākaraṇa*, the *gāthā*, the *udāna*, the *nidāna*, the *itivṛttaka*, the *jātaka*, the *vaipulya*, the *adbhutadharma*, and the *avadānopadeśa*.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if one does not understand the deeds of Māra when they have been explained, this too should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Moreover, Subhūti, having approached a bodhisattva mahāsattva, someone will speak to him thus:

"Son of good family, you do not possess any thought of awakening (bodhicitta) at all, nor are you irreversible, nor will you be able to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
since you do not recognize these kinds of deeds of Māra that have been described.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a spiritual friend of ill omen (pāpamitra) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti, someone may approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a Buddha and say:
"Noble son, the eye is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self."
Form is empty of self and of what belongs to self;
likewise, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of self and of what belongs to self;
eye-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to self.

In this way, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; eye-contact is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;
likewise, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self.
Feeling conditioned by eye-contact is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self;

likewise, feeling conditioned by ear-contact, feeling conditioned by nose-contact, feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, feeling conditioned by body-contact, and feeling conditioned by mind-contact are empty of a self and of what belongs to a self.
The perfection of generosity is empty of self and of what belongs to self;

likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are empty of self and of what belongs to self;
the applications of mindfulness are empty of self and of what belongs to self.

In this way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the paths—even up to the unique qualities of a Buddha—are empty of both a self and what belongs to a self.
What will you achieve by awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment if you do not point out and teach such deeds of Māra?
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a pratyekabuddha and say:
"Son of good family, the eastern direction is empty of Buddhas, Blessed Ones, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas; here there is no Buddha, no awakening, no bodhisattva, and no śrāvaka.
Likewise, all ten directions are empty."
By the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, and the Śrāvakas, it has been taught that herein there is no Buddha, no awakening, no Bodhisattva, and no Śrāvaka;
those who do not point out such deeds of Māra as these, Subhūti, should be known as the evil friends of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a śramaṇa, will divert a bodhisattva mahāsattva from the mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects and will instruct and advise them with mental engagements associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti, one who does not point out such a deed of Māra as this should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a preceptor or a teacher, [addresses] a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
He will cause him to turn away from the conduct of a bodhisattva; he will cause him to turn away from mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects;

he will urge him toward the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; and he will urge him toward emptiness, the signless, and the wishless, saying:
"Having realized these very dharmas, realize the stage of a śrāvaka!"
"What will he do for you toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he who does not point out nor teach such deeds of Māra as these?
Subhūti, this should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s evil friend.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a mother or father, will speak thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva:"

"Come, son of good family, apply yourself to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; apply yourself to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. What is the use of your awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, for the sake of which you have wandered through saṃsāra for incalculable and immeasurable eons?"

Subhūti, one who does not instruct or explain such deeds of Māra as these— deeds by which one wandering in saṃsāra must experience the cutting off of hands and the cutting off of feet— should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a monk, will teach that form is impermanent by way of apprehension;

he will teach that form is suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension; and he will teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus he will teach by way of apprehension;
he will teach that consciousness is suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
he will teach that the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent, suffering, non-self, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension.
In this way, up to the applications of mindfulness, he will teach that they are impermanent, suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by means of apprehension;

likewise, he will teach that the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are impermanent, suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless.
Even as far as the Buddha-qualities, he will teach that they are impermanent, suffering, selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, and wishless by way of apprehension;
and whoever does not point out or declare such deeds of Māra— Subhūti, this too should be known as a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and having recognized him, he should be avoided.
Thus ends the second section on being accompanied by a spiritual friend.
Having thus explained the fourfold limb of penetration, Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, it is said 'bodhisattva, bodhisattva. Blessed One, what is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Blessed One replied:
The term "bodhisattva," Subhūti, is a term for a non-entity. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, neither the arising of awakening nor its existence or non-existence is found or perceived;
therefore, Subhūti, the term "bodhisattva" is a term for a non-entity.
Such is the essential nature of the lineage (*gotra*).
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the track of a bird in the sky is neither found nor perceived;
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
Subhūti, just as, for example, the track of a dream does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
just as, for example, Subhūti, the track of an illusion does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
just as, Subhūti, the track of a mirage does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as there is no locus for an echo, a reflection, an image, a city of the Gandharvas, or a magical creation, and these are not perceived, even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not perceived.
This is the support for the stage of Heat (uṣmagata).
Subhūti, just as, for example, no trace of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) exists and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
just as, for example, Subhūti, no trace of suchness (tathatā) exists and is not apprehended.

In the same way, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended; likewise, the referent of the term for suchness, non-erroneous suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and truth (*satyatā*) does not exist and is not apprehended.
In this very way, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Thus is the support for reaching the summit.
Subhūti, just as, for example, no track of the form of an illusory person exists and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for feeling, perception, and mental formations, and just as for the consciousness of an illusory person no track is found and nothing is apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" is found and nothing is apprehended.
Subhūti, just as, for example, the referent of the eye of an illusory person does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
and the same is true for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of a phantom person’s mind does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of a phantom person’s forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, for an illusory person, the referents of the terms "eye," "form," and "eye-consciousness" do not exist and are not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

In the same way, Subhūti, the referent of the ear, sounds, ear-consciousness; the nose, odors, nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness; and the body, tangibles, body-consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, for example, Subhūti, the referent of the mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness of an illusory person does not exist and is not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Thus is the basis for those who have attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Subhūti, just as for an illusory person practicing in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended in a phantom person practicing external emptiness;
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended in a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended in a phantom person practicing internal-and-external emptiness.

In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended; this should be understood in detail.
Just as, Subhūti, for an illusory person practicing in the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, Subhūti, for an illusory person there is no such thing in the perfections, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a buddha, the aggregates, the elements, or the sense-fields.
While practicing the dependent originations, the meditations, the formless attainments, and the superknowledges, the referent-object of "bodhisattva" is neither found nor apprehended;
in the same way, Subhūti, while a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of "bodhisattva" is neither found nor apprehended.
This is the support for those who have reached the supreme dharmas.
Subhūti, just as, for example, the referent of the term "form" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, just as, for example, the referent of the terms "feeling," "perception," "formative predispositions," and "consciousness" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended in a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, just as, for example, the referent of the term "eye" does not exist and is not apprehended in a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha...
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the referents of the terms "ear," "nose," "tongue," "body," and "mind" do not exist and are not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, just as the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor apprehended in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while practicing from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence,
even so, Subhūti, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor apprehended in a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, just as, for example, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha courses in all the factors conducive to enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the term "conditioned realm" does not exist and is not apprehended within the unconditioned realm,
and the term "unconditioned realm" does not exist and is not apprehended within the conditioned realm;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Thus is the basis for the path of seeing.
Subhūti, just as the referent of the term "non-arising" does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, just as, for example, the referent-objects of non-ceasing, non-conditioning, non-manifestation, non-apprehension, and non-defilement do not exist and are not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended; just as, for example, Subhūti, the referent-object of non-purification does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the referent of the term "arising" of form does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the referent of "arising" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Why is that?
Subhūti, regarding form, the category of phenomena consisting of cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction does not exist and is not apprehended;

Subhūti, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the category of phenomena consisting of cessation, volitional formation, manifestation, apprehension, and affliction does not exist and is not apprehended.
Why is that?
Subhūti, the referent of the purification of form does not exist and is not apprehended;
Subhūti, the referent of the purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the very same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the entity of arising does not exist and is not apprehended in the individual or collective aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination;
and so on, up to the point that the entity of purification does not exist and is not apprehended within the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination.

In the same way, the entity of arising does not exist [for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the analytical knowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities].
In this way, up to the point where the referent-object of purification does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, the referent-objects of the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to the referent-objects of affliction and purification, do not exist and are not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Just as, Subhūti, because form is absolutely secluded, the referent of the term "sign" does not exist and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Of feeling, perception, and mental formations— just as, Subhūti, because consciousness is absolutely secluded, no basis for signs exists and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in the case of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination—whether taken individually or collectively—a basis for signs does not exist and is not apprehended because they are absolutely secluded;
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in the case of the applications of mindfulness, a basis for signs does not exist and is not apprehended because they are absolutely pure.

In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent-object of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended; likewise, because the right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, immeasurables, meditative concentrations, formless attainments, superknowledges, analytical knowledges, ten powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a buddha are absolutely pure, the referent-object of signs does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.

Just as, Subhūti, in the purification of the self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer, no footprint exists and is not apprehended—
on account of the non-existence of the self, the sentient being, the living soul, the nourisher, the person, the individual, the human, the man, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
This is the basis of the path of cultivation.
Just as, Subhūti, when the sun rises, no footprint of its radiance exists and is not apprehended, so it is with this.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
This is the support of the counteragent.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is just as when the conflagration at the end of an aeon is occurring, [all] conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)...
No such thing as a "footstep" exists and is not apprehended;
in the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "bodhisattva" exists and is not apprehended.
Thus ends the basis for the abandonment of opposing factors.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in the morality of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, no basis for immorality exists and is not apprehended;
even so, Subhūti, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, no referent for the term "Bodhisattva" exists and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in the concentration of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, no basis for distraction exists and is not apprehended.
In the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the term "lack of wisdom" does not exist and is not apprehended;
in the liberation of the Tathāgata, the term "non-liberation" does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
Subhūti, just as, for example, in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, no basis for the vision of the knowledge of liberation exists and is not apprehended,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended.
This is the support for the abandonment of conceptualizations regarding the counter-factors and their opposites.
Subhūti, just as no trace of the radiance of the sun and moon is found or perceived,
even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
Thus ends the section on the basis of wisdom and compassion.

Subhūti, just as there is no trace and nothing to be found of the radiance of the light of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, planets, constellations, or precious jewels, even so, Subhūti, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "Bodhisattva" has no existence and is not to be found.
Thus [he is] the locus of uncommon qualities.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, with the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the gods of Brahmā’s Retinue, the gods of Brahmā’s Ministers, and the Mahābrahmā gods.

Just as no trace of the radiance of the gods, up to and including the Akaniṣṭha gods, is found or perceived, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is neither found nor perceived.
Thus ends the support for the sequence of the welfare of others.

Subhūti, just as for example the footprint of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha cannot be found and is not apprehended, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" cannot be found and is not apprehended. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, the awakening by which the referent of the term "bodhisattva" exists, and that referent of the term "bodhisattva" itself—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless and invisible.
They are non-obstructive and of a single characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the non-attachment to and the non-existence of all dharmas,
by means of non-conceptualization and further non-conceptualization.
Moreover, Subhūti, all phenomena must be realized by the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus, that which is called the "basis for knowledge proceeding without effort" is stated to be the basis for practice.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are all dharmas?
Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the non-existence of all dharmas?"
“Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand all phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
“All phenomena are said to be wholesome and unwholesome, determinate and indeterminate, mundane and supramundane, with outflows and without outflows, conditioned and unconditioned, and common.”
And those that are non-common; these, Subhūti, are called all dharmas, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in their non-existence.
These, Subhūti, are all dharmas that must be fully understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus Subhūti spoke regarding the nature of the objective support:
"Blessed One, what are the wholesome worldly dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:
"Worldly wholesome qualities are said to be:
filiality toward one's mother, filiality toward one's father, proper conduct toward recluses, proper conduct toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in the family."
This gift is a basis for meritorious action; this morality is a basis for meritorious action;
this cultivation is a basis for meritorious action;
and skill in means accompanied by service.
The ten paths of wholesome action, and the nine worldly perceptions:

the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a putrefying corpse, the perception of a bloody corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, and the perception of a scattered corpse.
The perception of a skeleton, the perception of a burning corpse,
the four worldly meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments,
and the five worldly supernormal knowledges.
The ten worldly recollections are as follows:

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of the deities, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of death, and recollection directed toward the body;
these are called wholesome worldly dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the unwholesome worldly dharmas?
The Blessed One said:
Taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view— these are the ten unwholesome paths of action;
anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, harmfulness, envy, avarice, pride, and false pride—
these are called the unwholesome worldly dharmas.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the indeterminate dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:
Indeterminate bodily action, indeterminate vocal action, and indeterminate mental action.
The four great elements are indeterminate;
the five sense faculties are indeterminate;
the six sense bases are indeterminate.
The formless aggregates, elements, and sense bases that are indeterminate;
the indeterminate results of maturation—
all these are called indeterminate phenomena.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the worldly wholesome dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:

The five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten wholesome paths of action, the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five superknowledges, and whatever other mundane phenomena there may be—
these are called mundane wholesome phenomena.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what are the supramundane wholesome dharmas?
The Blessed One said:
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path;
the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known.
Concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought;
and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Knowledge and liberation, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and appropriate mental attention;
what are the eight liberations? They are:
one who possesses form sees forms. (PvsP1-2: 26)
This is the first liberation;
being percipient of the formless internally, one sees forms externally—
this is the second liberation.
One becomes resolved upon the beautiful;
this is the third liberation, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form.
With the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space;
this is the fourth liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, [one attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness].
Thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation,
through the complete transcendence of the sphere of nothingness.
He does not attain and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the eighth liberation;
these are the eight liberations.
The nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling:
The four meditative absorptions:

secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion;

with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness, equanimous and mindful"—thus he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.

And through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental gladness and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Having attained it, he dwells therein;

by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
These are the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling:
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these are called supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Subhūti said:
“What, Blessed One, are the dharmas with outflows?
The Blessed One said: “The five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.”
These are called the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, which are the uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)?"

The Blessed One said: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four grounds of self-confidence.
The four analytical knowledges up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these are called the untainted dharmas.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, what are conditioned phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
“The realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, and whatever other phenomena are included within the three realms.”
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and so forth— these are called conditioned phenomena.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, what are unconditioned phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
“Those phenomena for which neither arising, nor cessation, nor alteration is perceived; namely, the destruction of passion, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.”

Suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*):
these are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharmāḥ*).
Subhūti said:
“What, Blessed One, are the common dharmas?
The Blessed One replied: “The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges.”
These are called the common dharmas.
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, what are the uncommon dharmas?"

The Blessed One said: "The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the three gateways to liberation, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these are called the uncommon dharmas."
In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not form any attachment to phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics;
rather, all phenomena should be realized through non-dual yoga,
by means of both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
Thus having spoken regarding the objective support for practice,
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, as for that which is called 'a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva'— "
"For what reason, Blessed One, is he called a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, he will bring about the leadership over a great mass of beings, over a great multitude of beings."
For that reason, Subhūti, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is this great mass of beings, this great assembly of beings, among whom the bodhisattva mahāsattva shall exercise leadership?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti,

it is called a 'multitude of great beings' and a 'community of great beings' because, starting from the first production of the thought of awakening, there are those on the stage of the lineage, those on the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas."
Up until they become irreversible— this is that great mass of beings, that great assembly of beings, whom the bodhisattva mahāsattva will lead to preeminence.
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated a mind like a diamond (vajra), should bring about leadership over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings.
Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, what is the generation of a mind like a diamond?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the following thought:
'Having donned the armor for an immeasurable saṃsāra, I must become one who relinquishes all possessions.'"
I must generate a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
I must lead all sentient beings to final nirvana through the three vehicles;
yet, even after I have led all sentient beings to final nirvana, not a single sentient being has been led to final nirvana. Why is that?
I must realize the non-arising of all phenomena;
with a mind of omniscience that is unconfused, I must practice the six perfections;
and I must train in the perfection of penetrating all phenomena, which is universally pervasive.
I must realize all phenomena as a single unity;

I must train in all phenomena for the sake of penetrating the realization of the perfections; and I must train in all phenomena for the sake of penetrating the realization of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
"I must train in the dharmas for the sake of realizing and penetrating the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the superknowledges;
I must train in the dharmas for the sake of realizing and penetrating the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in which the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the preeminence over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings.
He will cause it to be made,
and that by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought as follows:

"However many beings there may be who experience painful sensations—whether they be in the hells, among the animals, or in the world of Yama—for their sake I would experience those painful sensations myself. In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate such a thought:
"For the sake of even a single being, I would undergo the suffering of the hells, the animals, or the world of Yama for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons."
"Until those beings have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder,
by this means I shall experience that suffering of the hells and so forth on behalf of all beings,
until those beings have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Afterwards, having planted the roots of merit performed by myself, may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment after hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.

Subhūti, this is the diamond-like production of the thought of awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which he will bring about leadership over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must possess a noble mind, a mind by which he shall bring about leadership for all beings.
In this regard, the noble-mindedness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, they do not give rise to a mind of passion,
they do not give rise to a mind of hatred, and they do not give rise to a mind of delusion.
He does not give rise to a mind of violence;
he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka; he does not give rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, this is the magnanimity of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva by which he shall bring about the preeminence of all sentient beings, yet he does not conceive pride because of that mind.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must possess a mind that is unshakable.
In this regard, Subhūti, the unshakable state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which does not even conceive of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all aspects;
this, Subhūti, is the unshakable state of mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should maintain a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings.

In this regard, Subhūti, the mind of benefit and happiness belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which consists in the protection of all sentient beings and the non-abandonment of all sentient beings, and yet he does not conceive of himself by means of that;

this, Subhūti, is the mind of benefit and happiness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. For it is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, [acts] for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be one who delights in the Dharma, who finds joy in the Dharma, and who is devoted to the practice of delighting in the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the Dharma?
It is, namely, the non-differentiation of all phenomena.
This is called the Dharma; therein, what is delight in the Dharma?
That which is joy in the Dharma is called delight in the Dharma.
In that regard, what is delighting in the Dharma (*dharmārāmatā*)?
It is the cultivation and frequent practice of that Dharma;

this is called delighting in the Dharma. For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attains the preeminence over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings.
It should be caused to be made by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in internal emptiness, having stood in external emptiness, having stood in internal-and-external emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence—

Abiding therein, one should exercise leadership over a great mass of beings, a great assembly of beings, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should abide in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, in the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

Abiding in the qualities of a Buddha, one should exercise leadership over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having stood in the diamond-like samādhi, and so on, up to standing in the space-like, unattached, liberated, and stainless samādhi, [should do so] for the sake of the great mass of beings, the great...
One should exercise leadership over the multitude of beings by means of non-apprehension.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, while remaining established in these dharmas, should exercise leadership over the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings;
therefore, he is called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Thus [is] the greatness of the mind that is supreme among all beings.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'."
The Blessed One said:
"Let it occur to you, Śāriputra, by what meaning a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'.
Śāriputra said:

O Blessed One, [it is so] because of the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a living soul, the view of a creature, the view of a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, a doer, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer; because of the view of annihilation, the view of eternalism, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of the aggregates, the view of the elements, the view of the sense-bases, the view of dependent origination, the view of the factors conducive to awakening, the view of the powers and the grounds of self-confidence, and the view of the unique qualities of a Buddha.

He teaches the Dharma through the application of non-apprehension for the sake of abandoning all these views: the view of maturing sentient beings, the view of purifying the buddha-field, the view of the bodhisattva, the view of the Buddha, and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma.
For that reason, he is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, venerable Śāriputra, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva have a view of form?"
“Does there arise a view of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Śāriputra replied:
“In this case, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes unskilled in means.”
Having perceived form, he produces a view by means of perception;

in this way, in detail, having perceived the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination—both individually and collectively—up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair, he produces a view.

Likewise, having perceived the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the perfections, the superknowledges, the syllables, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, he produces a view.

Thus, having apprehended the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by way of apprehension, one gives rise to a [false] view.
This is the greatness of abandonment.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"It occurs to me also, Blessed One, for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'.
The Blessed One said:
"Let it occur to you, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, even regarding that bodhicitta—the mind of equality with the unequaled, the mind not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—one is unattached even to that mind. Why is that?
Because that mind of omniscience is untainted and not included within the three realms; one is unattached even to that mind, and for that reason, a bodhisattva is reckoned as a 'mahāsattva'."
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind that is equal to the unequaled, the mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
Subhūti replied:
In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the arising or the cessation of any dharma;

he does not perceive decrease or increase, coming or going, defilement or purification. And in that, venerable Śāriputra, where there is neither defilement nor purification, neither coming nor going, neither decrease nor increase, neither arising nor cessation—
And that is neither the mind of a śrāvaka nor the mind of a pratyekabuddha;
this, Śāriputra, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unequaled and equal mind, a mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra said:

As for what the Venerable Subhūti has said— that one is unattached even to the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— is it not the case, Venerable Subhūti, that form (*rūpa*) is also unattached by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)?
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unattached.
Subhūti said: "So it is, venerable Śāriputra; form is also unattached, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unattached."
To the extent that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination—both individually and collectively—are unattached, even up to old age and death;
likewise, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are unattached;

and so on, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are all unattached.
Śāriputra said:
"As for what the Venerable Subhūti has said— that this mind of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned— "
"Venerable Subhūti, is not even the mind of ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*aparyāpanna*), by reason of its natural emptiness (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*)?

Is it not likewise the case that even the minds of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and perfectly enlightened buddhas (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) are untainted and unconditioned, by reason of their natural emptiness?
Subhūti replied:
"It is so, Venerable Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"Form also, Subhūti, is without outflows and unconditioned, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Subhūti, are also untainted and unattached by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness;

likewise, venerable Subhūti, are not the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha untainted and unattached?
“By virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Subhūti said:
“It is so, Venerable Śāriputra, just as you say; even the minds of foolish commoners are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.”
Based on the fact that even the minds of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and perfectly enlightened buddhas are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of their natural emptiness;

and based on the fact that even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are untainted and unconditioned by virtue of their natural emptiness.
Śāriputra said: "As for what the Venerable Subhūti has thus said— that because it is non-mind, one is unattached even to that mind— "

"Venerable Subhūti, is it not the case that form is unattached even in form; feeling is unattached even in feeling; perception is unattached even in perception; formations are unattached even in formations;
and consciousness is unattached even in consciousness?
Subhūti replied:
"It is so, Venerable Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"But surely, Venerable Subhūti, even in the applications of mindfulness, the applications of mindfulness are unattached?"

In this same way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the perfections, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so on, up to the unique qualities of a Buddha— even the unique qualities of a Buddha are unattached. Subhūti said:
It is so, venerable Śāriputra, just as you say.
Venerable Śāriputra, form is unattached even in form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattached even in consciousness.

Likewise, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, both individually and collectively, as well as the truths, dependent origination, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, are all unattached.

The perfections, the superknowledges, the factors of enlightenment, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and even among the unique qualities of a Buddha, the unique qualities of a Buddha are unattached. Thus, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, by that also—

By means of the thought of awakening— the thought that is peerless and equal, the thought not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— one does not conceive pride nor does one adhere [to anything], through the yoga of the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
This is the greatness of realization.
When this summary of practice had been spoken, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Lord, it occurs to me also as to the sense for which a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'."
The Blessed One said: "May it occur to you, Pūrṇa.
Pūrṇa said: "O Blessed One, that being is one girt with the great armor; O Blessed One, that being has set out upon the Great Vehicle; that being, O Blessed One, is a bodhisattva by virtue of that."
"He is called a 'Great Being'.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Pūrṇa, to what extent is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be 'armed with the great armor'?"

Pūrṇa said: "In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing for the sake of awakening does not, while established in the perfection of giving, give gifts for the sake of limited beings;
rather, he gives gifts while established in the perfection of giving for the sake of all beings.

Likewise, while practicing for the sake of awakening, he does not do so for the sake of limited beings when established in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditative concentration; [the same applies] when established in the perfection of wisdom."
Abiding [in this way], he cultivates the perfection of wisdom;
moreover, for the sake of all sentient beings, he abides in the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not don the great armor by means of delimiting sentient beings.
"I shall lead this many beings to final nirvana; I shall not lead this many beings to final nirvana; I shall establish this many beings in awakening."
"I will not establish this many beings in enlightenment"—
on the contrary, he girds himself with the armor for the sake of all beings,
and it occurs to him thus:
"I myself shall fulfill the perfection of generosity and shall also establish all sentient beings in the perfection of generosity;

likewise for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration; and I myself shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom."
"I shall establish all sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom," and likewise,
"I shall cultivate for myself the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments, and I shall establish all sentient beings in them."

"Up to the point where one thinks, 'I myself shall abide in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and I shall establish all sentient beings in them as well'— to this extent, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be 'armed with the great armor. Thus is the nature of practice.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he makes that gift common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the armor of the perfection of giving for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while bestowing gifts.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom bestows gifts,

that which consists in the avoidance of the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects— this too is the armor of the perfection of giving.
This is the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [that which pertains to] those...
Forbearance, illumination, and thorough investigation—
this is called the armor of the perfection of patience for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom...

When one gives with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, that non-laxity of vigor— having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings— one dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
this is the armor of the perfection of vigor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, that one-pointedness of mind through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects— which leaves no room for the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the armor of the perfection of meditative concentration belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving gifts.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving gifts,
that perception of being created by illusion which is established through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects does not at all [arise].
He perceives neither the giver, nor the recipient, nor the gift;
this is the armor of the perfection of wisdom for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift.
For, Venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not take those six perfections as signs and does not apprehend them.
For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is armored with the great armor.
Thus ends the first hexad on the armor of the perfection of generosity.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline [should train] with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

With mental attentions, he gives gifts, having made them common to all sentient beings, and dedicates them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment by way of non-apprehension; this, Śāriputra, is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, there is a lack of longing for the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone for the level of ordinary persons.
This is the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, it is that forbearance, appreciation, and thorough investigation of phenomena through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.

This is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline, that state of non-laxity and non-dejection in his mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline and dwells with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he does not allow any opportunity for the arising of thoughts associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas; it is the dedication toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of those roots of goodness which have been made common to all sentient beings.
This is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, the perception that all phenomena are like illusions is present; yet he does not conceive of that ethical discipline, nor does he apprehend it.
"Venerable Śāriputra, this is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of ethical discipline.

For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of ethical discipline embraces all six perfections; by that, he comes to be reckoned as one who is 'armed with the great armor.'"
Thus ends the second hexad on the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience, he gives gifts with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with those associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas.
By means of mental attentions, he makes that root of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience.

In this way, for one practicing the perfection of patience, there are the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience applies himself, through wisdom and with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, to the full realization of all Buddha-dharmas and to the maturation of all sentient beings.

When he does not dedicate that root of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by means of mental engagements associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but instead makes it common to all sentient beings,
this is the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience embraces the six perfections; by that, he is reckoned as one who has donned the great armor.
Thus ends the third section: the sixfold armor of the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor gives gifts with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects, not with mental orientations associated with the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor;
likewise, for one practicing the perfection of vigor, there are the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor and cultivating the perfection of wisdom establishes the perception that all phenomena are like illusions.

With mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with mental attentions associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
this is the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor embraces the six perfections; by that, he comes to be reckoned as "one who has donned the great armor.
Thus ends the fourth section: the sixfold armor of the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration gives gifts with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not with mental engagements associated with the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration;

likewise, for one practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, there are the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration and cultivating the perfection of wisdom establishes the perception that all phenomena are like illusions.

By means of mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not by means of mental attentions associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
this is the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of meditation embraces the six perfections; by that, he comes to be reckoned as "one who has donned the great armor.
Thus ends the fifth section: the sixfold armor of the perfection of meditation.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift purified in the three spheres, with mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects and not with mental orientations associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas; and having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, for one practicing the perfection of wisdom, there are the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates the perfection of wisdom.
In him, regarding all the perfections and all phenomena, there arises the perception that they are like an illusion, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, and a magical creation;
this occurs through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and not through mental engagements associated with the disciples or solitary buddhas.
And having made that root of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of wisdom:
namely, when, O Venerable Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not take these six perfections as signs and does not apprehend them.
For in this way, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is girt with the great armor;
and furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by abiding in each individual perfection, fulfills all six perfections.
Thus ends the sixth [section], the hexad of the armor of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) yet does not relish them, is not captivated by them, and is not reborn under their influence;
likewise, he enters into the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), yet does not relish them, is not captivated by them, and is not reborn under their influence.
This should be understood as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that has entered into skillful means (*upāyakauśala*).

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) by means of the vision of seclusion, and he dwells by means of the vision of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
yet he does not personally realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is the armor of skillful means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva" because he is armored with the great armor.

And for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus armored with the great armor, Venerable Śāriputra, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions, utter words of exultation, proclaim his praise, and celebrate his name.
They cause the sound of that bodhisattva mahāsattva to be heard and raise their voice, proclaiming:

"In such-and-such an extension of world-systems, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, armored with the great armor, is maturing sentient beings and purifying a buddha-field. Thus concludes the summary of the sixfold armor.
Thus the practice of armor has been explained.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Pūrṇa, to what extent is a bodhisattva mahāsattva one who has set out in the Great Vehicle and mounted upon the Great Vehicle?"

Pūrṇa said: "In this case, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity dwells, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and born of seclusion, filled with joy and happiness."
Having attained it, he dwells therein; likewise the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
and likewise having attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells therein.

These are the meditations and formless attainments of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of generosity, enters into and emerges from these meditations and these formless attainments by way of the forms, signs, and marks of space,
and having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, [dedicates them] toward unexcelled...
He dedicates it toward perfect enlightenment;
this is the perfection of giving of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The same should be said for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and enters the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
and when that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of these meditative concentrations and these formless attainments,
as he enters and emerges from these meditative concentrations and formless attainments, he attends to the forms, signs, and characteristics of space.

While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he takes those roots of merit and others as well, makes them common to all sentient beings through mental applications associated with the knowledge of all aspects, and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections, armored in the great armor, brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field.
Thus is the practice of emerging from and entering the meditative absorptions and formless attainments.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated a mental attention associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [teaches] the Dharma to all sentient beings for the destruction of their afflictions.
He generates the thought, "I shall teach," and this is the perfection of generosity of the bodhisattva mahāsattva,
in that the bodhisattva mahāsattva, with those very mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters and teaches the first dhyāna.

And therein he establishes himself in the first dhyāna, granting no opportunity for other mental states associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s ungrasped perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*),
in that it is associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
While dwelling in the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), it occurs to him:
"I shall teach the Dharma for the sake of the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings.
This extends as far as the endurance, appreciation, investigation, realization, and profound contemplation of those mental orientations.

This is the perfection of patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having made all roots of merit common to all sentient beings through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, dedicates them to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And he does not slacken his vigor;
this is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

in that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters into the meditative concentrations and formless attainments and yet does not perceive them.
This is the perfection of meditation of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:

that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, [contemplates] the factors of the first meditation, the factors of the second, the third, and the fourth meditations by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of non-self.
He contemplates with the aspect of peace, the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of signlessness, and the aspect of wishlessness, yet he does not apprehend them;
this is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This, venerable Śāriputra, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Thus is the setting forth of the six perfections. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that which cultivates all aspects of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.

He cultivates in every way the concentrations on the doors of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and he cultivates in every way the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Venerable Śāriputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus is the setting forth upon the noble path.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness— vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rival, unobstructed, harmless, all-pervading, well-spoken, reaching as far as the limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), extending to the furthest reaches of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*)— [regards] the entire world...
Having pervaded one quarter of the world, he dwells having attained it; likewise, having pervaded the ten directions, he dwells having attained them—

thus with a mind accompanied by compassion, accompanied by sympathetic joy, and accompanied by equanimity, which is vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from rivalry, unobstructed, and unhindered.

With well-spoken words that follow everywhere throughout the world as far as the limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and as far as the end of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), he dwells having pervaded and attained the entire world—
first one direction, and so on, until he dwells having pervaded and attained the ten directions. These are called the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and directs [his mind] toward the thought, "I must rescue all sentient beings.

He enters the concentration of compassion (*karuṇā-samādhi*) and directs [his mind] toward a state of compassionate pity for sentient beings. He enters the concentration of sympathetic joy (*muditā-samādhi*) and directs [his mind] toward sentient beings with the thought, "I myself shall cause them to rejoice."
He enters into equanimity and meditative concentration, and he dedicates the destruction of the outflows toward all sentient beings;
this is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables,

when the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from the forms, signs, and characteristics of the meditative concentrations and immeasurables, and does not dedicate them to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but [dedicates them] otherwise.
This is the ungrasped perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables:
