when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells unmixed with those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, he does not long for these two—the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha—but rather all-aspect omniscience alone is acceptable and pleasing to him; this is the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables.

The perfection of patience is practiced when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with a sense of unflagging responsibility, through mental states associated with the knowledge of all modes, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome dharmas and attaining wholesome dharmas;
this is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), these immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and these formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), yet does not take rebirth through the power of those concentrations, immeasurables, or formless attainments, and does not relish them nor become captivated by them.
This is the perfection of meditative concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the immeasurables:

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, enters into and emerges from those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, regarding them by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of selflessness, and the aspect of peace.
He contemplates by way of the aspect of emptiness, the aspect of signlessness, and the aspect of wishlessness;

yet he does not enter the fixed course of the śrāvakas or the fixed course of the pratyekabuddhas. This is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the immeasurables. This, venerable Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus is the undertaking of the immeasurables.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that knowledge regarding internal emptiness which does not function through the mode of apprehension.
That knowledge regarding external emptiness which is not by way of apprehension;

that knowledge regarding internal-external emptiness which is not by way of apprehension; up to that knowledge regarding the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence which is not by way of apprehension—this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is that wherein the mind does not train in any phenomena; that is concentrated wisdom. This too is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is...
When the knowledge arises regarding this that it is neither permanent nor impermanent,
neither suffering nor non-suffering, and neither pleasure nor non-pleasure;
Neither "self" nor "non-self," neither "peaceful" nor "not peaceful," neither "empty" nor "not empty."

Knowledge proceeds neither as "sign" nor as "signless," neither as "wishful" nor as "wishless. This too, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
That knowledge which does not operate in the past time, does not operate in the future time, and does not operate in the present time;
Furthermore, ignorance regarding the three times does not arise for him, and that occurs through the yoga of non-apprehension. This too, Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Moreover, Śāriputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva:
That which is such that knowledge does not operate in the desire realm, knowledge does not operate in the form realm, and knowledge does not operate in the formless realm,
yet ignorance does not operate for him regarding the desire, form, or formless realms— this being by way of non-apprehension— this too, Śāriputra, is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that in which knowledge does not operate with respect to mundane or supramundane phenomena,

nor with respect to contaminated or uncontaminated phenomena, nor with respect to conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; yet, he possesses no ignorance regarding these mundane, supramundane, contaminated, uncontaminated, conditioned, or unconditioned phenomena.
And that is by way of non-apprehension. Venerable Śāriputra, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus is the setting forth by way of non-apprehension.
Śāriputra said:
"To what extent, Venerable Pūrṇa, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to be 'mounted upon the Great Vehicle'?
Pūrṇa replied: "In this regard, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, mounts the perfection of giving."
He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor the giver, nor the recipient, nor the gift; he does not perceive them by way of non-perception.
It is in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "mounted upon" the perfection of giving.

Likewise, he is mounted upon the perfection of ethical discipline, mounted upon the perfection of patience, mounted upon the perfection of vigor, and mounted upon the perfection of meditative concentration. While practicing the perfection of wisdom, he [does not perceive] the perfection of wisdom.
He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor the bodhisattva, nor mental attention, by way of non-perception.
It is in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "mounted upon the perfection of wisdom.
This is the setting forth of the purity of the three spheres.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment with an unadulterated production of the mind set on omniscience, for the purpose of cultivation and thorough cultivation, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
It is in this way, venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with an unadulterated production of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all aspects,

cultivates the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness for the purpose of cultivation and non-cultivation, and that by way of non-apprehension. It is in this way, venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have mounted the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with an unadulterated production of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all aspects,

cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, for the purpose of cultivation and thorough cultivation, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. It is thus, venerable Śāriputra.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "mounted upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives in this way: "That which is called 'bodhisattva' is a mere conventional designation," based on the non-apprehension of a sentient being.
This too is a mere name, namely form, by virtue of the non-apprehensibility of form; feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise];
this too is a mere name, namely consciousness, by virtue of the non-apprehensibility of consciousness.
This which is called "eye" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the eye;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, and body are mere names, and this which is called "mind" is a mere name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the mind.

Thus, whether taken individually or collectively, the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are mere names.

That is to say, from internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence—since even the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is unapprehendable, these are mere names.
Furthermore, based on the non-apprehensibility of both Buddha-qualities and non-Buddha-qualities, these are mere names.

This which is called suchness, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—is merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of the limit of reality.

This which is called awakening (*bodhi*) and a Buddha is also merely a name, based on the non-apprehensibility of a Buddha. It is in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have "embarked upon the Great Vehicle. Thus concludes the section on the presentation of the subject matter.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the attainment of awakening, in the interval between these, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, because of the perfection of the superknowledges, brings sentient beings to maturity and travels from buddhafield to buddhafield.
In every buddhafield, he honors, reveres, respects, and worships the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
whatever method of appropriate worship and honor belongs to each Buddha, he performs it for those Blessed Buddhas, and from them he hears the Dharma,
namely, this very Mahāyāna.
Having mounted the Bodhisattva-vehicle there, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field,
purifies buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity;
yet neither the notion of a "buddha-field" nor the notion of "sentient beings" arises for him.
Abiding on the stage of non-duality, he intentionally assumes such a physical form as is capable of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings;
he is never separated from that Great Vehicle until he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus, having attained the knowledge of all aspects through the application of the superknowledges, he turns the wheel of Dharma,
which cannot be turned by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor by the world of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, or asuras.
When he has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, speak his praise, raise their voices, and proclaim his fame.

In this extension of world-systems, such-and-such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having mounted the Mahāyāna, has attained all-aspect omniscience; and having attained all-aspect omniscience, [he turns] the wheel of Dharma.

Likewise, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, the northeastern, the southeastern, the southwestern, the northwestern, the nadir, and the zenith—in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—there are Buddhas, Blessed Ones.
They speak of his color, they utter his voice, and they proclaim his fame, saying:
"In such an extension of world-systems, such-and-such a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained all-aspect omniscience;
having attained all-aspect omniscience, he has set in motion the wheel of Dharma. Thus indeed, venerable Śāriputra, is a bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva is said to be "mounted upon the Great Vehicle. Thus, the setting forth toward the knowledge of all aspects has been described; this concludes the practice of setting forth.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it is said that 'the bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who has donned the great armor, one who has donned the great armor.
To what extent, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to have donned the great armor?"
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor of the Mahāyāna— namely, the armor of the perfection of generosity,
the armor of the perfection of ethical discipline, the armor of the perfection of patience, the armor of the perfection of vigor, and the armor of the perfection of meditative concentration— "
He dons the armor of the perfection of wisdom; having donned the armor of the applications of mindfulness,
he dons the armor of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path.
Having donned the armor of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments;
having donned the armor of internal emptiness; having donned the armor of external emptiness;
Having donned the armor of internal and external emptiness, up to having donned the armor of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature,
and having donned the armor of the powers of supernormal knowledge;
Having donned the armor of the grounds of self-confidence, having donned the armor of the analytical knowledges, and having donned the armor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Having donned the armor of the knowledge of all aspects and having donned the armor of the body of a Buddha,
he pervades the great trichiliocosm with his radiance.

It causes the entire hellish realm to tremble in six ways; having extinguished that mass of fire and pacified the sufferings of the beings in the hells, the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that they are all turned toward nirvāṇa.
Thus he utters this word and causes this sound to be heard: "Homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One!
Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness;

through that very happiness and mental well-being, they emerge from those hells and are reborn in that world-system where they behold the Blessed Buddhas, please them, and attain birth among gods and humans.
And they take hold [of them];

thus, having emerged from the animal realm and the world of Yama, they are reborn in those world-systems where they behold the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and please them, as well as attaining rebirth among gods and humans.
And so it is in the eastern direction, the southern, the western, the northern, the northeastern, and the southeastern.

In the south-western, north-western, downward, and upward directions, he pervades world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with his radiance and causes them to tremble in six ways; having extinguished the masses of fire in all the hellish abodes and pacified the sufferings of the sentient beings in those hells, he leads them all toward Nirvana.
Having understood this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva utters such a word and proclaims this sound: "Homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha!
Then those beings in the hells, having heard that sound of the Buddha, obtain happiness.

By means of that very bliss and mental joy, they emerge from those hells and are reborn here and there in various world-systems, wherever they behold the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and bring them satisfaction;
and they take up birth among gods and humans.
Likewise, emerging from the animal realms and the worlds of Yama, they are reborn here and there in various world-systems, wherever...
In that state, they behold the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, please them, and take up rebirth among gods and humans.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to [manifest] a great multitude of people at a major crossroads.

In front of them, he conjures up hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama; having conjured these, he causes those beings to hear the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," and the sound of "Saṅgha.
Then, by means of that sound of Buddha, the sound of Dharma, and the sound of Saṅgha, they emerge from those hells, animal realms, and worlds of Yama, and are reborn among gods and humans.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, has any being at all been raised up from the states of hell, the animal realm, or the world of Yama by that magician or the magician’s apprentice?
Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:

"In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has liberated beings from the three lower realms in incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite world-systems, not a single being has been liberated. Why is that?"
Why is that? Subhūti, this is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), based on the illusory nature of all things.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has mounted the Great Vehicle and is girt with the great armor is so called. Thus ends the equipment of compassion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity and donning the great armor, transforms the great trichiliocosm into lapis lazuli; having transformed it into lapis lazuli, he transforms it into the array of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); and having transformed it into the array of a universal monarch, he gives food to those who lack food.

In this way, up to providing clothing, vehicles, perfumes, garlands, flowers, incense, ointments, powders, and various requisites; or dwellings, beds, seats, coverings, life-sustaining necessities, medicines, gold, silver, jewels, gems, coral, conch shells, stones, pearls, and ornaments— up to giving any kind of requisite whatsoever— he, having given food to those seeking food and up to having given any kind of requisite, teaches the Dharma to those beings.
That is to say, this very teaching connected with the six perfections;

moreover, those beings, having heard that Dharma teaching, shall never be separated from those perfections until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva—
A great being is said to be "one girded with the great armor.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled magician or a magician’s apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great multitude of people, were to conjure up a vast crowd of people and, having conjured them, give food to those who desire food.
One should give various kinds of requisites to those who need them. What do you think, Subhūti? Would anything at all have been given by that illusionist or his apprentice to anyone?
Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having manifested even the array of a universal monarch, [should give] food..."
While giving food to those seeking food, and while giving various other human requisites, no human requisites whatsoever have been given to any sentient being. Why is that?

Subhūti, this is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), based on the illusory nature of all phenomena. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."
Thus is the equipment of generosity.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, through the intentional assumption of rebirth, is born into a family of universal monarchs;
staying there, he establishes beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.
He establishes them in the four meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
he establishes them in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
And those beings are never deprived of that teaching of the Dharma until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads of four great roads and establish them in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Just as one might establish beings in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, yet by establishing that many beings in those qualities of a Buddha, not a single being has actually been established in the qualities of a Buddha; even so, Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established those many beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Even when he has established [beings] in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), not a single sentient being has actually been established in those Buddha-qualities. Why is that?

Subhūti, this is the very nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, based on their illusory nature (*māyādharmatā*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor. Thus ends the equipment of ethical discipline (*śīlasambhāra*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, encourages, introduces, and establishes sentient beings in patience.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, encourage, introduce, and establish sentient beings in patience?
Here, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Thus he dons the armor, thinking:

"Even if all sentient beings were to strike me with sticks, clods of earth, fists, or weapons, I must not give rise to even a single thought of agitation; rather, I must establish all sentient beings in such patience as this."

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads, and all of them were to strike that illusionist with sticks, clods of earth, fists, or weapons;
yet he would not give rise to even a single thought of agitation toward them, and he would establish those created beings in such patience.
In that way, although he has established that many beings in patience, not a single being has been established in patience;
even so, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established those many beings in patience, not a single being has been established in patience.
This, Subhūti, is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is because all phenomena have the nature of an illusion. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
This concludes the equipment of patience.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, encourages, introduces, and establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of vigor.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, cause all sentient beings to take up, enter, and be established in the perfection of vigor? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in physical and mental vigor through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects,
causes all sentient beings to take up, enter, and be established in physical and mental vigor.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads and, with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, establish them in physical and mental vigor; even though he has established that many beings in physical and mental vigor, not a single being has actually been established in physical and mental vigor.

In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established that many beings in physical and mental vigor, not a single being has actually been established in physical and mental vigor.
Why is that?
Subhūti, this is the very nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of all things. It is for this reason, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor."
Thus is the equipment of vigor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, encourages all sentient beings toward the perfection of meditative concentration, settles them in it, and establishes them in it.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, encourage all sentient beings toward the perfection of meditative concentration, settle them in it, and establish them in it?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the equality of all phenomena, does not perceive the distraction or non-distraction of any phenomenon whatsoever.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the perfection of meditative concentration; he likewise encourages, introduces, and establishes all sentient beings in the perfection of meditative concentration.
And they have been encouraged, settled, and established [in this way],
so that they are never deprived of the perfection of meditative concentration until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist.

Suppose, Subhūti, that at a great crossroads, having manifested a vast multitude of people before a great crowd of beings, one were to establish that crowd in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Even though by that means one has established all those beings in the perfection of meditative concentration, not even a single being among them would have been established in the perfection of meditative concentration.

In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes all beings in the perfection of meditative concentration, no being at all has been established in the perfection of meditative concentration.
For what reason?
Subhūti, this is the true nature of phenomena, based on the illusory nature of phenomena. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
Thus ends the equipment of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourages all sentient beings toward the perfection of wisdom, settles them in it, and establishes them in it.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encourage all sentient beings toward the perfection of wisdom, settle them in it, and establish them in it?
It is because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the near shore or the far shore of any dharma whatsoever.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the perfection of wisdom; he likewise encourages all sentient beings toward it, leads them into it, and establishes them therein.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were at a great crossroads before a vast multitude of people.
Having manifested a great multitude of people before him, he incites them to the perfection of wisdom, settles them in it, and establishes them in it;
yet, although he has established that many beings in the perfection of wisdom, not even a single being has been established in the perfection of wisdom.
In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes all beings in the perfection of wisdom, no being at all has been established in the perfection of wisdom.
It is so. For what reason?

Subhūti, this is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), based on the fact that all phenomena have the nature of an illusion. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
Thus ends the equipment of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, armored with the great armor, in the eastern direction—

in as many world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā— exhorts, introduces, and establishes all those beings in the perfection of giving, just as he himself abides in the perfection of giving.

In this way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes others in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom;
and he teaches the Dharma, namely, that which is connected with these very six perfections.
And having heard it, they shall never again be separated from the six perfections until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; likewise,

as many beings as there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the southern, western, northern, northeastern, southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, downward, and upward directions— [all hear it].
Just as he himself stands in the perfection of generosity, he likewise encourages, introduces, and establishes all of them in the perfection of generosity;

in the same way, he encourages, introduces, and establishes them in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
And he teaches the Dharma, namely this very teaching connected with the six perfections;
and having heard it, they shall never again be separated from the six perfections until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to manifest a great multitude of people before a vast crowd at a major crossroads, and then encourage, establish, and settle that manifested multitude in the six perfections. What do you think, Subhūti?
Has any actual being been encouraged by that illusionist or his apprentice in the six perfections?
"Or it would have been established or fixed.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has established that many beings in the six perfections, not a single being has been established in the six perfections. Why is that?"
This is the true nature of phenomena, Subhūti, based on the illusory nature of all things. For it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be "armed with the great armor.
Furthermore, Subhūti, having donned the great armor and dwelling with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he allows no opportunity for other thoughts to arise, such as:
"I must establish so many beings in the perfection of generosity, and so many I must not establish."

Likewise, regarding the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration, one should not think: "I must establish this many beings in the perfection of wisdom, but I must not establish that many"; nor should one think: "I must establish this many beings in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, but I must not establish that many."

"...that so many sentient beings are to be established in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and so many are not to be established; that so many sentient beings are to be established in the fruit of stream-entry and so many are not to be established;
and likewise in the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning—that so many sentient beings are to be established in arhatship and so many..."

One should not think: "This many beings are to be established in the state of a Pratyekabuddha and this many are not to be established; this many beings are to be established in omniscience and this many are not to be established.
Rather, indeed, incalculable and immeasurable beings are to be established in the six perfections.

In this way, they should be established in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and immeasurable, incalculable beings should be established in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and in Buddhahood.
Thus is the equipment for calm abiding (*śamatha*).

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist were to create at a great crossroads a vast multitude of people—incalculable and immeasurable—and establish them in the six perfections, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects endowed with the supreme of all modes; even so, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva...

When a Mahāsattva has established those countless and immeasurable beings in the six perfections, up to establishing them in the knowledge of omniscience endowed with the excellence of all aspects, not a single being has been established in the six perfections. Why is that?
"Subhūti, this is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena, namely, that they are based upon this illusory nature of phenomena.
Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, it should be known that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is, indeed, 'armed with non-armour,' by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā)."
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, form is empty of form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness.
The eye is empty of the eye;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the mind;
form is empty of form.
In this way, sound, odor, taste, the tangible, and mental phenomena are empty of mental phenomena;
visual consciousness is empty of visual consciousness;
and likewise, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness are empty of mental consciousness.
Eye-contact is empty of eye-contact;
likewise, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of mind-contact.
[This is] the feeling conditioned by eye-contact.
It is empty of the feeling conditioned by eye-contact; likewise, it is empty of the feeling conditioned by ear-contact,
and the feeling conditioned by nose-contact.
The feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, the feeling conditioned by body-contact,
and the feeling conditioned by mind-contact are empty of the feeling conditioned by mind-contact.
O Blessed One, the perfection of generosity is empty of the perfection of generosity;

likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are empty of the perfection of wisdom;
and internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness.
External emptiness is empty of external emptiness;
internal-external emptiness is empty of internal-external emptiness;
up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which is empty of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty of the factors of enlightenment;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata are empty of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the grounds of self-confidence are empty of the grounds of self-confidence.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
a bodhisattva, O Blessed One, is also empty of a bodhisattva;

and the armor of the Great Vehicle, O Blessed One, is also empty of the armor of the Great Vehicle. By this method, O Blessed One, it should be understood that a bodhisattva is one who is armored with non-armoring.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, just as you say. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the knowledge of all aspects is uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned."
Those beings, too, are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned,
for whose sake the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has donned this great armor.
Subhūti said:

For what reason, Blessed One, is omniscience uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned, and why are those very beings for whose sake the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has donned the great armor also uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, based on the non-apprehension of an agent, all-aspect omniscience is uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned; those sentient beings as well are uncreated, unaltered, and unconditioned. Why is that?"
For indeed, Subhūti, form does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
nor do feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness act, transform, or construct.
The eye does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not act, do not transform, and do not construct; form does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.

Sound does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; smell does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; taste does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; the tangible does not act, does not transform, and does not construct; mental phenomena do not act, do not transform, and do not construct. Eye-consciousness does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness do not act, do not transform, and do not construct.
Eye-contact does not act, does not transform, and does not construct;
ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact do not act, do not transform, and do not construct.
The feeling conditioned by eye-contact does not act, does not transform, and does not construct.

He does not produce, does not transform, and does not construct the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, nor the feeling conditioned by nose-contact, nor the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, nor the feeling conditioned by body-contact, nor the feeling conditioned by mind-contact. For what reason?
For in this way, all these do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
Subhūti, the self does not act, does not transform, and does not perform formative acts;

likewise, the sentient being, the life-principle, the nourisher, the person, the individual, the human, the youth, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer do not act, do not transform, and do not perform formative acts.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, all these things do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
A dream, Subhūti, does nothing, does not transform anything, and does not bring anything about through volitional formation.
In this way, an echo, a reflection, a mirage, and a magical creation do not act, do not transform, and do not perform any formative activity. Why is that?
Because, in an ultimate sense, all these things do not exist and are not apprehended.
Subhūti, internal emptiness does not act, does not transform, and does not perform any formative activity. Why is that?
For in this way, internal emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense, by virtue of its ultimate non-apprehensibility;
external emptiness does not act, does not transform, and does not construct. Why is that?
For indeed, external emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended, based on its absolute non-apprehensibility;
internal-external emptiness does not act, does not transform, and does not construct. Why is that?

For in this way, internal-external emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended, because it is absolutely non-apprehensible; and so on, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, which neither acts, nor transforms, nor constructs. Why is that?
For thus, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence does not exist and is not apprehended,
by virtue of its absolute non-apprehensibility.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment do not act, do not transform, and do not perform formative activity. Why is that?
Because they absolutely do not exist and are not apprehended.

Likewise, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not act, do not transform, and do not perform formative activity. Why is that? Because they absolutely do not exist and are not apprehended.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, they do not exist and are not perceived in an absolute sense.
Suchness does not act, does not transform, and does not construct. For what reason?
For suchness (*tathatā*), Subhūti, does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense;

likewise, non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-otherness (*ananyatathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), awakening (*bodhi*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) do not act, do not transform, and do not perform any formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*). Why is that?
For they do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
Subhūti, by this method, omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) is uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned;
those sentient beings as well are uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned.

"For the sake of whom the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has donned this great armor. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is said to be 'donned in the great armor. Thus [ends] the equipment of insight.
Subhūti said:
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken,
form, O Blessed One, is neither bound nor liberated;
so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
“Consciousness, Blessed One, is neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said: “Venerable Subhūti, you say that form is neither bound nor liberated.”
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Subhūti, you say are neither bound nor liberated.
Subhūti replied:
"It is so, venerable Pūrṇa.
Pūrṇa asked: "Venerable Subhūti, what is that form which is neither bound nor liberated?
What are those feelings, perceptions, and mental formations?"
"What is that consciousness which is neither bound nor liberated?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Pūrṇa, that form which is like a dream is neither bound nor liberated."
Those feelings, perceptions, and mental formations which are like a dream,

and this consciousness which is like a dream— that is neither bound nor liberated. Likewise, O Venerable Pūrṇa, those things which are like an echo, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a reflection are neither bound nor liberated.
Form is like a magical creation; it is neither bound nor liberated.
Those feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and that consciousness which are like a magical creation are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
Venerable Pūrṇa, past form is neither bound nor liberated; past feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise]; Venerable Pūrṇa, past consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.

In the same way, Venerable Pūrṇa, future form is unbound and unliberated; present feeling, perception, and formations are unbound and unliberated; and, Venerable Pūrṇa, present consciousness is unbound and unliberated. For what reason?
Venerable Pūrṇa, because form does not exist, in that way, that form is neither bound nor liberated; Venerable Pūrṇa, because feeling, perception, and mental formations do not exist...

Because it does not exist, Venerable Pūrṇa, consciousness is thus neither bound nor liberated; likewise, because it is secluded, peaceful, empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, and unarisen, it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither afflicted nor free from affliction, neither blameworthy nor blameless, and neither with outflows nor without outflows.
Worldly and supramundane, defiled and purified—Venerable Pūrṇa, form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because form is non-existent, thus that form is neither bound nor liberated; so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
"Venerable Pūrṇa, consciousness—whether afflicted or purified—is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because consciousness is non-existent; thus, that consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.
Furthermore, Venerable Pūrṇa, all phenomena (dharmas) are also neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?"
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
The perfection of generosity, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is also neither bound nor liberated;

likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, O Venerable Pūrṇa, are also neither bound nor liberated.
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated; likewise, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Even internal emptiness, O Venerable Pūrṇa, is neither bound nor liberated.
Outer emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is also neither bound nor liberated; inner-and-outer emptiness, venerable Pūrṇa, is also neither bound nor liberated;
up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, venerable Pūrṇa, is also neither bound nor liberated. For what reason?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated; likewise, because they are secluded, up to because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
O Venerable Pūrṇa, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are neither bound nor liberated.
In this way, Āyuṣman Pūrṇa, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated; likewise, because they are secluded, and so on, up to because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Venerable Pūrṇa, awakening also is unbound and unliberated;
venerable Pūrṇa, omniscience also is unbound and unliberated;
even the bodhisattva is unbound and unliberated.
For what reason? Because of its non-existence, it is neither bound nor liberated;
likewise, because of its solitude, up to its unarisen nature, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Furthermore, Venerable Pūrṇa, suchness is neither bound nor liberated;

non-falsity, non-otherness, the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, and the limit of reality—Venerable Pūrṇa, these too are neither bound nor liberated. For what reason?
Because they do not exist, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Thus, because they are secluded, up to: because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
For in this way, venerable Pūrṇa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither bound nor liberated;
likewise, the six perfections are also neither bound nor liberated.
Even omniscience itself is neither bound nor liberated; even those beings whom he will lead to final nirvana are neither bound nor liberated.
They too are neither bound nor liberated;
even those Buddha-fields that he will purify are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whom he shall attend upon, they too are unbound and unliberated;
the Dharma which he shall hear, that too is unbound and unliberated;
and he shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, being himself unbound and unliberated.
He will not be devoid of the superknowledges, being neither bound nor liberated;
he will not be devoid of the five eyes, being neither bound nor liberated; likewise, he will not be devoid of other meditative concentrations, being neither bound nor liberated.
He will bring forth the knowledge of the aspects of the path, which is neither bound nor liberated;
he will realize the knowledge of all aspects, which is neither bound nor liberated;
and he will turn the wheel of Dharma, which is neither bound nor liberated.
Being himself unbound and unliberated, he will lead beings—who are likewise unbound and unliberated—to final nirvana by means of the three vehicles.

For it is thus, Venerable Pūrṇa, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being unbound and unliberated through the six perfections, will fully awaken to all dharmas on the basis of their non-existence; and so on, on the basis of their seclusion, up to their non-arising.
"Thus, venerable Pūrṇa, the great armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood as neither bound nor liberated. This concludes the equipment for the path of union.
Then, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, Blessed One, is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has set out in the Great Vehicle to be known? From where will that vehicle depart?"
"Where will that vehicle abide? Or who will set out by means of that vehicle?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Regarding what you have said, Subhūti:
"What is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? Subhūti, the six perfections are the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. What are the six?
The perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of generosity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects;
that is to say, having made internal and external things common to all sentient beings, [he gives them] for the sake of unsurpassed..."
He dedicates it toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and encourages others therein by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this is the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"What, Blessed One, is the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects,"

He himself undertakes and abides in the ten paths of wholesome action, and he also encourages others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this is the ungrasped perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, what is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with mental states associated with the knowledge of all aspects,”
He himself attains patience and encourages others to attain patience through the yoga of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this is the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
“What, Blessed One, is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One said:
“In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, never laying down the burden regarding the five perfections.”
And he encourages others in those five perfections by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the knowledge of all aspects,
yet he is not reborn under the power of those [afflictions]."
And he encourages others in the meditative concentrations by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"Lord, what is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with the knowledge of all aspects, does not adhere to any phenomena and contemplates the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."

And by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, he encourages beings toward the contemplation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Subhūti, this is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti, this is the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus is the equipment of skill in means.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, and the emptiness of non-dispersal.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of the nature of non-existence,
the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature.
In that regard, what is internal emptiness?
Internal phenomena are said to be the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Among these, the eye is empty of the eye, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The ear is empty of the ear, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
The nose is empty of the nose, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
This is its very nature:
the tongue is empty of a tongue, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
The body is empty of the body, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
The mind is empty of the mind, by reason of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is its very nature; this is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*)?
As for external phenomena, namely forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects:
therein, form is empty of form, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature: likewise, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
phenomena are empty of phenomena, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is their intrinsic nature;
this is called external emptiness.
In that regard, what is internal-external emptiness?
The six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases— this is called internal-external emptiness.
In that regard, which internal phenomena are empty of external phenomena?

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are internally empty of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects, by virtue of their being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is their very nature.
In that regard, which external phenomena are empty of internal phenomena?
Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena are empty of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, by virtue of their being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is their very nature; this is called internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of emptiness?
It is that which is the emptiness of all phenomena, and it is empty by means of that very emptiness, because it is neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of emptiness.
In that regard, what is the great emptiness?
The eastern direction is empty of the eastern direction.

In the same way, the southern, western, northern, northeastern, southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, downward, and upward directions are empty of the upward direction, by virtue of their being neither immutable nor indestructible.
Why is that? Because this is their very nature.
This is called the great emptiness.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the ultimate?
The ultimate is said to be nirvāṇa.
And that [nirvana] is empty of nirvana, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
In that regard, what is conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
The "conditioned" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therein, the desire realm is empty of the desire realm, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature:
the form realm is empty of the form realm, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is its very nature.
The formless realm is empty of the formless realm by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is its very nature;
this is called the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*)?
That which is called "unconditioned" is that which has no arising, no cessation, no duration, and no alteration;
this is called the unconditioned.
It is empty of the unconditioned by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature;
this is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
That whose limit is not apprehended is absolutely empty by means of its absoluteness, on account of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature.
This is called absolute emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end (*anavarāgraśūnyatā*)?
It is that for which neither a beginning nor an end is perceived.
It has no middle;
and for that which neither beginning, middle, nor end is perceived, there is neither coming nor going.
Even the beginning, middle, and end are empty of beginning, middle, and end, by virtue of being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. For what reason is that?
This is their intrinsic nature;
this is called the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-dispersal?
For that dharma there is no "dispersal" (*avakāra*); dispersal means scattering, casting away, or relinquishing.
It is non-dispersal because it is empty of non-dispersal, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason is that?
This is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)?

That which is the nature of all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, is not made by Śrāvakas, nor made by Pratyekabuddhas, nor made by Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is neither altered nor diminished. Nature is empty of nature, on account of its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. Why is that?
This is its intrinsic nature; this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

"All dharmas" refers to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects;

eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; and eye-contact, ear-contact, [nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact].

Olfactory contact, gustatory contact, tactile contact, mental contact; feeling conditioned by visual contact, feeling conditioned by auditory contact, feeling conditioned by olfactory contact, feeling conditioned by gustatory contact, feeling conditioned by tactile contact, and feeling conditioned by mental contact— these are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharmas*).
These unconditioned phenomena are called "all phenomena. In this regard, phenomena are empty of phenomena, by virtue of being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of all phenomena.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of specific characteristics?
Form is without characteristic by way of form.
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; perception has the characteristic of grasping; and mental formations have the characteristic of volitional construction.
Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing; this should be explained in detail.

Furthermore, whatever is the characteristic and non-characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and whatever is the characteristic and non-characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), all these phenomena are empty of their own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), on account of their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. Why is that?
This is their intrinsic nature; this is called the emptiness of specific characteristics.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-apprehension?
Those phenomena that are past, future, and present are not apprehended. Why is that?
Because the past is not apprehended in the future, nor is the future apprehended in the past;
and the past and future are not apprehended in the present.

Nor is this non-apprehension of them in the past and future something present; because they are pure from the beginning, it is based on their being neither immutable nor subject to destruction. Why is that?
This is their very nature; this is called the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*)?
There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to any conditioned phenomenon (*saṃyogika-dharma*) because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
A conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is empty of conjunction, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason?
This is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of existence?
"Existence" refers to the five aggregates of clinging;
and that existence is empty of existence, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because this is its very nature.
This is called the emptiness of existence.
In that regard, what is the emptiness of non-existence?
Non-existence refers to the unconditioned.
And that unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
This is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

For intrinsic nature is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), which is non-perversion; its emptiness by means of itself, based on its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction, is not produced by knowledge or vision. Why is that?
This is its very nature;
this is called the emptiness of intrinsic being (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
In that regard, what is the emptiness of other-being (*parabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains constant: the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the fixed order of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), suchness (tathatā), non-falsity (avitathatā), unalterable suchness (ananyatathatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
The emptiness of that [nature] by way of itself, based on its being neither immutable nor subject to destruction—this is called the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
It was not made by another. For what reason?
This is its very nature; this is called the emptiness of other-nature (parabhāva-śūnyatā).
This, Subhūti, is called the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
This is the equipment of knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:
Namely: the samādhi called Śūraṅgama,
the samādhi called Ratnamudra,
and the samādhi called Siṃhavikrīḍita.
the concentration named Sucandra, the concentration named Candradhvajaketu,
and the concentration named Sarvadharmodgata.
The samādhi called "Beholding the Summit," the samādhi called "Determined by the Dharmadhātu," and the samādhi called "The Banner of Certainty."
the concentration called "diamond-like," the concentration called "seal of entry into phenomena," and the concentration called "well-established king of concentrations."
the concentration named "Emission of Rays," the concentration named "Array of Powers," and the concentration named "Exalted."
the samādhi called "Entry into Etymological Explanations," the samādhi called "Thorough Entry into Designations," and the samādhi called "Beholding the Directions."
The samādhi called the Seal of the Foundation,
the samādhi called Unforgotten,
and the samādhi called the Ocean Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas.
The samādhi called Pervading Space,
the samādhi called Radiant, and the samādhi called Immeasurable Illumination.
The concentration named "unattached and unobstructed," the concentration named "the complete cutting off of the activity of all phenomena," and the concentration named "abandoning conflict."
the samādhi named Vairocana, the samādhi named Animisha, and the samādhi named Aniketasthita;
the concentration named "Thoughtless," the concentration named "Stainless Lamp," and the concentration named "Infinite Radiance."
the concentration named Prabhākara, the concentration named Samantāvabhāsa,
and the concentration named Śuddhasāra;
the samādhi named Vimalaprabha, the samādhi named Ratikara, and the samādhi named Vidyutpradīpa;
The concentration named Inexhaustible,
the concentration named Vajra-maṇḍala,
and the concentration named Free from Inexhaustibility.
the concentration called "immovable," the concentration called "unveiled," and the concentration called "sun-lamp."
the concentration named Moon-Pure,
the concentration named Pure Radiance, and the concentration named Light-Maker;
The concentration called "the maker of actions," the concentration called "banner of knowledge," and the concentration called "like a diamond."
the concentration called "stability of mind," the concentration called "universal illumination," and the concentration called "well-established."
the concentration named Jewel-Crest, the concentration named Seal of the Sublime Dharma,
and the concentration named Equality of All Phenomena;
the concentration named "Abandoning Delight," the concentration named "Exalted and Fulfilled in All Dharmas," and the concentration named "Dispersion."
The concentration called "The Distinction of All Dharma-Phrases," the concentration called "Equal Syllables," and the concentration called "Transcending Syllables."
The concentration called "severing of objective referents," the concentration called "unchanging," and the concentration called "without mode."
the concentration called non-entry into names and signs, the concentration called wandering without a home,
and the concentration called free from darkness;
the concentration named Endowed with Conduct, the concentration named Immovable,
and the concentration named Having Crossed Over the Sense Objects;

The concentration named "Attainment of the Accumulation of All Virtues," the concentration named "Certainty in the Stability of Mind," and the concentration named "Purity of the Blossoming of the Auspicious."
the concentration called "Possessing the Factors of Enlightenment," the concentration called "Infinite Radiance," and the concentration called "The Peerless Equal."
The samādhi called "Transcending All Phenomena," the samādhi called "Effecting Delimitation," and the samādhi called "Scattering Doubt."
the concentration called "without basis," the concentration called "single array," and the concentration called "accomplishment of forms."
The concentration named "Single-Form Array," the concentration named "Non-Engagement with Forms," and the concentration named "Piercing Through to the Foundation of All Phenomena."
The samādhi called "Entry into Conventional Sounds," the samādhi called "Liberated from the Syllables of Song and Resonance," and the samādhi called "Blazing Torch."
The concentration named Purification of Characteristics,
the concentration named Uncharacterized,
and the concentration named Endowed with the Excellence of All Aspects.
the concentration named "Rejoicing in Neither All Pleasure nor Pain," the concentration named "Inexhaustible Form," and the concentration named "Practice of the Dhāraṇī."
The samādhi called "the inclusion of all correctness and error," the samādhi called "the pacification of all obstructions and cessations," and the samādhi called "conformity and counter-conformity."
the samādhi named Vimalaprabha,
the samādhi named Sāravatī, and the samādhi named Paripūrṇacandravimala;
the concentration named Great Array, the concentration named Illuminator of All Aspects,
and the concentration named Equality of Concentrations;

The concentration named "convergence in the absence of conflict," the concentration named "convergence of all things in both the conflict-free and the having-a-refuge," and the concentration named "having no home in the wind."
the samādhi called "ascertained in the abiding of suchness," and the samādhi called "thoroughly crushing the defilement of the body."
The concentration called "Destroyer of Verbal Quarrels," the concentration called "Equal to the Sky," and the concentration called "Unstained Liberation through Non-attachment to Space."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called Śūraṅgama?
It is that samādhi by which one experiences the range of all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named Śūraṅgama.
In that regard, what is the samādhi called the "jewel-seal"?
That samādhi by which all samādhis are sealed is called the samādhi named the "jewel-seal."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "lion’s sport"?
That concentration in which, having remained, one sports with all concentrations—
this is called the concentration called "lion’s sport."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Beautiful Moon"?
That concentration in which, having remained, one illuminates all concentrations— this is called the concentration named "Beautiful Moon."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Moon Banner Emblem"?
That which upholds the banner of all samādhis is called the samādhi named "Moon Banner Emblem."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Surpassing All Phenomena"?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one rises above all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi "Surpassing All Phenomena."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "Beholding the Summit"?
It is that samādhi in which, having remained, one beholds the summits of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi named "Beholding the Summit."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "fixed in the realm of phenomena"?
That concentration in which, having remained, one attains certainty regarding the realm of phenomena—
this is called the concentration called "fixed in the realm of phenomena."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called "the banner of certainty" (niyatadhvajaketu)?
When one abides in this samādhi, one upholds the banner of certainty of all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named "the banner of certainty."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "diamond-like"?
That concentration in which, having remained, one is not broken by any concentrations—
this is called the concentration called "diamond-like."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called the Seal of Entry into Dharmas?
It is that samādhi wherein, having remained, one enters the seal of all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named the Seal of Entry into Dharmas.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Well-Established King of Concentrations"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one is established by means of the excellent establishment of the king of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named "Well-Established King of Concentrations."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Emission of Rays"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one emits rays from all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named "Emission of Rays."
In that regard, what is the concentration called the Array of Powers?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one maintains the array of powers of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named the Array of Powers.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Exalted" (*samudgata*)?
That concentration in which, having remained, all concentrations arise—
this is called the concentration named "Exalted."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "entry into the explanation of etymologies"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the explanation of the etymologies of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration named "entry into the explanation of etymologies."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "entry into designations"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one enters into the designations and names of all concentrations;
this is called the concentration "entry into designations."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Beholding the Directions"?
When one abides in this concentration, the directions of all concentrations are beheld;
this is called the concentration named "Beholding the Directions."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called the Seal of Support (*ādhāraṇamudra*)?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one maintains the seal of all samādhis;
this is called the samādhi named the Seal of Support.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "unfailing"?
When one abides in this concentration, all concentrations are not lost; this is called the concentration named "unfailing."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called the "Ocean-Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas"?
When one abides in this samādhi, all samādhis reach a state of inclusion and convergence;
this is called the samādhi named the "Ocean-Seal of the Convergence of All Dharmas."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "pervading space"?
It is the concentration wherein, having abided, one pervades all concentrations by means of the pervasion of space;
this is called the concentration called "pervading space."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Possessing Radiance" (*tejovatī*)?
It is the concentration in which, having abided, one blazes with the brilliance and wisdom of all concentrations;
therefore it is called the concentration "Possessing Radiance."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "immeasurable radiance"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained therein, the immeasurable becomes radiant;
therefore it is called the concentration "immeasurable radiance."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "unattached and unobstructed"?
It is the concentration in which, by abiding, one shines forth unobstructed by virtue of being free from all attachments; therefore it is called the concentration "unattached and unobstructed."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the severance of the activity of all phenomena"?
It is that concentration by which, when one abides therein, one severs the activity regarding all phenomena; therefore it is called the concentration "the severance of the activity of all phenomena.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "the abandonment of strife"?
Abiding in which concentration one abandons even the signs of all concentrations, let alone other signs of the afflictions;
therefore, it is called the concentration named "the abandonment of strife."
In that regard, what is the samādhi called Vairocana?
It is the samādhi in which, having remained, one illuminates, heats, and shines radiantly upon all samādhis;
therefore it is called the samādhi named Vairocana.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "unblinking"?
It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not seek any phenomenon;
therefore it is called the "unblinking" concentration.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "dwelling without a home"?

It is the concentration in which, having remained, one does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as a home among all concentrations; therefore it is called the concentration "dwelling without a home.
In that regard, what is the concentration called "thoughtless"?
Abiding in which concentration one does not give rise to inferior mental states and mental factors, it is therefore called the concentration named "mindless" (*niścitta*).
In that regard, what is the concentration named "stainless lamp" (*vimalapradīpa*)?
Abiding in which concentration one holds the lamp of all concentrations, it is therefore called the concentration named "stainless lamp."
In that regard, what is the concentration called "Infinite Radiance"?

It is the concentration by staying in which one produces infinite radiance; therefore it is called the concentration "Infinite Radiance. In that regard, what is the concentration called "Light-Maker"?
The concentration by abiding in which one produces the radiance of all concentrations is therefore called the concentration named "Light-Maker" (*prabhākara*).

In that regard, what is the concentration named "Universal Illumination" (*samantāvabhāsa*)? It is that concentration through the simultaneous attainment of which all the gateways of concentration are illuminated.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Universal Illumination.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Pure Essence"?
It is the concentration abiding in which one attains the pure equality of all concentrations.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Pure Essence.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Stainless Radiance"?
It is that concentration by remaining in which one draws forth the power of all concentrations and manifests all concentrations.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light).
In that regard, what is the concentration named Ratikara (Delight-Maker)?
It is that concentration by abiding in which one experiences the delight of all concentrations.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Producer of Delight.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Lightning Lamp"?
It is the concentration in which, having abided, one acts as a lamp for all concentrations.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Lightning-Lamp.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Inexhaustible"?
It is that concentration in which, having remained, one perceives neither the inexhaustibility nor the exhaustion of all concentrations.
Therefore, it is called the concentration named "Inexhaustible.
In that regard, what is the concentration named "Vajra-maṇḍala"?
It is the concentration by abiding in which one upholds all maṇḍalas of concentration.
This is called the samādhi named Vajramaṇḍala.
In that regard, what is the samādhi named Akṣayāpagata?
