That vehicle is equal to space; just as for space no eastern direction is discerned, nor a southern, nor a western, nor a northern, nor an intermediate direction, nor a downward, nor an upward direction— just so, Subhūti, for that vehicle no eastern direction is discerned, nor a southern, nor a western, nor a northern, nor an intermediate direction, nor a downward, nor an upward direction.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space is neither long nor short, neither round nor square, neither even nor uneven, and neither blue nor yellow nor red nor white nor crimson nor the color of crystal or silver;
in the very same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither long nor short, neither round nor square, neither even nor uneven, and neither blue nor yellow nor red nor white nor [crimson].
It is not madder-red, nor is it the color of crystal or silver;
therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space is neither past, nor future, nor present.
In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither past, nor future, nor present; therefore it is said that this vehicle is equal to space.
Just as, Subhūti, there is neither decrease nor increase in space, so it is with this vehicle.
In the same way, Subhūti, there is neither decrease nor increase in that Great Vehicle; therefore it is said, "That vehicle is equal to space.
Just as, Subhūti, for space there is neither defilement nor purification, so it is with that vehicle.
In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle has neither affliction nor purification; therefore it is said, "That vehicle is equal to space.
Just as, Subhūti, for space there is no arising, no cessation, no staying, no remaining, and no alteration of its state, so too is that vehicle.
In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle has no arising, no cessation, no staying, no persisting, and no alteration while staying; therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space.

Just as, Subhūti, space is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither defined nor undefined, even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither defined nor undefined; therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space."

Subhūti, just as space is not seen, not heard, not thought, and not cognized, even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is not seen, not heard, not thought, and not cognized; therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space. Subhūti, just as space is neither knowable nor unknowable, neither fully knowable nor to be fully known, neither to be abandoned nor to be realized, nor to be cultivated.

In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is not something to be known, nor something not to be known; it is not to be fully understood, nor is it to be fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, nor is it to be realized, nor is it to be cultivated. Therefore it is called "that vehicle which is equal to space.
Just as, Subhūti, space is neither a karmic result nor subject to the nature of maturation, so too is that vehicle.
In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither a karmic maturation nor subject to the nature of maturation; therefore it is called "that vehicle is equal to space.

Just as, Subhūti, space is not included within the desire realm, not included within the form realm, and not included within the formless realm, even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is not included within the desire realm, not included within the form realm, and not included within the formless realm; therefore it is called "that vehicle is equal to space."

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in space there is no first production of the thought [of awakening], no second, no third, no fourth, no fifth, no sixth, no seventh, no eighth, no ninth, nor a tenth;

even so, Subhūti, in that Great Vehicle there is no first production of the thought, no second, no third, no fourth, no fifth, no sixth, no seventh, no eighth, no ninth, nor a tenth production of the thought. Therefore, it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space."

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in space there is no stage of bright insight (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), no stage of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), no stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), no stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), no stage of refinement (*tanū-bhūmi*), no stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), and no stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*);

even so, Subhūti, in that Great Vehicle there is no stage of bright insight, no stage of the lineage, no stage of the eighth person, no stage of seeing, no stage of refinement, no stage of freedom from passion, and no stage of one who has completed what was to be done. Therefore, it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space."

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in space there is no fruit of stream-entry, no fruit of once-returning, no fruit of non-returning, no state of arhatship, no state of a pratyekabuddha, and no state of buddhahood;

even so, Subhūti, in that Great Vehicle there is no fruit of stream-entry, no fruit of once-returning, no fruit of non-returning, no state of arhatship, no state of a pratyekabuddha, and no state of buddhahood. Therefore, it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space."
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, in space there is no stage of a śrāvaka, no stage of a pratyekabuddha, and no stage of a perfectly enlightened buddha;

even so, Subhūti, within that Great Vehicle there is no stage of a śrāvaka, no stage of a pratyekabuddha, and no stage of a perfectly enlightened buddha. Therefore, it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space is neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, and neither conjoined nor disjoined.

In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither material nor immaterial; it is neither visible nor invisible; it is neither resistant nor non-resistant; it is neither joined nor disjoined. Therefore, it is called "that vehicle which is equal to space.
Just as, Subhūti, space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither peaceful nor unpeaceful; [so too is that vehicle].

In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither happiness nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither peaceful nor unpeaceful; therefore it is called "that vehicle is equal to space.

Just as, Subhūti, space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither wishless nor non-wishless, even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither wishless nor non-wishless; therefore it is called "that vehicle is equal to space."
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space is neither secluded nor non-secluded, neither light nor darkness;

even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither secluded nor non-secluded, neither light nor darkness. Therefore, it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space cannot be obtained and is not apprehended.
In the same way, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is not found and is not apprehended; therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space.

Just as, Subhūti, space is neither an expression nor a non-expression, even so, Subhūti, that Great Vehicle is neither an expression nor a non-expression; therefore it is said that "that vehicle is equal to space."
Thus is the departure through equanimity.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti said:
"Just as in space there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings,"
"In the same way, there is room within that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is; just as there is room in space for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings."
In the same way, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings. For what reason?
Subhūti, because of the non-existence of sentient beings, the non-existence of space should be understood;
because of the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Great Vehicle should be understood.
By this method also, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, those beings, that space, and that Great Vehicle—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of beings, the non-existence of space should be understood.
Through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Great Vehicle is to be known;
through the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of the immeasurable is to be known.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: those beings, that space, and that Great Vehicle—all this is non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of beings, the non-existence of space is to be known;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Great Vehicle is to be known.
Through the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of incalculable beings should be understood;
for in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, those who are beings, that which is space, that which is the Great Vehicle, and that which is the incalculable—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of sentient beings, the non-existence of the Tathāgata is to be known;
by the non-existence of the Tathāgata, the non-existence of space is to be known;
and by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be known.
By the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of immeasurable beings is to be understood;
for in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: those beings, that space, that Great Vehicle, and that which is immeasurable—all this is not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of beings, the non-existence of the Tathāgata is to be known;
by the non-existence of the Tathāgata, the non-existence of space is to be known.
Through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be known;
through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of the unconditioned is to be known;
through the non-existence of the conditioned, the non-existence of the immeasurable is to be known.
By the non-existence of the immeasurable, the non-existence of the incalculable is to be known;
by the non-existence of the incalculable, the non-existence of the infinite is to be known;
by the non-existence of the infinite, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be known.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, those who are sentient beings, the Tathāgata, space, the Great Vehicle, the unconditioned, the immeasurable, the incalculable, the infinite, and all dharmas—all these are not apprehended.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, one should understand the non-existence of a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer;
by the non-existence of a knower and a seer, one should understand the non-existence of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
and by the non-existence of the limit of reality, one should understand the non-existence of the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite.
Through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that there is room within that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, the self, and so on up to the knower and the seer, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the immeasurable, the incalculable, the infinite, and all phenomena—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, the non-existence of everything up to a knower and a seer is to be understood;
by the non-existence of a knower and a seer, the non-existence of the inconceivable realm is to be understood;
and by the non-existence of the inconceivable realm, the non-existence of the aggregate of form is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of the aggregate of form, the non-existence of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should be understood;
through the non-existence of the aggregate of consciousness, the non-existence of space should be understood;
and through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Great Vehicle should be understood.
Through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings is to be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that in this Mahāyāna there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, the self, up to and including all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of the knower and the seer, it should be known; by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, the non-existence of the eye should be known.
Through the non-existence of the eye, the non-existence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is to be understood;
through the non-existence of the mind, the non-existence of space is to be understood;
and through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be understood.
By the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings should be understood;
by the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena should be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that there is room within that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, up to and including all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of one who knows and one who sees, [this] should be understood;
by the non-existence of one who knows and one who sees, the non-existence of the perfection of generosity should be understood.

Through the non-existence of the perfection of generosity, the non-existence of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom should be known;
through the non-existence of the perfection of wisdom, the non-existence of space should be known;
and through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Great Vehicle should be known.
Through the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings is to be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room within that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, and so forth, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, one should understand the non-existence of the knower and the seer; by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, one should understand the non-existence of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and so on, up to the non-existence of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
By the existence of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the non-existence of space is to be known;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be known;
by the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite is to be known.
Through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the self, up to and including all phenomena—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of one who knows and one who sees, should be understood;

by the non-existence of one who knows and one who sees, the non-existence of the foundations of mindfulness should be understood; by the non-existence of the foundations of mindfulness, the non-existence of the right efforts should be understood.
Through the non-existence of the right efforts, the non-existence of the bases of psychic power is to be known;
through the non-existence of the bases of psychic power, the non-existence of the faculties is to be known;
through the non-existence of the faculties, the non-existence of the powers is to be known.
Through the non-existence of strength, the non-existence of the factors of enlightenment is to be known;
through the non-existence of the factors of enlightenment, the non-existence of the path is to be known;
through the non-existence of the path, the non-existence of the immeasurables is to be known.
Through the non-existence of the immeasurables, the non-existence of the meditative absorptions is to be understood;
through the non-existence of the meditative absorptions, the non-existence of the formless attainments is to be understood;
through the non-existence of the formless attainments, the non-existence of the analytical knowledges is to be understood.
Through the non-existence of the analytical knowledges, the non-existence of the ten powers is to be known;
through the non-existence of the ten powers, the non-existence of the grounds of self-confidence is to be known;
through the non-existence of the grounds of self-confidence, the non-existence of the unique qualities of a buddha is to be known.
Through the non-existence of the unique qualities of a Buddha, the non-existence of space should be known;
through the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna should be known;
through the non-existence of the Mahāyāna, the non-existence of the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite should be known.
Through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the self, and so on, up to all phenomena—all these are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, one should understand the non-existence of the knower and the seer;
by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, one should understand the non-existence of the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi);
and by the non-existence of the stage of the lineage, one should understand the non-existence of the stage of the eighth person (aṣṭamaka).
By the non-existence of the eighth stage, the non-existence of the stage of seeing should be understood;
by the non-existence of the stage of seeing, the non-existence of the stage of refinement should be understood;
by the non-existence of the stage of refinement, the non-existence of the stage of freedom from passion should be understood.
By the non-existence of the stage of one free from passion, the non-existence of the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done should be understood;
by the non-existence of the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done, the non-existence of space should be understood;
and by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna should be understood.
Through the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings is to be understood;
through the non-existence of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, the non-existence of all phenomena is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that in that Great Vehicle there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, and so forth, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of the self and sentient beings, up to the non-existence of the knower and the seer should be understood;
by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, the non-existence of the stream-enterer should be understood.
Through the non-existence of the stream-enterer, the non-existence of the once-returner is to be known;
through the non-existence of the once-returner, the non-existence of the non-returner is to be known;
through the non-existence of the non-returner, the non-existence of the arhat is to be known.
By the non-existence of Arhats, the non-existence of Pratyekabuddhas is to be understood;
by the non-existence of Pratyekabuddhas, the non-existence of all dharmas—up to space, the Mahāyāna, the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the infinite—is to be understood.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that in this Mahāyāna there is room for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings. Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: the self, and so on, up to all dharmas—all these are non-apprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the non-existence of a self and a sentient being, one should understand the non-existence of the knower and the seer;
by the non-existence of the knower and the seer, one should understand the non-existence of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
By the non-existence of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the non-existence of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is to be known;
by the non-existence of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the non-existence of the Tathāgata is to be known.
By the non-existence of the Tathāgata, the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is to be known;
by the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects, the non-existence of space is to be known;
by the non-existence of space, the non-existence of the Mahāyāna is to be known.
By the non-existence of the Great Vehicle, the non-existence of all phenomena up to that point is to be understood.
For in this way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the self, and so on, up to all phenomena—all these are not apprehended.

Subhūti, just as there is room within the realm of nirvāṇa for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, even so, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings. Subhūti, just as there is room in space for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings, [so it is with the Great Vehicle].
In the same way, Subhūti, there is room in that Great Vehicle for immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings.
This is the departure for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said:

"Furthermore, neither the coming nor the going of that Great Vehicle is seen, nor is its staying seen. It is thus, Subhūti: neither the coming nor the going of that Great Vehicle is seen, nor is its staying seen. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are immovable; they do not go anywhere, they do not come from anywhere, and they do not stay anywhere. For what reason?"

For indeed, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere; nor does the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, Subhūti, come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the suchness of form does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere;
[the same is true] for feeling, perception, mental formations, and Subhūti, the suchness of consciousness does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of form does not come from anywhere, it does not go anywhere, and it does not abide anywhere.

The intrinsic nature of feeling, the intrinsic nature of perception, the intrinsic nature of mental formations, and the intrinsic nature of consciousness, Subhūti, do not come from anywhere, they do not go anywhere, and they do not abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the characteristic of form does not come from anywhere, it does not go anywhere, and it does not abide anywhere;
the characteristic of feeling, the characteristic of perception, the characteristic of mental formations, and the characteristic of consciousness, Subhūti, do not come from anywhere,
they do not go anywhere, and they do not abide anywhere.

Subhūti, the nature of the eye does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere— neither its suchness, nor its intrinsic being, nor its characteristic. Likewise, Subhūti, the nature of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere— neither their suchness, nor their intrinsic being, nor their characteristic.
Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the earth element does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor does its suchness, its self-nature, or its characteristic.

Likewise, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor does their suchness, their self-nature, or their characteristic.
Subhūti, the nature of the dharma-realm does not come from anywhere, it does not go anywhere, and it does not abide anywhere;
neither the suchness, nor the intrinsic nature, nor the defining characteristic of the dharma-realm comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or abides anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of suchness does not come from anywhere, it does not go anywhere, and it does not abide anywhere.
The suchness of suchness does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; it has no intrinsic nature and no characteristic.
Subhūti, the nature of the limit of reality does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere;
the suchness of the limit of reality, the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality, and the characteristic of the limit of reality do not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of the inconceivable realm does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere.

Subhūti, the suchness of the inconceivable realm, the intrinsic nature of the inconceivable realm, and the characteristic of the inconceivable realm do not come from anywhere, do not go anywhere, and do not abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of the perfection of generosity does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere.

The suchness of the perfection of generosity does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor does the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, nor its characteristic. Likewise, the nature of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.

The suchness of the perfection of wisdom does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere; nor does the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, nor the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom, come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the fundamental nature of the applications of mindfulness likewise does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.

The suchness of the applications of mindfulness does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere; nor does the intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness, nor their characteristic.

Likewise, the nature of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path does not come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.

The suchness of the noble eightfold path does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere; nor, Subhūti, does the nature of the noble eightfold path, nor its characteristic, come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere.
The intrinsic nature of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere;
nor does the suchness of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments, nor their intrinsic nature [come from anywhere, go anywhere, or abide anywhere].
The characteristic of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of the ten powers of a Tathāgata does not come from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere;

neither the suchness of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the characteristic of the ten powers of a Tathāgata comes from anywhere, does not go anywhere, and does not abide anywhere.
It goes nowhere and does not abide anywhere;

likewise, Subhūti, the nature of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not come from anywhere nor go anywhere.
It goes nowhere and does not abide anywhere;

the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere; the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere; the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere.
It goes nowhere and does not remain anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and remains nowhere;

neither the suchness (*tathatā*) of awakening, nor the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of awakening, nor the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of awakening comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or remains anywhere.
Subhūti, the nature of the unconditioned does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere.
Neither the suchness of the unconditioned, nor the intrinsic nature of the unconditioned, nor the characteristic of the unconditioned comes from anywhere, goes anywhere, or abides anywhere.
This is the effortless departure.
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said:

"No beginning of this vehicle is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended; that vehicle is equal throughout the three times; therefore it is called the 'Great Vehicle,' the Great Vehicle.
So it is, Subhūti, so it is.

No beginning of this vehicle is apprehended, no end is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended; that vehicle is equal throughout the three times. Therefore, it is called the "Great Vehicle," the Great Vehicle.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the past time is empty of the past time.
The future time is empty of the future time;
the present time is empty of the present time;
the equality of the three times is empty of the equality of the three times.

The Mahāyāna is empty of the Mahāyāna; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. Subhūti, emptiness is not one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten. Therefore, by virtue of the equality of the three times, this vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is equal.
Nor is anything even or uneven perceived therein;
nor is passion perceived therein, nor is the absence of passion;
nor is hatred perceived, nor is the absence of hatred.
Neither delusion nor non-delusion is apprehended; neither name nor non-name is apprehended; and so on, until neither the wholesome nor the unwholesome is apprehended.
Neither the contaminated is perceived nor the uncontaminated; neither the blameworthy is perceived nor the blameless; neither affliction is perceived nor the absence of affliction.
Neither the destruction of afflictions nor the non-destruction of afflictions is apprehended;
neither the mundane nor the supramundane is apprehended;
neither defilement nor purification is apprehended.
Neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa is perceived;
herein neither permanence nor impermanence is perceived,
and neither pleasure nor suffering is perceived.
Neither a self nor a non-self is apprehended; neither the peaceful nor the unpeaceful is apprehended;
neither the realm of desire is apprehended nor the transcendence of the realm of desire.
The realm of form is not apprehended, nor is the transcendence of the realm of form;
the formless realm is not apprehended, nor is the transcendence of the formless realm. Why is that?
Because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended.
Subhūti, past form is empty of past form; future form is empty of future form;
present form is empty of present form. Likewise, past feeling, perception, and mental formations [are empty].
Past consciousness is empty of past consciousness; future consciousness is empty of future consciousness;
present consciousness is empty of present consciousness. For what reason?
In emptiness, past form is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended within emptiness—how much less could past form be apprehended within emptiness?
In emptiness, past feeling is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty...
It is not apprehended within emptiness;
how much less could past feeling be apprehended within emptiness?
Past perception is not apprehended within emptiness.
Emptiness itself is indeed empty; emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.

How, then, could past perception be apprehended within emptiness? Past formations are not apprehended within emptiness; emptiness itself is indeed empty; emptiness is not apprehended within emptiness.
Furthermore, how could past formations be apprehended in emptiness?
Past consciousness is not apprehended in emptiness; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could past consciousness be apprehended in emptiness?
Thus, in emptiness, future form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not apprehended.
In emptiness, present form is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended even within emptiness—how much less could present form be apprehended in emptiness?
In emptiness, present feeling is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended even within emptiness—how much less could present feeling be apprehended within emptiness?
In emptiness, present perception is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended even within emptiness.
Furthermore, how could a present perception be apprehended in emptiness?
Present formations are not apprehended in emptiness; since emptiness itself is empty and is not apprehended within emptiness, how then could present formations be apprehended in emptiness?

In emptiness, present consciousness is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended within emptiness—how much less could present consciousness be apprehended within emptiness?
In emptiness, past, future, and present form is not apprehended; since emptiness itself is empty, it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, moreover, could past, future, or present form be apprehended within emptiness?
Within emptiness, past, future, or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are not apprehended; for emptiness itself is empty, and it is not apprehended within emptiness.
How, then, could past, future, or present feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended within emptiness?
Subhūti, the perfection of giving is not apprehended from the perspective of the past;
Subhūti, the perfection of giving is also not apprehended from the perspective of the future;
Subhūti, the perfection of giving is also not apprehended from the perspective of the present.
Through the equality of the three times, the perfection of generosity is not apprehended.
Subhūti, within the equality of the three times, a past time is not apprehended; indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.
How much less, then, could the perfection of generosity—past, future, or present—be apprehended within that equality?
Thus, the perfection of ethical discipline is not apprehended in the past, future, and present time periods;
the perfection of patience is not apprehended in the past, future, and present time periods;
and the perfection of vigor is not apprehended in the past, future, and present time periods.
The perfection of meditation is not apprehended in the past, future, or present time-frames.

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended from the perspective of the past; Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended from the perspective of the future; and Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is also not apprehended from the perspective of the present.

Through the equality of the three times, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended. Subhūti, within equality, a past time is not apprehended, nor is a future or a present time apprehended; indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.
How much less, then, could the perfection of wisdom—past, future, or present—be apprehended within equality?
Furthermore, Subhūti, the foundations of mindfulness are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle; the foundations of mindfulness are not apprehended in the equality of the three times.
Subhūti, in equality the past, future, and present times are not apprehended;
indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.
How much less, then, will the foundations of mindfulness—past, future, and present—be apprehended within equality?
Likewise, the right efforts are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle;
the bases of psychic power are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle.

The faculties are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle; the powers are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle; the factors of enlightenment are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle.
The noble eightfold path is not apprehended in the past, future, or middle;
the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle;
and the ten powers of a Tathāgata are not apprehended in the past, future, or middle.
The four grounds of self-confidence are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle;
the four analytical knowledges are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle; and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle.

Due to the equality of the three times, the unique attributes of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are not apprehended; for, Subhūti, within equality, the past, future, and present times are not apprehended. Indeed, even equality itself is not apprehended within equality.

How much less, then, could the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— past, future, and present— be apprehended within that sameness? Furthermore, Subhūti, an ordinary person is not apprehended from the perspective of the past limit,
nor is an ordinary person apprehended from the perspective of the future limit.
From the perspective of the present, an ordinary person is not apprehended;
by the equality of the three times, an ordinary person is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because of the non-apprehension of sentient beings.

In this way, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas do not perceive a Tathāgata from the perspective of the past, they do not perceive a Tathāgata from the perspective of the future, and they do not perceive a Tathāgata from the perspective of the present.
The Tathāgata is not apprehended through the equality of the three times. Why is that?
Because of the non-apprehension of sentient beings.
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, [does not apprehend the Tathāgata] in the three times.
Having trained, one must fulfill omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva through the equality of the three times;
established herein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, will set forth toward omniscience.
Thus ends the departure from the extremes.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! This Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas has been well-spoken by the Blessed One."
In this regard, Blessed One, by training in this Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, of the past attained omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);
those Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, of the future who train in this Mahāyāna will also attain omniscience;

and those Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who are currently present, Blessed One, in the world-systems throughout the ten directions in incalculable universes, they too, having trained in this Mahāyāna, [will attain] omniscience.
"Therefore, Blessed One, this Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is indeed the equality of the three times.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
"Having trained in this Mahāyāna, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have attained, will attain, and are attaining omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Then Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this Elder Subhūti has been commissioned by the Tathāgata with respect to the perfection of wisdom; he would consider that the Mahāyāna should be taught."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"May it not be, O Blessed One, that I teach the Mahāyāna by overstepping the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
For indeed, Subhūti, you do not teach that the Mahāyāna conforms to the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, whatever wholesome factors conducive to awakening there may be—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all of them are included within and converge upon the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what are those wholesome factors conducive to awakening— the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas— which enter into and converge within the perfection of wisdom?"

The Blessed One said: "Namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,
the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— the four immeasurables, the four meditative concentrations, and the four..."

The formless attainments; the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;

the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness, and the state of dwelling in constant equanimity—these, Subhūti, are the wholesome factors conducive to awakening, the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas, which are all comprised within the perfection of wisdom.
They go to the assembly.

And, Subhūti, that which is the Great Vehicle, and that which is the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity;
and that which is form, and feeling, and perception, and mental formations, and consciousness—[all these are non-dual].
That which is the eye, that which is the ear, that which is the nose, that which is the tongue, that which is the body, and that which is the mind;
that which is form, that which is sound, that which is odor, that which is taste, that which is tangibility, and those which are mental phenomena;
and that which is visual consciousness, that which is auditory consciousness, that which is olfactory consciousness, and that which is gustatory consciousness...
And body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; and eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact;
and the feeling born of eye-contact, the feeling born of ear-contact, and the feeling born of nose-contact.
The feeling born of tongue-contact, the feeling born of body-contact, and the feeling born of mind-contact;
and the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and the immeasurables.
the meditative concentrations and the formless attainments; the powers of a Tathāgata and the grounds of self-confidence;
the four analytical knowledges and the [three] doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the unconditioned phenomena;
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and the realm of desire and the realm of form.
And that which is the formless realm, and internal emptiness, and external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness,

up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; and those meditative concentrations, and those gateways of mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī), and up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—

The Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), and nirvāṇa—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
By this method, Subhūti, you describe the Great Vehicle as being in conformity with the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, the Great Vehicle is not one thing and the perfection of wisdom another, nor the perfection of meditation another, nor the perfection of vigor another, nor the perfection of patience another, nor the perfection of ethical discipline another, nor the perfection of generosity another.
Thus, the Great Vehicle and the perfections of wisdom, meditation, vigor, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual; they are not divided into two.

Nor, Subhūti, is the Great Vehicle one thing and the applications of mindfulness another. For indeed, the Great Vehicle and the applications of mindfulness are non-dual; they are not divided into two.

Thus, the Great Vehicle is not one thing and the right efforts, bases of miraculous power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path another; for the Great Vehicle and the right efforts, bases of miraculous power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path are non-dual and indivisible. The Great Vehicle is not one thing and the immeasurables, dhyānas, and formless attainments another; for the Great Vehicle and the immeasurables, dhyānas, and formless attainments are non-dual and indivisible.

The Mahāyāna is not one thing and the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha another; for the Mahāyāna and the Buddha-qualities are non-dual and indivisible.
For this reason, Subhūti, you correctly designate the Mahāyāna as conforming to the perfection of wisdom.
Thus ends the departure by attainment.
Subhūti said:
"Moreover, Bhagavān, a bodhisattva does not come from the past limit,
nor does a bodhisattva come from the future limit."
A bodhisattva does not approach from the middle.
One should understand that because form is limitless, a bodhisattva is limitless;
likewise, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, a bodhisattva is to be understood as limitless. Form...
Even as "bodhisattva," it does not exist and is not apprehended;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not "bodhisattva."
Even so, it does not exist and is not apprehended;

for in this way, O Blessed One, since I do not apprehend and do not perceive a bodhisattva in any way whatsoever, in its entirety and in every respect, which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?
Moreover, Blessed One, this which is called "bodhisattva" is merely a name.
Just as one speaks of a "self, self," yet the self is ultimately unproduced,
so too, among phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, what form is there that is unproduced?
In the same way, feeling, perception, and mental formations are thus. What is that consciousness which is unarisen?

That which is unarisen is not form, feeling, perception, or mental formations; and that which is unarisen is not consciousness. Therefore, how shall I instruct this non-arising in the perfection of wisdom, which is itself non-arising?
Furthermore, apart from non-arising, no bodhisattva is apprehended who would course toward awakening.

If, when this is thus taught, the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become despondent, and his mind does not feel regret; if he is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, do you say this: 'A bodhisattva does not come from the prior limit'?"
A bodhisattva is not apprehended from the future limit,
nor is a bodhisattva apprehended from the middle.
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus?

"By the boundlessness of form, the boundlessness of the bodhisattva is to be known; likewise, by the boundlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the boundlessness of the bodhisattva is to be known.
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus?"

"Form is a bodhisattva"— even this is not found and is not apprehended; likewise, "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are a bodhisattva"— [this too is not found and is not apprehended].

Even so, it does not exist and is not apprehended; thus, not apprehending and not perceiving a bodhisattva mahāsattva in any way whatsoever, in any manner whatsoever, which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this: that "Bodhisattva" is merely a name?

Just as "self" is spoken of as "self," yet the self is ultimately unarisen, so too, among phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence, what is that form which is unarisen? What are those feelings, perceptions, and mental formations? What is that consciousness which is unarisen? And that which is unarisen is not [a thing].
Form is unarisen, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen; that which is unarisen is not consciousness.
How then shall I instruct and admonish that which is unarisen within the unarisen perfection of wisdom?
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this: that apart from the non-arising [of phenomena], no bodhisattva is apprehended who would practice for the sake of awakening?
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this?

If, when this is thus taught, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become dejected, does not feel regret, and his mind does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, by reason of the non-existence of a sentient being, a bodhisattva does not come from the past;
Venerable Śāriputra, by reason of the emptiness of a sentient being, a bodhisattva does not come from the past."
Venerable Śāriputra, because a sentient being is isolated, a bodhisattva is not apprehended from the perspective of the past;
venerable Śāriputra, because a sentient being lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva is not apprehended from the perspective of the past.
The same should be said for the future and the middle. For what reason?
Because existence and non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and intrinsic nature are not apprehended in the prior limit and so forth,

and because existence, non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and intrinsic nature are not one thing while the bodhisattva and the prior limit and so forth are another— indeed, that which is existence and non-existence, up to that which is the middle— all this, through the non-existence of form, does not approach a bodhisattva from the perspective of the prior, posterior, or middle limits.
By way of the emptiness of form, the seclusion of form, and the lack of intrinsic nature of form, a bodhisattva does not approach [it] from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle;
likewise, by way of the non-existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, a bodhisattva does not approach them from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle;

by way of the emptiness of consciousness, the seclusion of consciousness, and the lack of intrinsic nature of consciousness, a bodhisattva does not approach it from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle.

In this way, it should be said that a bodhisattva does not approach [the concept of] the sense bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), or the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) from the perspective of the past limit, the future limit, or the middle.

Because of the non-existence of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), a bodhisattva does not approach [the concept of] a bodhisattva from the perspective of the past limit, the future limit, or the middle;

because of the emptiness of the perfection of generosity, the seclusion of the perfection of generosity, and the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, a bodhisattva does not approach [the concept of] a bodhisattva from the perspective of the past limit, the future limit, or the middle.

In this way, by means of the existence of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle.

By means of the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, the seclusion of the perfection of wisdom, and the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, in the existence, emptiness, and seclusion of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom—
Within the absence of intrinsic nature, the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle are not apprehended.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, non-existence is not one thing, emptiness another, detachment another, the absence of intrinsic nature another, and the bodhisattva another;

nor is the perfection of generosity another, the perfection of ethical discipline another, the perfection of patience another, the perfection of vigor another, the perfection of meditative concentration another, the perfection of wisdom another, and the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle another.

Thus, venerable Śāriputra, that which is non-existence, up to the state of having non-existence as its intrinsic nature, the six perfections, the bodhisattva, and the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle— all this, venerable Śāriputra, is such that a bodhisattva does not approach it within the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle. By way of the non-existence of internal emptiness, by way of emptiness, by way of solitude, and by way of the absence of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva does not approach [anything] from the perspective of the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle.

In this way, up to the point of the existence, emptiness, detachment, and lack of intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] from the past limit, the future limit, or the middle. Why is that?

Because, venerable Śāriputra, within the existence, emptiness, detachment, and lack of intrinsic nature of internal emptiness, up to the existence, emptiness, detachment, and lack of intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, the past limit, the future limit, and the middle are not apprehended.

Moreover, Śāriputra, non-existence is not one thing, emptiness another, detachment another, the absence of intrinsic nature another, and the bodhisattva yet another; nor are the past, future, and middle [extremes] different.

For indeed, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is internal emptiness—non-existence, emptiness, detachment, and the absence of intrinsic nature, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities—non-existence, emptiness, detachment, and the absence of intrinsic nature, and that which is the bodhisattva: [these are all one].

And those things which belong to the past limit, the future limit, and the middle—all this is non-dual. In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva does not approach [as a real entity] within the past, future, and middle limits.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, because of the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), a bodhisattva does not approach [as a real entity] within the past, future, and middle limits.

In this way, by virtue of the non-existence, emptiness, isolation, and lack of intrinsic nature of the right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, limbs of enlightenment, path, immeasurables, meditative concentrations, formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
a bodhisattva does not approach them in the past, future, or middle. Why is that?

For indeed, Venerable Śāriputra, within the non-existence, emptiness, seclusion, and lack of intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness, up to the non-existence, emptiness, seclusion, and lack of intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the prior limit, the later limit, and the middle are not apprehended;
nor, Śāriputra, is non-existence, emptiness, seclusion, and lack of intrinsic nature one thing, and the applications of mindfulness another.

In this way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the other eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the other [factors] such as the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle— O Venerable Śāriputra, it is because the non-existence, emptiness, seclusion, and lack of intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness, up to and including... [is likewise].

That which is the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and that which is the Bodhisattva, and those which are the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle— all this is non-dual. In this manner, venerable Śāriputra,
a Bodhisattva does not approach [them] in terms of the prior limit, the subsequent limit, or the middle.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, because of the non-existence of all samādhis, the non-existence of all doors of dhāraṇī, the non-existence of the dharma-realm, the non-existence of suchness, the non-existence of the limit of reality, the emptiness of the limit of reality, the seclusion of the limit of reality, and the lack of intrinsic nature of the limit of reality, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] in the past, future, or middle. Why is that?

For indeed, Venerable Śāriputra, within the non-existence of samādhi, up to the non-existence of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the emptiness of the limit of reality, the seclusion of the limit of reality, and the lack of intrinsic nature of the limit of reality, there are no prior limits, posterior limits, or middle; nor, Śāriputra, is non-existence one thing, emptiness another, seclusion another, lack of intrinsic nature another, the bodhisattva another, samādhi another, the entrance to the dhāraṇīs another, the dharma-realm another, suchness another, or the limit of reality another.

The others are the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle. Thus, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-existence of samādhi, up to and including the non-existence of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—emptiness, solitude, and the absence of intrinsic nature—and that which is the bodhisattva and those which are the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle:
all this is non-dual. In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva does not approach [any of] the prior limit, the posterior limit, or the middle.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, by way of the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the *śrāvaka*, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] in the past, future, or middle;

by way of the non-existence of the *pratyekabuddha*, the non-existence of the bodhisattva, the non-existence of the omniscient one (*sarvajña*), the emptiness of the omniscient one, the solitude of the omniscient one, and the lack of intrinsic nature of the omniscient one, a bodhisattva does not approach [them] in the past, future, or middle. Why is that?

For indeed, Venerable Śāriputra, within the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the śrāvaka, and so on up to the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the omniscient one, neither the prior limit, the subsequent limit, nor the middle are perceived. Furthermore, Śāriputra, non-existence is not one thing, emptiness another, solitude another, lack of intrinsic nature another, the śrāvaka another, the pratyekabuddha another, the bodhisattva another, and the omniscient one another.

The others are the past, the future, and the middle. Thus, venerable Śāriputra, the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the śrāvaka, up to the non-existence, emptiness, solitude, and lack of intrinsic nature of the omniscient one, and that which is the bodhisattva and those which are the past, the future, and the middle— [all these are empty].
All this is non-dual. In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva does not approach [anything] in the past, the future, or the middle.
Thus, regarding the departure [from saṃsāra], there is the negation of that which is to be attained.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as for what you said:

For what reason should the boundlessness of the bodhisattva be understood through the boundlessness of form; and why should the boundlessness of the bodhisattva be understood through the boundlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Form, venerable Śāriputra, is equal to space;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, are equal to space. For what reason?
Venerable Śāriputra, it is just as, for example, no prior limit of space is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended;
yet, because it is infinite and boundless, it is conventionally designated as "space.
In the very same way, Venerable Śāriputra, no prior limit of form is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended. Why is that?
Based on the emptiness of form. Furthermore, neither a prior limit, nor a subsequent limit, nor a middle is apprehended in emptiness;
likewise, for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, no prior limit is apprehended, no subsequent limit is apprehended, and no middle is apprehended. For what reason?
Based on the emptiness of consciousness. Furthermore, neither a prior limit, nor a later limit, nor a middle of emptiness is apprehended;
yet it is conventionally designated as "emptiness.
By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, one should understand that because form is limitless, the bodhisattva is likewise limitless.
Through the boundlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the boundlessness of the bodhisattva is to be understood.

Likewise, among the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, both individually and collectively, and throughout dependent origination up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair;

and among the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.
The unique qualities of a Buddha, Venerable Śāriputra, are equal to space. Why is that?

It is because, Venerable Śāriputra, just as in the case of space, neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle can be apprehended; it is designated as "space" only because it is infinite and boundless. In the very same way, Venerable Śāriputra, for the qualities of a Buddha, there is neither a beginning nor an end.
A middle is not apprehended, by reason of the emptiness of the Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore, neither a prior limit, nor a subsequent limit, nor a middle is apprehended within emptiness.
By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, one should understand that because the Buddha-dharmas are limitless, the Bodhisattva is likewise limitless.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as for what you said: "For what reason is it that 'form is a bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended, nor do feeling, perception, and mental formations [exist and are not apprehended]?"
"Is it that even 'consciousness is a bodhisattva' does not exist and is not apprehended?
"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form; feeling, perception, and mental formations [are likewise empty]."
Consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, is empty of consciousness. For what reason?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, form does not exist in emptiness, nor does a bodhisattva exist in emptiness; nor do feeling, perception, or mental formations exist.
Consciousness does not exist in emptiness,
nor does a bodhisattva exist in emptiness. By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, form is a bodhisattva.
Even so, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist and are not apprehended as "a bodhisattva."
Even so, it does not exist and is not apprehended.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of generosity is empty of the perfection of generosity;
the perfection of ethical discipline is empty of the perfection of ethical discipline.
The perfection of patience is empty of the perfection of patience;
the perfection of vigor is empty of the perfection of vigor;
the perfection of meditation is empty of the perfection of meditation.
The perfection of wisdom is empty of the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because within emptiness the perfection of generosity does not exist, nor does the bodhisattva exist within emptiness;
likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration [do not exist].
In emptiness, the perfection of wisdom is not found; in emptiness, the bodhisattva is not found. Venerable Śāriputra, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness;
likewise, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, that is empty of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
The foundations of mindfulness are empty of the foundations of mindfulness.

In this way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses,
the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The dharma-realm is empty of the dharma-realm; meditative concentration is empty of meditative concentration; the gateways of mnemonic formulas are empty of the gateways of mnemonic formulas; omniscience is empty of omniscience; the knowledge of the aspects of the path is empty of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;

the knowledge of all aspects is empty of the knowledge of all aspects; the vehicle of the śrāvakas is empty of the vehicle of the śrāvakas; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas is empty of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.

The Buddha-vehicle is empty; by means of the Buddha-vehicle it is empty. A śrāvaka is empty of being a śrāvaka; a pratyekabuddha is empty of being a pratyekabuddha; a Tathāgata is empty of being a Tathāgata. For what reason?
Because within emptiness no Tathāgata is found, and within emptiness no bodhisattva is found.
In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, "form is a bodhisattva" does not exist and is not apprehended;
likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations [do not exist and are not apprehended].
"Consciousness is a bodhisattva"—
even this is neither found nor apprehended.
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Śāriputra said:
For what reason do you speak thus:
"Since I do not apprehend and do not perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva in any way whatsoever, in any manner whatsoever, which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?"
Form, venerable Śāriputra, does not exist and is not apprehended within form;
form does not exist and is not apprehended within feeling;
feeling does not exist and is not apprehended within feeling.
Feeling does not exist and is not apprehended in form;
both form and feeling do not exist and are not apprehended in perception;
perception does not exist and is not apprehended in perception.
Perception does not exist and is not apprehended in form;
perception does not exist and is not apprehended in both form and feeling;
form, feeling, and perception do not exist and are not apprehended in mental formations.
Formations do not exist and are not apprehended within formations;
formations do not exist and are not apprehended within form, feeling, and perception;
form, feeling, perception, and formations do not exist and are not apprehended within consciousness.
Consciousness does not exist and is not perceived in consciousness;
consciousness does not exist and is not perceived in form, feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Furthermore, O Venerable Śāriputra, the eye does not exist and is not perceived in the eye.
The eye is not found and is not perceived in the ear; the ear is not found and is not perceived in the eye;
and the eye and the ear together are not found and are not perceived in the nose.
The nose does not exist and is not perceived in the nose;
the nose does not exist and is not perceived in the eye or the ear;
the eye, ear, and nose do not exist and are not perceived in the tongue.
The tongue does not exist and is not perceived in the tongue;
the tongue does not exist and is not perceived in the eye, ear, or nose;
the eye, ear, nose, and tongue do not exist and are not perceived in the body.
The body does not exist and is not perceived within the body;
the body does not exist and is not perceived within the eye, ear, nose, or tongue;
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body do not exist and are not perceived within the mind.
The mind does not exist and is not apprehended within the mind;
the mind does not exist and is not apprehended within the eye, ear, nose, tongue, or body.
Form does not exist and is not perceived in form;
form does not exist and is not perceived in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Sound does not exist and is not perceived in sound, odor, or taste.
Sound does not exist and is not perceived in others; likewise, odor does not exist and is not perceived in odor or in others;
taste does not exist and is not perceived in taste or in others.
Contact does not exist and is not perceived in contact, nor in other things; phenomena do not exist and are not perceived in phenomena, nor in others.
Eye-consciousness does not exist and is not perceived in eye-consciousness, nor in anything else.
The others do not exist and are not perceived within one another;
likewise, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness do not exist and are not perceived within mind-consciousness,
nor do they exist and are not perceived within the others.
Eye-contact does not exist and is not apprehended within eye-contact;
it does not exist and is not apprehended in other things either;
and therein, those other things do not exist and are not apprehended.
In the same way, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact do not exist and are not apprehended in mind-contact;
nor do they exist and are not apprehended in the others;
for therein the others neither exist nor are apprehended.
Feeling born of eye-contact does not exist and is not perceived within feeling born of eye-contact;
therein, and likewise in others, it does not exist and is not perceived.
In the same way, [feeling] born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, and feeling born of body-contact [are to be understood].
Feeling born of mental contact does not exist and is not apprehended within feeling born of mental contact;
therein, one is not found in the other, nor is it apprehended.
The foundations of mindfulness do not exist and are not apprehended within the foundations of mindfulness.
In this way, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,

the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha [are included] within the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They do not exist and are not apprehended among the qualities of a Buddha;
likewise, those [qualities] do not exist and are not apprehended within one another.

Internal emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended within internal emptiness; internal emptiness, moreover, does not exist and is not apprehended up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
the emptiness of the nature of non-existence does not exist and is not apprehended within the emptiness of the nature of non-existence.
Even the emptiness of the nature of non-existence does not exist and is not apprehended within internal emptiness.
Concentration does not exist and is not apprehended within concentration;
concentration does not exist and is not apprehended within the dhāraṇīs.
A dhāraṇī does not exist and is not apprehended within a dhāraṇī; dhāraṇīs do not exist and are not apprehended within a samādhi.
The stage of an ordinary person does not exist and is not apprehended within the stage of an ordinary person.

In this way, the stage of the lineage, the stage of the eighth person, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from passion, the stage of one who has completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata— even the stage of omniscience— is not found and is not apprehended within the stage of omniscience.
The stream-enterer is not found and is not apprehended in the state of being a stream-enterer.
In this way, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha do not exist and are not apprehended in the state of a pratyekabuddha;
the bodhisattva does not exist and is not apprehended in the state of a bodhisattva; and the Tathāgata does not exist and is not apprehended in the state of a Tathāgata.
The perfection of wisdom does not exist and is not apprehended in the perfection of wisdom;
the instruction and admonition do not exist and are not apprehended in the perfection of wisdom; and the perfection of wisdom does not exist and is not apprehended in the instruction and admonition.
For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, because all phenomena are non-existent and unapprehendable, the bodhisattva is neither existent nor apprehendable.
Thus, regarding the departure through attainment, there is the negation of the attainer.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as for what you have said:
For what reason is this a mere name, namely "bodhisattva"?
For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus?
This designation "bodhisattva" is adventitious and merely superimposed;

for, Venerable Śāriputra, a name does not come from anywhere among the ten directions, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it abide anywhere. Even the name of bodhisattvas, which is itself a dharma, does not come from anywhere.
It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, nor does it abide anywhere;

this is merely an adventitious designation. For that which is called "form," "feeling," "perception," "formative factors," or "consciousness"—that designation is not form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formative factors, nor consciousness. Why is that?
For indeed, that which is called "name" is empty of the intrinsic nature of a name, and that which is empty is not a name;
for that reason it is said that "Bodhisattva" is merely a designation.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, this which is called "perfection of generosity" is merely a designation.
There is no perfection of giving in the name, nor is there the perfection of giving in the name.
Why is that?
Because both that which is the name and that which is the perfection of giving—neither of these exists, nor is either apprehended.
Therefore, "bodhisattva" is merely a name;
likewise, "perfection of ethical discipline," "perfection of patience," "perfection of vigor," and "perfection of meditative concentration" are merely names;
and even "perfection of wisdom" is merely a name, for there is no name within the perfection of wisdom, nor...
Regarding the name "Perfection of Wisdom," for what reason is that?
