Because both that which is the name and that which is the Perfection of Wisdom— neither of these two exists nor is it apprehended.
Therefore, this which is called "bodhisattva" is a mere name;
this designation "bodhisattva" is adventitious and has been superimposed.

This is merely a name, namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. Yet, within internal emptiness there is no name, nor is there internal emptiness within the name;
and this applies to external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
For what reason?

Because that which is called "name," and internal emptiness, and external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence—all these do not exist.
In this manner, Venerable Śāriputra, this is a mere name, namely, "bodhisattva."
Śāriputra, this designation "foundations of mindfulness" is adventitiously applied;
yet there is no name in the foundations of mindfulness, nor are the foundations of mindfulness in the name. Why is that?
Because both that which is the name and those which are the foundations of mindfulness—both of these do not exist and are not apprehended.

In this way, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges—
these are adventitious names that have been superimposed; namely, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Thus, among the Buddha-qualities there is no name, nor are the Buddha-qualities in the name. Why is that?
Because both the name and the Buddha-qualities do not exist and are not apprehended; this designation "samādhi" is a mere adventitious appellation, superimposed [upon them].
Up to omniscience, there is no name in omniscience, nor is there omniscience in the name. Why is that?
Because both that which is the name and that which is omniscience—neither of these exists, nor is either perceived.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as for what you said: "For what reason is it said that 'self, self' is spoken of,
yet the self is ultimately unproduced?"
Śāriputra, the self (*ātman*) does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense; how then could there be its production?

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a sentient being (*sattva*), a living soul (*jīva*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*puruṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), a human (*manuja*), a youth (*mānava*), an agent (*kāraka*), an experiencer (*vedaka*), a knower (*jānaka*), or a seer (*paśyaka*) does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
How, then, could there be the arising of this?
Venerable Śāriputra, form does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense;
how, then, could there be the arising of this?
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—
Venerable Śāriputra, consciousness does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be its arising?
Venerable Śāriputra, the eye does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
how then could there be its production?
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The mind does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense;
how, then, could its arising occur?
Form also does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense.
From where, then, will its arising come about?
In this same way, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles— dharmas do not exist at all, nor are they perceived.
How, then, will there be the arising of these?
Since visual consciousness absolutely does not exist and is not apprehended,
how, then, will there be its arising?
Thus, in an ultimate sense, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness do not exist and are not apprehended;
how, then, could there be the arising of these?
In an ultimate sense, visual contact does not exist and is not apprehended.
How, then, could there be the arising of this?
In the same way, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact do not exist and are not apprehended;
how, then, could there be the arising of these?
Mind-contact does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense;
how then could its production occur?
Feeling born of eye-contact does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
How, then, could there be the production of this?
Sensation born of ear-contact, sensation born of nose-contact, sensation born of tongue-contact, and sensation born of body-contact do not exist and are not apprehended in an ultimate sense.
How, then, could its arising occur?
Feeling born of mental contact does not exist and is not apprehended in an absolute sense;
how, then, could its arising occur?
Ultimately, the perfection of generosity does not exist and is not apprehended;
how, then, could there be its arising?
Likewise, ultimately, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration do not exist and are not apprehended.
How, moreover, could there be the arising of this?
Since the perfection of wisdom does not exist and is not apprehended in an ultimate sense,
how, moreover, could there be the arising of it?
Ultimately, internal emptiness does not exist and is not apprehended;
how, then, could there be its arising?
Likewise, ultimate external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, do not exist and are not apprehended.
How, then, will its manifestation come about?
Since the foundations of mindfulness do not exist and are not perceived in an ultimate sense,
how, then, will their manifestation come about?

Thus, in an ultimate sense, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path do not exist and are not apprehended;

likewise, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges do not exist and are not apprehended— how then could there be the manifestation of these?
Ultimately, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist and are not apprehended;
how then could their manifestation ever occur?
Ultimately, the meditative concentrations and the gateways of mnemonic formulas do not exist and are not apprehended.
How, then, could there be the manifestation of these?
Since, in an absolute sense, the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha do not exist and are not apprehended,
how, then, could there be the manifestation of these?
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, it is said that "self,
self," yet the self is absolutely unproduced.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as to what you have said:
"All dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature"—this is so. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, there is no composite intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, of what is there no inherent nature produced by combination?
Subhūti replied:
Venerable Śāriputra, form has no inherent nature produced by combination;
venerable Śāriputra, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no inherent nature produced by combination;
the eye has no inherent nature produced by combination.

In this way, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind have no inherent nature arising from conjunction; likewise, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena have no inherent nature arising from conjunction;
and visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness have no inherent nature arising from conjunction.

There is no inherent nature produced by conjunction in visual contact, auditory contact, olfactory contact, gustatory contact, tactile contact, or mental contact; nor is there such an inherent nature in the feeling born of visual contact, the feeling born of auditory contact, the feeling born of olfactory contact,
the feeling born of gustatory contact, the feeling born of tactile contact, or the feeling born of mental contact.
There is no inherent nature produced by combination in the feeling conditioned by eye-contact, nor in the feeling conditioned by ear-contact, nor in the feeling conditioned by nose-contact,
nor in the feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, nor in the feeling conditioned by body-contact, nor in the feeling conditioned by mind-contact.
There is no inherent nature produced by combination;

there is no inherent nature produced by combination in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom. By this, O Venerable One...
“Śāriputra, in another sense, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, all phenomena are impermanent, not by way of the departure of anything.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, which are those impermanent all dharmas that do not exist through the departure of anything?
Subhūti replied:
"Form, venerable Śāriputra, is impermanent, not through the departure of anything."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, are impermanent, not by way of the departure of anything. For what reason?

Because, venerable Śāriputra, that which is impermanent is non-existence and exhaustion. Likewise, all phenomena—whether painful, selfless, peaceful, empty, signless, or wishless—are not by way of the departure of anything; they are wholesome and blameless.
They are untainted, free from afflictions, supramundane, purified, and unconditioned. Why is that?

Because, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is unconditioned is non-existence and exhaustion; thus, Venerable Śāriputra, by this method all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, not through the disappearance of anything. Furthermore, Śāriputra, they are immutable...
"All dharmas are indestructible.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, are all dharmas neither immutable nor indestructible?"
Subhūti said: "Form, venerable Śāriputra, is neither immutable nor indestructible. For what reason? This is its very nature."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Śāriputra, are neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that?
Because this is their very nature.

Thus, it is wholesome, unwholesome, faulty, faultless, with outflows, without outflows, afflicted, free from affliction, mundane, supramundane, conditioned, unconditioned, affliction, purification, saṃsāra, and nirvāṇa—neither immutable nor subject to destruction. Why is that?
Because this is its very nature.
"By this method, Venerable Śāriputra, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:
'For what reason is form unconditioned? Likewise, for what reason are feeling, perception, and mental formations unconditioned? For what reason is consciousness unconditioned? Subhūti replied:"
For in this way, venerable Śāriputra, form is unproduced; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unproduced. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, there is no agent of volitional construction; the eye, venerable Śāriputra, is unconstructed. Why is that?
For it is thus, venerable Śāriputra: there is no agent of volitional construction;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unconstructed. Why is that?
For it is thus, venerable Śāriputra: there is no agent of volitional construction.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are unconditioned. Why is that?
Because an agent who conditions them is not apprehended; indeed, all phenomena are unconditioned. Why is that?
Because an agent who conditions them is not apprehended.
"In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unproduced. Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:
'For what reason is that which is unproduced not form, not feeling, not perception, not mental formations, and not consciousness?
Subhūti replied:"
For in this way, venerable Śāriputra, form is empty by nature; and that which is empty by nature has neither arising nor passing away;
and for that which has neither arising nor passing away, no alteration is perceived.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty by nature; and that which is empty by nature has neither arising nor passing away.
That which has neither arising nor passing away is not perceived to undergo change.

Thus, up to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), they are empty by nature; and those which are empty by nature have neither arising nor passing away, and for those which have neither arising nor passing away, no change is perceived.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, that which is unproduced is not form, not feeling, not perception, not formations, and not consciousness.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as for what you asked: "For what reason do you speak thus? [it is because]...
Therefore, how could I instruct or admonish non-arising within non-arising Prajñāpāramitā?
For, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is non-arising is Prajñāpāramitā, and that which is Prajñāpāramitā is non-arising.
Thus, Prajñāpāramitā and non-arising are non-dual; this is an undifferentiated unity. It is by this method, Venerable Śāriputra, that I speak thus.
"So then, how shall I instruct and admonish non-arising in the perfection of wisdom which is itself non-arising?
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as for what you said:
'And apart from non-arising, no bodhisattva is found who would course toward awakening'—"

For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive non-arising as one thing and the bodhisattva as another; for non-arising and the bodhisattva are non-dual and indivisible.
Apart from non-arising, he does not perceive form.
One does not perceive feeling, perception, or mental formations other than non-arising;
one does not perceive consciousness other than non-arising.
For indeed, non-arising and form are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and feeling, perception, and mental formations are non-dual; this is an undifferentiated unity.
For thus, non-arising and consciousness are non-dual; this is an undifferentiated unity.
For thus, non-arising and the eye are non-dual; this is an undifferentiated unity.
For thus, non-arising and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are non-dual;
this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and eye-consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and mind-consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and eye-contact are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-arising and mind-contact are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-attachment and the feelings conditioned by eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.

For thus, non-attachment and the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
For thus, non-attachment and the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.

For thus, non-attachment and the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are non-dual; they are not divided into two.
For thus, non-attachment and the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Up to:
for thus, non-attachment and all phenomena are non-dual; they are not divided into two.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who would practice for the sake of awakening is not apprehended apart from non-arising.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked: "For what reason do you speak thus? [the answer is: because there is no other way.

If, when this is being taught in this way, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not shrink back, does not sink down, does not become regretful, and his mind does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into fear, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
For in this way, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as devoid of activity;

he perceives them as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shimmering optical illusion, like a magical creation, and like a city of the Gandharvas.

In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is thus instructed, his mind does not shrink back, does not sink down, and does not become regretful; his mind is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall into terror.
Thus the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena,
at that time he does not approach form, does not take it up, does not dwell upon it, does not adhere to it, and does not designate it as 'this is form.'"

Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena, at that time he does not approach, does not grasp, does not settle upon, does not adhere to, and does not designate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "this is consciousness.
At that time, he does not approach, does not grasp, does not settle upon, does not adhere to, and does not designate the eye as "this is the eye."

In this way, he does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not become attached to, and does not designate the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind as "this is the mind. Furthermore, Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena, at that time he does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not become attached to, and does not designate the perfection of generosity.

"This is the perfection of generosity. Likewise, at that time, he does not approach, grasp, dwell upon, adhere to, or designate the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as "this is the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, he does not approach, grasp, dwell upon, adhere to, or designate internal emptiness as "this is internal emptiness."

At that time, he does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not become attached to, and does not designate external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, thinking, "This is the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena...
At that time, one does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not adhere to, and does not designate the foundations of mindfulness as "these are the foundations of mindfulness.

At that time, one does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not adhere to, and does not designate the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as "this is the path."

At that time, he does not approach, does not grasp, does not abide in, does not adhere to, and does not designate the immeasurable meditative concentrations, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments as "these are the attainments.

At that time, he does not approach, does not grasp, does not abide in, does not adhere to, and does not designate the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as "these are the Buddha-qualities."

Furthermore, Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena, at that time he does not approach, does not grasp, does not dwell upon, does not become attached to, and does not designate these gateways of all the samādhis and dhāraṇīs, thinking, "These are the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī. Why is that?

For in this way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive anything up to the individual and collective aggregates,

elements, and sense-bases, nor dependent origination; he does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he does not perceive the perfections, nor the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
...up to the point that he does not perceive omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). For what reason?

Because, Blessed One, that which is the non-arising (*anutpāda*) of form is not that form; that which is the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not that consciousness. Thus, consciousness and non-arising are non-dual.

This is non-dual. Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of the eye is not the eye; that which is the non-arising of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind is not the mind. For the mind and non-arising are non-dual; this is non-dual. Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of generosity is not the perfection of generosity.

That which is the non-arising of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and that which is the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom— that is not the perfection of wisdom; for indeed,
the perfection of wisdom and non-arising are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of internal emptiness is not internal emptiness;
that which is the non-arising of external emptiness is not external emptiness;
that which is the non-arising of internal-and-external emptiness is not internal-and-external emptiness.
That which is the non-arising of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not that emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
for indeed, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence and non-arising are non-dual and indivisible.
O Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of the foundations of mindfulness is not those foundations of mindfulness.

In this way, Blessed One, the non-arising of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges—that which is the non-arising of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is not those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; for these Buddha-qualities and non-arising are non-dual.
Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is not that realm of phenomena.

That which is the non-arising of suchness, the realm of space, the limit of reality, the inconceivable realm, and awakening—that which is the non-arising of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not that omniscience; for omniscience and non-arising are non-dual and indivisible. Why is that?
Because non-arising is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the non-arising of omniscience is not that omniscience.
Blessed One, that which is the cessation of form is not form;
that which is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
Thus, the aggregates and their cessation are non-dual and indivisible. For what reason?
For in this way, passing away is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the passing away of the five aggregates is not those five aggregates.
Blessed One, that which is the passing away of the perfection of generosity is not that perfection of generosity;
likewise, [that which is the passing away] of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration—

That which is the exhaustion of the perfection of wisdom is not that perfection of wisdom; for indeed, the perfection of wisdom and exhaustion are non-dual, they are not divided into two. Why is that?
Because exhaustion is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the exhaustion of the perfections is not those perfections.
Blessed One, that which is the exhaustion of internal emptiness is not that internal emptiness.
Thus, internal emptiness and passing away are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity. Why is that?

Because passing away is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct. Therefore, that which is the passing away of internal emptiness is not itself internal emptiness. Likewise, that which is the passing away of external emptiness is not itself external emptiness.

That which is the cessation of internal-external emptiness is not internal-external emptiness; likewise, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence is not the emptiness of the nature of non-existence.
For indeed, the emptiness of the nature of non-existence and cessation are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Why is that?

For indeed, cessation is not one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the cessation of the emptiness of non-existent intrinsic nature is not itself the emptiness of non-existent intrinsic nature.
O Blessed One, that which is the cessation of the applications of mindfulness is not those applications of mindfulness;
for thus the applications of mindfulness and their cessation are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity. Why is that?
For indeed, cessation is not one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the cessation of the applications of mindfulness is not those applications of mindfulness.

Likewise, that which is the cessation of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path is not that path. For the path and cessation are non-dual, an indivisible unity. Why is that?
For in this way, cessation is not one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct; therefore, that which is the cessation of the path is not the path.

Likewise, that which is the cessation of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the analytical knowledges, the fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, those are not the Buddha-qualities.
Thus, the Buddha-qualities and their passing away are non-dual; this is not a duality. For what reason?
Because passing away is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor distinct. Therefore, that which is the passing away of the Buddha-qualities is not those Buddha-qualities.
Furthermore, Blessed One, as for what is said:
"Form"— this is a designation made for the non-dual;
"feeling," "perception," and "formative predispositions," and furthermore, that which is called "consciousness"— this too is a designation made for the non-dual.
Furthermore, as for that which is said, from "form" up to "the knowledge of all aspects," this is the enumeration of non-duality.
Thus, in the context of attainment and departure, there is a negation of the relationship between the object to be attained and the attainer.
Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"How, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, examine these dharmas? And who, venerable Subhūti, is a bodhisattva?"
"What is the perfection of wisdom?
What is the act of examining?
Subhūti replied:
Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you ask, "Who is a bodhisattva?": it is awakening itself that is the being; therefore, one is called a bodhisattva.
And by means of that awakening, one knows the aspects of all phenomena, yet one does not become attached to them.
Of which phenomena does one know the aspects?
One knows the aspects of form, yet one does not become attached to them.
He knows the aspects of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
yet he does not become attached to them.

In this way, he knows the aspects of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, both individually and collectively, as well as those of dependent origination and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, yet he does not become attached to them.

Likewise, he knows the aspects of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the perfections, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, yet he does not become attached to them.
Śāriputra said:
“What, Subhūti, are those aspects of all dharmas?
Subhūti said:
“Those aspects, venerable Śāriputra, by which, those marks by which, and those signs by which form, sound, smell, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena [are characterized]...”
Whether they be internal or external phenomena, conditioned or unconditioned, those which are manifested are called the aspects (ākāra) of all phenomena.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as for what you asked:
"What is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?"
It has desisted, O Venerable Śāriputra; it has reached cessation. Therefore it is called "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā).
From what has it desisted, from what has it reached cessation?

From the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), the sense bases (āyatanas), and dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); from the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom.

He has desisted, he has desisted from: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; he has desisted, he has desisted from the applications of mindfulness.

They have desisted from, they have desisted beyond, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; they have desisted from, they have desisted beyond, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments; they have desisted from, they have desisted beyond, the powers and the grounds of self-confidence.

To turn away from and to have desisted from the analytical knowledges and the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to turning away from and having desisted from omniscience— this is what is called the perfection of wisdom.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, it is the perfection of wisdom that is the desisting and the state of having desisted.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:
"What is examination? [it is this very thing].

In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not examine form as permanent, nor as impermanent; not as happiness, nor as suffering; not as self, nor as non-self; not as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful;
not as empty, nor as non-empty; not as having signs, nor as signless; nor as wishless.
Thus, he does not examine it as "wishless," nor does he examine it as "secluded" or "not secluded";
he does not [examine] feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations.

One does not examine consciousness as permanent, nor as impermanent; one does not examine it as pleasant, nor as painful; as self, nor as non-self; as peaceful, nor as unpeaceful; as empty, nor as non-empty; as having signs, nor as signless; as having a wish, nor as wishless.
He does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.

Likewise, he examines the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as "not permanent," nor as "impermanent"; nor as "happiness," nor as "suffering"; nor as "self," nor as "non-self"; nor as "peaceful," nor as "not peaceful."
He does not examine them as "empty" or "not empty," nor as "with signs" or "signless," nor as "wishful" or "wishless"; he does not examine them as "secluded" or "not secluded.
In this same way, he does not examine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as "permanent" or "impermanent."

He does not examine them as "pleasant" or "unpleasant," nor as "self" or "not-self," nor as "peaceful" or "not peaceful," nor as "empty" or "not empty," nor as "with signs" or "signless," nor as "wishful" or "wishless"; he does not examine them as "secluded" or "not secluded."
In this way, one examines eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as being neither permanent nor impermanent;

one examines them as being neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither calm nor uncalm, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, and neither with aspiration nor without aspiration.
One does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.
In the same way, one does not examine eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as "permanent" nor as "impermanent";
nor as "pleasure," nor as "suffering"; nor as "self," nor as "non-self"; nor as "peaceful."

He does not examine it as "not peaceful" nor as "empty," nor as "not empty"; he does not examine it as "with signs" nor as "signless," nor as "with aspiration" nor as "without aspiration"; he does not examine it as "secluded" nor as "not secluded.
In the same way, [he does not examine] feeling conditioned by eye-contact, feeling conditioned by ear-contact, or feeling conditioned by nose-contact.
He examines that feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, feeling conditioned by body-contact, and feeling conditioned by mind-contact are neither permanent nor impermanent;
neither pleasant nor painful; neither self nor non-self; neither calm nor uncalm; neither empty nor non-empty; neither with signs nor signless; and neither with aspirations nor without aspirations.
Thus he examines them as neither "wishless" nor "not wishless," and he examines them as neither "secluded" nor "not secluded.

In this way, he examines the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom as neither "permanent" nor "impermanent."

He examines them as neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither peaceful nor unpeaceful; he examines them as neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither with aspiration nor aspirationless; he examines them as neither secluded nor non-secluded.

In this way, he examines that internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, is neither permanent nor impermanent;
he examines it as neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither calm nor uncalm, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither wishless nor unwishless;
he examines it as neither secluded nor non-secluded.

In this way, he examines the applications of mindfulness as neither permanent nor impermanent; he examines them as neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither calm nor uncalm, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, and neither with aspirations nor aspirationless.

One does not examine them as being secluded, nor as being non-secluded; likewise for the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He examines that the concentrations, all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, and omniscience are neither permanent nor impermanent;

he examines them as neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither peaceful nor unpeaceful, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither wishless nor unwishless; he examines them as neither secluded nor non-secluded.
"For it is thus, Venerable Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, examines these dharmas.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus?"
That which is the non-arising of form is not form; that which is the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
Thus, with respect to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, both individually and collectively; in the factors of dependent origination; in the perfections; in all the modes of emptiness;

in all the factors conducive to enlightenment; in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; in the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges; in the doors of concentration and mnemonic formulas; in the superknowledges; and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
"That which is the non-arising of omniscience is not omniscience.
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form."
And that which is emptiness, venerable Śāriputra, is not form, nor is it arising.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of form is not form; [it is likewise] not feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Consciousness is empty of consciousness;
and that which is emptiness, Venerable Śāriputra, is neither that consciousness nor its arising.
In this manner, Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not consciousness.
The perfection of giving, venerable Śāriputra, is empty of the perfection of giving;
and that which is emptiness is neither the perfection of giving nor its arising.
In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of giving is not the perfection of giving.
In this way, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration,
and the perfection of wisdom are empty of the perfection of wisdom;
and that which is emptiness is neither the perfection of wisdom nor its arising.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom.
Internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness;
and that which is emptiness is neither internal emptiness nor arising.
Venerable Śāriputra, by this method, that which is the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom;
internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness,
and that which is emptiness is neither internal emptiness nor arising.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of internal emptiness is not internal emptiness;
likewise, external emptiness is empty of external emptiness,
and internal-external emptiness is empty of internal-external emptiness.
Up to the point that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty by way of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
and that which is emptiness is neither the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence nor production.
By this method, O Venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-production of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is not itself the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Venerable Śāriputra, the foundations of mindfulness are empty of the foundations of mindfulness;
and that which is emptiness is neither those foundations of mindfulness nor their arising.
Venerable Śāriputra, by this method, that which is the non-arising of the foundations of mindfulness is not those foundations of mindfulness.

In this way, Āyuṣman Śāriputra, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the superknowledges, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the concentrations, the dhāraṇīs, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— all these, as well as omniscience itself, are empty by virtue of omniscience.
And that which is emptiness is neither omniscience nor arising.
"In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the non-arising of all-aspect-knowledge is not that all-aspect-knowledge.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, do you speak thus?"
That which is the passing away of form is not form; that which is the passing away of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
Thus, among the individual and collective aggregates, elements, sense-bases, factors of dependent origination, and factors conducive to awakening;

among the perfections, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; and among the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whatever is the cessation of omniscience in all its aspects, that is not omniscience in all its aspects.
Subhūti said:

"For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, that which is cessation and that which is form, and that which is non-duality, and that which is feeling, and that which is perception, and those which are mental formations, and that which is consciousness—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive."

They have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics; thus it is with respect to all phenomena— whether taken individually or collectively— such as the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, perfections, superknowledges, emptinesses, factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique buddha-qualities, the samādhis, and the gateways of dhāraṇīs.
That which is cessation, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and that which is non-duality—all these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
they are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive;
they have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, that which is the cessation of form is not form;
likewise, that which is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness.
In this way, regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and emptiness— whether taken individually or collectively— as well as the factors conducive to awakening,

the superknowledges, the perfections, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, the gateways of concentration and mnemonic formulas, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects: that which is the cessation of the knowledge of all aspects is not the knowledge of all aspects.
Śāriputra said:
"For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, do you say this: that what is called 'form' is merely a designation made for that which is non-dual?"
Feeling, perception, and mental formations—
this which is called "consciousness" is a designation made for the non-dual; and so on, up to this which is called "the knowledge of all aspects," which is a designation made for the non-dual.
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, non-arising is not one thing and form another;
non-arising itself is form."
Form itself is non-arising;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not other than non-arising, nor is non-arising other than consciousness.
Consciousness itself is non-arising, and non-arising itself is consciousness.
In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, that which is called "form" is reckoned as non-dual;
so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
This which is called "consciousness" is merely a designation for the non-dual.

In this same way, [this designation applies] to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, whether considered individually or collectively; to the perfections, the factors of enlightenment, all the modes of emptiness, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the powers, and the grounds of self-confidence.

Regarding the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and the gateways of meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs: for in this way, venerable Śāriputra, non-arising is not one thing and omniscience another; non-arising itself is omniscience, and omniscience itself is non-arising.
"In this way, venerable Śāriputra, that which is called 'omniscience' (sarvākārajñatā) is designated as a reckoning of non-duality.
Furthermore, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, examines these phenomena, at that time he perceives the non-arising of form."
Based on ultimate purity,
one perceives the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
based on ultimate purity.

One perceives the non-arising of the self, by way of its ultimate purity; likewise, one perceives the non-arising of a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer.
Based on ultimate purity,
he thus perceives the non-arising of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the superknowledges, both individually and collectively,
based on ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the perfection of generosity,
by virtue of its ultimate purity; likewise,
he perceives the non-arising of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Based on ultimate purity,
one perceives the non-arising of internal emptiness,
based on ultimate purity.
Thus, by means of ultimate purity, he perceives the non-arising of external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
he perceives the non-arising of the applications of mindfulness.

Based on ultimate purity, he perceives the non-arising of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the superknowledges, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the doors of concentration and dhāraṇī, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the knowledge of all aspects.
Based on ultimate purity,
one perceives the non-arising of the ordinary person;
based on ultimate purity.
He perceives the non-arising of the dharmas of ordinary beings,
by virtue of their ultimate purity.

In this way, he perceives the non-arising of the stream-enterer and the dharmas of a stream-enterer, of the once-returner and the dharmas of a once-returner, of the non-returner and the dharmas of a non-returner, of the arhat and the dharmas of an arhat, of the pratyekabuddha and the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha, of the bodhisattva and the dharmas of a bodhisattva, and of the Buddha.
On account of ultimate purity,
one perceives the non-arising of the Buddha-qualities,
on account of ultimate purity.
Śāriputra said:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Venerable Subhūti has spoken, form is non-arising; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising; even so, the aggregates, whether taken individually or collectively, are non-arising; the elements are non-arising."
The sense bases are non-arising; dependent origination is also non-arising; the perfections are non-arising; all the modes of emptiness are non-arising;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are non-arising; the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are non-arising; the gateways of concentration and mnemonic formulas are non-arising; and the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges are non-arising.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-arising; omniscience is non-arising; the ordinary person is non-arising; the qualities of an ordinary person are non-arising. Likewise, the stream-enterer and the qualities of a stream-enterer; the once-returner and the qualities of a once-returner; the non-returner and the qualities of a non-returner; the arhat and the qualities of an arhat; the pratyekabuddha and the qualities of a pratyekabuddha; the bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva are all non-arising.
The Buddha is non-arising; the qualities of a Buddha are non-arising.

Venerable Subhūti, if form is also non-arising, and even the qualities of a Buddha are non-arising, then, Venerable Subhūti, has the disciple already attained the enlightenment of a disciple, and has the one belonging to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas already attained the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha?
The Bodhisattva indeed attains omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*),
and there will be no distinction among the five destinies;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva indeed attains the fivefold awakening.
If, venerable Subhūti, all phenomena are non-arising,

for what purpose should the path be cultivated by a stream-enterer for the sake of abandoning the three fetters, and why should the path be cultivated by a once-returner for the sake of attenuating passion, hatred, and delusion?
The non-returner must cultivate the path for the abandonment of the five lower fetters;
the arhat must cultivate the path for the abandonment of the five higher fetters;
and those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha must cultivate the path for the attainment of pratyekabodhi.
For what reason does a bodhisattva practice the course of difficult deeds, undergoing those sufferings for the sake of sentient beings?
For what reason has the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
"For what reason was the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the attainment of an unarisen dharma, nor its realization."

I do not admit a stream-enterer of non-arising, nor the fruit of stream-entry; nor a once-returner, nor the fruit of once-returning; nor a non-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning; nor arhatship, nor the fruit of arhatship.
I do not desire for non-arising the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire a bodhisattva practicing a course of difficult deeds, nor does a bodhisattva practice with the perception of difficulty. Why is that?
Because, Venerable Śāriputra, it is not possible, while remaining in the perception of difficulty, to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, by generating the perception of a mother toward all sentient beings, and by generating the perception of a father, the perception of a brother, the perception of a son, and the perception of oneself, it is possible to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate this thought:
"Just as 'self' and 'self' are spoken of, yet the self is ultimately unarisen,
so too should one generate such a perception regarding all internal and external phenomena."
If he should produce such a perception, there will be no perception of difficulty. Why is that?
Because those bodhisattvas do not produce nor apprehend any phenomenon whatsoever, in any way, at all.
Venerable Śāriputra, I do not conceive of a Tathāgata in terms of non-arising.
Nor do I desire that unexcelled perfect enlightenment, nor the turning of the wheel of Dharma, nor the attainment of an unproduced attainment by means of an unproduced dharma.
Śāriputra said: "Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, is an arisen attainment attained by means of an unarisen dharma,
or is an unarisen attainment attained by means of an arisen dharma?"
Subhūti said:

"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not maintain that an unarisen attainment is being attained by means of an arisen dharma, nor do I maintain that an arisen attainment is being attained by means of an unarisen [dharma]."
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, do you desire attainment by means of an unarisen dharma, or do you desire attainment by means of an arisen dharma?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire attainment by means of an unarisen dharma, nor do I desire attainment by means of an arisen dharma."
Śāriputra said:
"But, venerable Subhūti, is it that there is no attainment and no realization?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, there is attainment and there is clear realization, yet they are not two.

Nevertheless, Venerable Śāriputra, it is by way of worldly convention that 'attainment' and 'clear realization' are designated; and it is by way of worldly convention that one is designated as a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha."

A bodhisattva or a buddha is merely designated; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no attainment and no realization, no stream-enterer, no once-returner, no non-returner, no arhat, no pratyekabuddha, no bodhisattva, and no buddha.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, it occurs to me to speak thus: 'A phenomenon is unarisen.
Subhūti said:
'Venerable Śāriputra, regarding what you say—that it occurs to you to speak thus, "A phenomenon is unarisen"—[it is so]. "
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, that which appears as speech regarding non-arising—why is that?

Because, Venerable Śāriputra, whatever dharma is unarisen, whatever eloquence there is, whatever expressions there are, and whatever non-origination there is—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive."
"They have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, even non-arising is a mantra."
Non-arising is eloquence; non-arising is the Dharma, and those dharmas are also unarisen concerning which one has the eloquence to speak.
Subhūti said: "It is so, Venerable Śāriputra; non-arising is the mantra."
Non-arising is eloquence; non-arising is the Dharma, and those dharmas upon which one relies to speak are themselves unarisen. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, form is non-arising.

In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising; likewise, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—both individually and collectively—are non-arising; the factors of dependent origination, the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, all the modes of emptiness, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are non-arising;
the superknowledges, the samādhis, the gateways of dhāraṇī, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-arising.

The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, the omniscient one, the knower of all modes, and even the state of the knower of all modes—these are non-arising.
Śāriputra said: "So it is, venerable Subhūti; non-arising is the mantra."

Non-arising is eloquence; non-arising is the Dharma. Those dharmas, concerning which one has the eloquence to speak, are themselves unarisen—namely, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the perfections, the factors conducive to awakening, all the emptinesses, all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, all the samādhis, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth.
"Even omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-arising.
Śāriputra said:
"But, venerable Subhūti, is it not the case that both attainment (*prāpti*) and clear realization (*abhisamaya*) exist only according to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*)?"
Thus, there is a differentiation of the five destinies by way of worldly convention, but not in the ultimate sense.
Subhūti said: "It is so, venerable Śāriputra; it is so."

Just as attainment and clear realization exist by way of worldly convention, so too does the differentiation of the five destinies exist by way of worldly convention; it is certainly not so, however, in the ultimate sense. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, in the ultimate sense there is no karma, no maturation, no arising, no cessation, no affliction, and no purification.
Śāriputra said:
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, does an unarisen dharma arise, or does an arisen dharma arise?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising of a dharma that has already arisen, nor do I desire the arising of a dharma that has not yet arisen.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, of which unarisen dharma do you not desire the arising?"
Subhūti said:

"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising of form, which is an unarisen dharma and empty of intrinsic nature; venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, which are unarisen dharmas and empty of intrinsic nature."

In this way, [he does not perceive] the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, whether taken individually or collectively; nor dependent origination; nor the perfections; nor the factors conducive to awakening;

nor the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments; nor the superknowledges; nor all the emptinesses; nor all the samādhis; nor the gateways of dhāraṇī; nor the powers; nor the grounds of self-confidence; nor the analytical knowledges; nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Venerable Śāriputra, I do not even desire the arising of awakening, which is unproduced and empty of intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra asked: "But, venerable Subhūti, does arising arise, or does non-arising arise?"
Subhūti said:
"Indeed, venerable Śāriputra, neither arising arises, nor does non-arising arise. Why is that?
Because, venerable Śāriputra, that which is arising and that which is [non-arising]..."

Furthermore, both these two dharmas—arising and non-arising—are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, arising does not arise, nor does non-arising arise.
By this method, venerable Śāriputra, non-arising is the mantra, and non-arising is the inspired eloquence.
"Non-arising is the nature of phenomena; those very phenomena are unarisen, concerning which it is possible to speak.
Śāriputra said:
"The Venerable Subhūti should be placed at the head of those who discourse on the Dharma. For what reason?"
For in this way, whatever the venerable Subhūti is questioned about, from that very point he emerges.
Subhūti said:

"This is the nature of things, venerable Śāriputra, for the disciples of the Tathāgata who are non-reliant upon all phenomena; from whatever they are questioned, from that very point they emerge. Why is that?"
"Indeed, it is because all dharmas are non-dependent.
Śāriputra asked:
"Venerable Subhūti, how are all dharmas non-dependent?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty by its very nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it apprehended between the two.
This is also true for feeling, perception, and mental formations."
"Venerable Śāriputra, consciousness is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it found between the two.
Venerable Śāriputra, the eye is empty by nature; it does not depend on the internal, it does not depend on the external, nor is it found between the two.

Likewise, venerable Śāriputra, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are empty by nature; they do not depend on the internal, they do not depend on the external, nor are they found between the two."
The perfection of giving, venerable Śāriputra, is empty by nature; it is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, venerable Śāriputra, are empty by nature; they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Internal emptiness is empty by nature; it is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In this way, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, are empty by their very nature; they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
The foundations of mindfulness are empty by their very nature; they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
Likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and the faculties [are empty].
The powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are empty by nature; they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

Likewise, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the samādhis, the gateways of dhāraṇī, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty by nature; they are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
In this manner, venerable Śāriputra, all phenomena are non-dependent,
by virtue of their intrinsic emptiness. Thus, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections must purify form,
and must purify feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this way, the aggregates, whether taken individually or collectively, as well as the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment,

the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, must be purified.
"Up to and including the all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is to be purified.
Thus [ends] the departure toward all-aspect omniscience.
Śāriputra said:
"How, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the six perfections, purify the bodhisattva path?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, there is a mundane perfection of giving and there is a supramundane [perfection of giving]."

In this way, there is the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation; there is the perfection of wisdom that is mundane and there is that which is supramundane.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the mundane perfection of generosity, and what is the supramundane?"
Subhūti said:

"Worldly, venerable Śāriputra, is the perfection of giving; here a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a donor, a master of giving, and a giver to ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, beggars, travelers, and supplicants."

He gives food to those who seek food; he becomes a giver of drink, vehicles, clothing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, flowers, incense, powders, fragrant substances, dwellings, shelters, requisites for life, bedding, seats, and medicines to those who seek drink, vehicles, clothing, bedding, seats, perfumes, garlands, ointments, flowers, incense, powders, fragrant substances, dwellings, shelters, and any other such articles of life, equipment, and medicine.
To those seeking a son, he gives a son;
to those seeking a daughter, he gives a daughter;
to those seeking a wife, he gives a wife.
He gives away his kingdoms to those who seek a kingdom; he gives away his head to those who seek his head; he gives away his limbs to those who seek his limbs.
He gives flesh, blood, and marrow to those who seek flesh, blood, and marrow;
and he relinquishes them with a basis,
thinking as follows:
"I give; he accepts; this is the gift; I am free from stinginess and renounce my entire possession; I carry out the command of the Buddha; I practice the perfection of generosity."
"Having made this gift common to all sentient beings, I dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by way of non-apprehension;
and by means of this gift and the fruit of the gift, may all sentient beings be happy in this very life and attain parinirvāṇa without clinging.
Yet, he gives the gift while being attached to the three spheres.
By which three?

Namely, by the notion of self, the notion of another, and the notion of giving. Bound by these three attachments, one gives a gift; this is called the mundane perfection of giving. For, venerable Śāriputra, it does not move away from the world, it does not transcend it, nor does it pass beyond it.
Therefore, it is called the mundane perfection of giving.
In that regard, what is the supramundane perfection of giving?
It is, namely, the complete purity of the three spheres. In that regard, what is the complete purity of the three spheres?

In this regard, O Venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not apprehend a self, he does not apprehend a recipient, he does not apprehend the gift, and he does not apprehend its maturation; this, Venerable Śāriputra, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s purity of the three spheres.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he offers that gift to all sentient beings;
yet he does not apprehend sentient beings,
nor does he apprehend a self.
And one dedicates that gift toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, yet does not apprehend enlightenment. This is called the supramundane perfection of giving.
For what reason is it called the supramundane perfection of giving?
For it is thus, Venerable Śāriputra, that it moves away from, rises above, and transcends the world; for that reason it is called the supramundane perfection of generosity,
and likewise the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation.
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, what is the mundane perfection of wisdom, and what is the supramundane?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, there is a worldly perfection of wisdom;
here, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift while relying on apprehension, thinking: 'I must suppress the mind of stinginess.'"

Relying on the notion of giving himself and other sentient beings, he renounces everything—whether an external or internal object, whether appropriated or unappropriated—there being nothing that he does not renounce;
and he dedicates that root of virtue toward enlightenment, making it common to all sentient beings while remaining dependent on apprehension.
Established in the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*), he practices ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Relying on the apprehension of body, speech, and mind,

while practicing those ten paths of wholesome action, he relies on the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and the view of wholesomeness; having apprehended awakening, he dedicates his morality— which is shared with all sentient beings— toward awakening, and that too by means of apprehension.
He exalts himself and disparages others.
He endures the misdeeds of all sentient beings,

yet relying on a view of patience regarding self and sentient beings, he dedicates that root of merit toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of apprehension, having made it common to all sentient beings.
He exerts vigor while perceiving the body, perceiving the mind, perceiving the accumulation of merit,
perceiving the accumulation of knowledge,
and perceiving a self.
Perceiving awakening through that exertion of vigor, he becomes conceited;
and having made that [merit] common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by means of the yoga of apprehension.
He cultivates loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; he enters into and emerges from the meditative attainments, and he relishes them.

Relishing those [wholesome roots], he conceives them as being shared with all sentient beings; yet, holding a view of objective apprehension (*upalambhadṛṣṭi*), he dedicates them toward awakening. This is called the mundane perfection of wisdom (*laukikī prajñāpāramitā*).
While cultivating emptiness, he perceives form as empty;
he perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty.
As long as one perceives even the enlightenment of a Buddha through the application of apprehension,
one makes those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
yet still by way of that application of apprehension.
One confesses all evil through the application of apprehension;
one rejoices in the merit of oneself and others;
and for the sake of oneself and others, while apprehending it, one entreats all the Buddhas.
If one transforms merit three times over for the sake of omniscience by means of an improper method, having made it common to all sentient beings, this is called worldly *prajñāpāramitā*.
In that regard, what is supramundane *prajñāpāramitā*?
By means of the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, the gift, and awakening, and through the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of giving.

For the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, ethical discipline, and awakening, and by means of the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of ethical discipline;
for the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, patience, and awakening, and by means of the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of patience;

and for the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, body, mind, vigor, merit, wisdom, and awakening, and by means of the purity of the three spheres, one purifies the perfection of vigor.

For the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, meditative absorption, concentration, and attainment, and by means of the purity of the three spheres, he purifies the perfection of meditation;
for the sake of awakening, through the non-apprehension of self, sentient beings, and all phenomena, and by means of the purity of the three spheres, he purifies the perfection of wisdom.

And he dedicates all roots of merit toward awakening, toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment, by means of a dedication that is without distinction, an unsurpassed dedication, and an unequaled dedication.
By means of inconceivable and incomparable transformation,
and by means of immeasurable transformation— this is called supramundane *prajñāpāramitā*.
For what reason is it mundane?
Those by which the world comes into being, or those by which one turns back from the world,
or those which are equal to the world;
Or those by which one gives to the world, or by which one emerges from the world,
or which lead to the existence of the world.
Those that exist in the world are mundane. Among them, which are supramundane?
They are those by which one transcends the world.
Those by which one delivers the world, or those by which one is delivered by the world,
or that which serves as illumination;
Alternatively, those by which one emerges from the world,
or those for the purpose of crossing over the world,
or those which are superior within the world— these are called "supramundane" (*lokottara*).
"In this way, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections purifies the path to awakening.
Śāriputra asked:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening?"
Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra, the four foundations of mindfulness are the path to awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
[so too are] the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of awakening."
The noble eightfold path; the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
all meditative concentrations; all gateways to the dhāraṇīs; the four immeasurables; the four dhyānas; and the four formless attainments.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion— this, Venerable Śāriputra, is called the path to enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, of which perfection is this the human effort?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra, this is the human effort of the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?"
For in this way, Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of all wholesome dharmas— of the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas;
the perfection of wisdom, Venerable Śāriputra, is the recipient of all wholesome dharmas— of the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
"O Venerable Śāriputra, by training in the perfection of wisdom, those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;

and, O Venerable Śāriputra, future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, too, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment only after training in this very perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves while teaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions—
they too have all awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment only after training in this very perfection of wisdom.
Moreover, Venerable Śāriputra, if, while this perfection of wisdom is being spoken, a bodhisattva...
It should be known that for the Mahāsattva there is no state of doubt and no state of hesitation.

O Venerable Śāriputra, it should be understood that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, never separated from this mental attention, namely, the mental attention of not abandoning any sentient being and the mental attention of great compassion for the sake of protecting all sentient beings.
Śāriputra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, as for what you have said—
that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of this dwelling and is never separated from this mental attention— "
"If that were so, Venerable Subhūti, then all sentient beings would also be bodhisattvas. Why is that?
Because, Venerable Subhūti, all sentient beings are never separated from mental attention.
Subhūti said:
Excellent, excellent, Venerable Śāriputra! I shall reprove you; indeed, the Venerable Śāriputra has grasped the very meaning by means of his statement of the true word. Why is that?
Venerable Śāriputra, through the non-existence of sentient beings, the non-existence of mental attention should be understood;
through the emptiness of sentient beings, the emptiness of mental attention should be understood.
Through the lack of intrinsic nature of sentient beings, the lack of intrinsic nature of mental attention should be understood;
through the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of mental attention should be understood;
through the non-awakening of sentient beings, the non-awakening of mental attention should be understood.

Through the non-existence of form, the emptiness of form, the lack of intrinsic nature of form, the seclusion of form, and the non-awakening to form, the non-awakening to mental attention should be understood.

Through the non-existence of feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; through the emptiness of consciousness, the lack of intrinsic nature of consciousness, the seclusion of consciousness, and the non-awakening to consciousness, the non-awakening to mental attention should be understood.

In this same way, it should be understood for the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination—both individually and collectively—as well as for the truths, the factors conducive to awakening, the perfections, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments.

In the superknowledges, in all the emptinesses, in all the meditative concentrations, in all the doors of dhāraṇī, in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges, and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should understand that there is no realization of mental attention because of the existence of omniscience, because of the emptiness of omniscience, because of the intrinsic nature of omniscience, because of the seclusion of omniscience, and because of the non-realization of omniscience.
"By this dwelling and by this mental attention, O Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not deprived [of these].
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, should be taught— just as you teach it— and indeed,
it is through the very power of the Tathāgata that a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva, should course in the perfection of wisdom just as you teach it.

Furthermore, while this chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom was being spoken by the Venerable Subhūti, the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system shook in six ways, rising and falling in the east, north, south, west, and the intermediate directions. Then, at that moment, the Blessed One smiled.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, just as the Tathāgata here in this world-system teaches the perfection of wisdom, even so in the eastern direction, in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones proclaim the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
In this way, throughout the ten directions, in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.

Now, while this teaching on the perfection of wisdom was being taught by Subhūti, twelve nayutas of beings among the gods and humans attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, [teach] this very perfection of wisdom.
As the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, were speaking, the minds of incalculable and immeasurable beings were set upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus is the departure by way of the path.
Thus has been explained the practice of departure;

thus has been explained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) in the Noble *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, as refined according to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*. This concludes the chapter on the knowledge of all aspects, the Subhūti Chapter.
